en: The Ritual for the Constant and Universal Prostration and Repentance of the Tenfold Vows and Practices at the Sea-Seal Bodhimanda from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*, Volume One.
Compiled by the State-Protecting Master Fahu (Dharma-Protector), the Śramaṇa Huìjué of Cí’ēn Temple on Mount Yún of Lán, during the Táng Dynasty, based upon the Sūtra.
Supplemented by the Śramaṇa Pūrui of Zai Guang Temple on Mount Cangshan during the Song Dynasty;
verified by the Buddhist disciple Mu Zeng, Provincial Governor of Sichuan, who was loyal and devoted to his sovereign;
and reviewed by the Śramaṇa Du Che of Ji Guang Temple on Chicken Mountain during the Ming Dynasty. Qīn Bāozhōngyì. Zhōngjìn. (Recorded).
The Tiantai Practitioner of Teaching and Contemplation, the Śramaṇa Zhengzhi, offers the first session of the *Zhiding* (Cultivating Samādhi),
with all-respectful homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.

First, the Extensive Cultivation of Offerings (based on the distinct and perfect teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*). These ten kinds of practices and vows are the sublime gateway for entering the inexhaustible realm of Vairocana. All you great assemblies, contemplate these ten kinds of practices and vows with careful discernment. Briefly, there are three gates [for this contemplation]. First, regarding the general characteristics:

the Sūtra states that after extensively explaining the inconceivable merits of the Tathāgata, it says: "If one wishes to accomplish this gateway of merit, one should cultivate ten kinds of vast practices and vows. As for those practices and vows, now...

If one were to explain in full the six aspects of perfect fusion and the ten layers of the profound gates, there is the simultaneous perfection of all practices and the instantaneous perfection of all practices. If based on the essential nature of the dharma-body and its attributes, they are fundamentally complete; if based on karmic function, they manifest wondrously according to capacities; if based on the arising from nature (*xingqi*), they are inherently possessed from the beginning;

if based on dependent origination (*yuanqi*), they should be newly cultivated through contemplation. Cause and effect are perfectly fused and mutually unobstructed. Because the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, at the very moment of the first aspiration for enlightenment, one attains the fruit of perfect awakening. Because the source of the cause is thoroughly penetrated, even though the fruit of Buddhahood is attained, one does not abandon the gateway of the cause.

Both being and non-being are present; they mutually negate and simultaneously sweep away [all extremes]. Regarding the four and six phrases of the realm of understanding and practice, that entry is the gate by which one enters; because one thereby plunges into the ocean of the fruit, it is called the "Inconceivable Chapter. II. Relying on...

Regarding the explanation of the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) as both sequential and circular (*xingbu-yuanrong*): the ten preceding gates are sequential; within their synthesis, there is circularity. To cite one is to possess all others; they are universally inclusive and mutually pervasive. One and many are naturally integrated; breadth and narrowness are unimpeded.

Whether possessing substance or lacking it, having power or lacking it, they interpenetrate and are identical. The number of phrases is manifold, as found in the *Huayan Dashi* (Great Commentary). This method of non-obstruction is like a mud puppet being pulled along; its arrival cannot be fixed to a single direction.

Thus, through this single gate of prostration, the net of Indra (*indrajāla*) of all sinful obstructions is extinguished, and the net of Indra of all merits is perfected. The other gates are likewise so. Master Qingliang said: "If one cannot see or hear this boundless and inexhaustible realm, [one cannot fulfill] Samantabhadra..."

If one is unable to fully cultivate [the practices], one should give rise to a mind of longing and joyful aspiration to observe and cultivate the ritual. Regarding the ten gates of mystery (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*), one may practice according to a single gate, as explained in Du Shun’s *Three Contemplations* (*San Guan*) and the Great Commentary (*Da Shu*).

Third, relying on the "Gate of Universal Inclusion" (*bian she men*), inferior capacities are guided and other types of practitioners are subsumed; for this reason, it is called the Gate of Universal Inclusion within this commentary. Now, relying on the three distinct gates as taught in the conventional teachings: 1. **Paying Homage to All Buddhas**:

To sever the obstacles of the seven, nine, or ten types of pride, and to obtain a body of noble majesty and sovereignty, perfected with the eighty-four thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). 2. **Praising the Tathāgatas**: To sever the four grave obstacles of speech and to obtain the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*catur-pratisaṃvid*).

The signs pervade everywhere. Being fully endowed with the ten kinds of perfect sounds. ○ Third, regarding the function of the offerings extensively cultivated to please all the Sages: the abundance of merit increases and flourishes; one obtains the two kinds of accomplishment through the Sage’s bestowal of grace.

The fault of not cultivating offerings is that what is undertaken does not succeed, and all things remain unsatisfactory. ○ Fourth, repenting of karmic obstructions: one severs the four obstacles and the ten obstacles, accomplishing all mundane and supramundane merits, and obtaining an excellent primary and secondary retribution.

○ Fifth, rejoicing in merit: one severs the obstacles of being displeased by the prosperity of others, jealousy, and so forth; one obtains immeasurable blessings, and all merits become perfectly fulfilled. ○ Sixth, requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma: one severs the transgression of opposing and slandering the Dharma.

7. [The obstacle of] equal dharmas and so forth; by obtaining the uncommon merit of great learning and wisdom, one severs the obstacles of those who hate the Buddha, slander the Buddha, harm the Buddha, or harbor malice toward Bodhisattvas and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and thus take no pleasure in the Buddha’s remaining in the world;

one attains an indestructible, adamantine body of long life. 8. [The obstacle of] constantly following the Buddha to study; by severing the obstacles of opposing the Buddha and all spiritual friends, being unable to accumulate merit, and lacking the resolve to cultivate the benefit of both self and others, one obtains the inexhaustible merits of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

9. [The obstacle of] always conforming to sentient beings; by severing the obstacles of sentient beings’ various natures—whether hostile or friendly, compliant or rebellious—which prevent one from conforming to the Buddha, displease the Buddha, or oppose the Buddha, one attains...

With vast spiritual friends as one’s retinue, one universally dedicates [merit] in ten ways. This eliminates the obstacle of narrow-mindedness and the failure to resolve for bodhicitta; it brings the perfection of the ten pāramitās and the attainment of the fruit of the ten bodies. As for this making of vows, it eliminates the obstacles of lack of aspiration and regression.

All the merits previously mentioned are here fully perfected. In this present life, one attains Sukhāvatī; thereafter, one wanders through the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha*). Now, based on the merit of eliminating obstacles according to the distinct teaching (*pratyekavidyā*), these have been briefly cited. The specific rituals for attaining Buddhahood in each case and so forth should be practiced according to the Dharma.
The Root Tantra states: "The ancient masters practiced only a single [method] and attained the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā Purity, thereby eliminating all suffering.
Then, these various assemblies of beings each knelt on their right knees and, holding incense and flowers, made offerings according to the ritual:
"May this ocean-like cloud of offerings pervade the realms of the ten directions—countless jewels, countless flowers, countless garlands, countless..."
Incalculable robes; incalculable parasols; incalculable banners; incalculable pennants; incalculable ornaments; incalculable attendants;
incalculable floor-spreads; incalculable ointments; incalculable powdered incenses;
incalculable blended incenses; incalculable burning incenses; incalculable deep faith; and incalculable affection.
Joy. Immeasurable pure minds; immeasurable reverence; immeasurable praise; immeasurable prostrations; immeasurable jewel thrones;
immeasurable flower thrones; immeasurable incense thrones; immeasurable garland thrones;
immeasurable sandalwood thrones; immeasurable cloth thrones; immeasurable vajra thrones; immeasurable...
There were *jīmūta* mani thrones; incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) thrones of precious silk; incalculable thrones of precious colors;
incalculable jeweled walkways; incalculable flower walkways; incalculable incense walkways;
incalculable garland walkways; incalculable cloth walkways; and incalculable walkways inlaid with various jewels.
Aśaṃkhyeya walkways of all kinds of precious silken brocades; aśaṃkhyeya walkways of all kinds of precious tala trees;
aśaṃkhyeya walkways of all kinds of precious balustrades; aśaṃkhyeya walkways completely covered by nets of all kinds of precious bells;
aśaṃkhyeya palaces of all kinds of precious materials; aśaṃkhyeya [palaces] of all kinds...
Flower palaces; incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) palaces of all kinds of incense; incalculable palaces of all kinds of garlands;
incalculable palaces of all kinds of sandalwood; and incalculable palaces of all kinds of solid, wondrous fragrant treasuries.
There were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) palaces of all kinds of vajras and incalculable palaces of all kinds of maṇi-jewels, all of which were exquisitely wonderful and surpassed those of the devas.
There were also incalculable trees of various miscellaneous jewels and incalculable trees of diverse fragrances.
There were incalculable trees of various precious garments; incalculable trees of various musical instruments;
incalculable trees of precious ornaments; incalculable trees of exquisite sounds; incalculable trees of inexhaustible jewels;
incalculable trees of precious silken fabrics; incalculable trees of precious earrings; and incalculable [trees] of all kinds of flowers, perfumes, banners, flags, garlands, and canopies.
The trees that serve as adornments—such as these trees with their spreading branches and dense foliage—provide shade and reflect light, adorning the palaces.

Furthermore, those palaces are adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) railings, incalculable windows, incalculable gate-towers, incalculable multi-storied pavilions, and incalculable crescent-shaped ornaments. Incalculable...
The pavilions were magnificently adorned. Immeasurable (*asaṃkhyeya*) vajras covered their surfaces; immeasurable incenses perfumed them everywhere on all sides;
and immeasurable garments were spread upon the ground. O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas used such various articles of worship as these.
Throughout immeasurable, incalculable, unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, they have purified their minds to revere, honor, and make offerings to all Buddhas, never regressing and without rest.
After each and every Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, they likewise honor and make offerings to all their relics. Having received these clouds of incense and flowers, they bring them to fruition.
The Radiant Terrace is wider than the boundless realm, immeasurable and infinite; may it perform the work of a Buddha. (Question:

Regarding this passage and those in the subsequent sutra where it says "fragrant flowers fill the realms of the ten directions" and so forth as offerings, how can such a multitude of offering implements be sufficient to make offerings to such a multitude of Buddhas? Answer:

According to the third chapter, the "Gate of Offerings," in the *Huayan Yuanqi Zhang* [Treatise on the Huayan Arising of Causes and Conditions], it is said: "Whatever a Bodhisattva provides—even a single incense, a single flower, a single robe, or a single canopy as an offering implement—none fail to accord with ultimate truth and are equal to the realm of empty space. Thus, by means of the whole...)

The body of the Dharma-realm travels through all Buddha-fields, making offerings to the Buddhas with things that accord with reality. For this reason, the Bodhisattva’s practice is not in vain; regarding the Buddhas encountered during their cultivation, they never miss the proper time.

All ritual implements are always accomplished in accordance with principle. Why is this? Because the gift of Dharma to the Buddhas accords with true principle. Thus the commentary states: "According to this, it refers to a single incense, a single flower, and so forth. Furthermore, it says: "Always accomplished in accordance with principle" means one should know that everything listed in the sutra is accomplished by being in accord with principle—whether it be one or many, and so on.

Therefore, for the practitioner, simply settle the mind in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*); then every object will naturally become manifold and pervade all Buddhas. Hence it is said: "May these clouds of incense and flowers fill the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas. [End of section] Next...

The Sutra below states: "Mental offerings made within a deluded mind are compared to making offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions (*koṭi-nayuta-kāla*) of Buddhas; even calculations, metaphors, sands, or atoms cannot equal one-tenth of one. All that is called "heaven" (*deva*) carries the meaning of spontaneity (*svabhāva*);

it signifies that within the *dharmadhātu*, there exists such inconceivable functioning as a natural law (*dharmatā*). All that is called "clouds" carries the meaning of following conditions (*pratyaya*); it signifies that they are perceived through the power of practice and vows (*caryā-praṇidhāna*).

This means that while these offerings manifest as distinct forms and characteristics, wisdom perceives them as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). They arise from the non-arising of phenomena within the emptiness of *dharma*. The seer and the seen are utterly without dependence. The application arises, yet its coming has no source; the application ceases, yet its departing reaches nowhere. Yet, they can contain compassion, raining down the Dharma-rain to benefit all things in their manifold layers.
Inexhaustible (therein are clouds of elephants).
Next, I offer as a gift the ocean of the self-nature of precious jewels interspersed with gems, together with the most excellent seven-jeweled mountains and so forth.
I bring forth such clouds of offerings as these and present them to all the Buddhas.
Oṃ sarva-tathāgata-arcana-pracarya-samagra-spharaṇa-samaye hūṃ.
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states: "There is a dhāraṇī named 'Infinite Varieties of Mantras,' which can accomplish all things and possesses great efficacy. The dhāraṇī says:
Oṃ sīmala sīmala mīmana sīkala mahāliṅga hūṃ. Regarding the *ratnacakra-dhāraṇī*:
when fashioning a jeweled wheel (*ratnacakra*) out of gold, silver, brass, or other materials, [one should place it] upon the maṇḍala.

Upon reaching the image of the Tathāgata, one offers these precious inlays at the sites of the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattvas, the *vīrya-jñāna* (valiant-knowledge) Brahmins, the *ṛṣis*, and the six realms of existence including the hungry ghosts (*preta*). Consequently, one obtains according to one's own various requests:
various palaces, various canopies, various elephants and horses, various chariots, various [objects] of the seven treasures, various garments, and various foods and drinks.
...and so forth; all these can be accomplished. Furthermore, from time immemorial, all past debts can be fully repaid.
Herein they are briefly compiled; the details are as explained in the sutras. Moreover, the *Pariṇāmacakra-sūtra* states:

"Once one has finished reciting this secret mantra, there immediately arises a great and wondrous cloud of offerings according to one's wishes, appearing before all Buddhas. If a son of good family..."

O virtuous woman, if you single-mindedly contemplate the Buddha, whether by day or by night, and recite this Wheel of Dedication, then, O son of good family or daughter of good family, all your transgressions will be extinguished, all afflictions will gradually diminish, and you will be able to attain all manner of merits.
By reciting it even once, one obtains the merit of Brahmā and shall constantly behold the Buddha in dreams. At the end of life...
Hereafter, one shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī, as extensively described in the sūtras.
Next, bind the Great Amoghapāśa Maṇi Mudrā and Mantra (Join the two hands in the vajra-palms gesture;
curl the two index fingers to form the shape of a jewel; extend both thumbs upright. This constitutes the recitation of the Amoghapāśa Maṇi Pūjā Dhāraṇī).
Oṃ amoghapāśa-mahāvidyārājñī tathāgatamūrdhābhiṣikta sarvamantrapralopa hūṃ.
By reciting this *Amoghapāśa Mahāmaṇi Pūjā Dhāraṇī* three times, one immediately achieves the state of non-... [omitted].
In the assembly of the Tathāgata Amitāyus and throughout infinite buddha-fields, there rained down immeasurable and vast offerings, namely: oceans of clouds of various kinds of ointments,
oceans of clouds of various kinds of flower garlands, oceans of clouds of various kinds of burning incense,
oceans of clouds of various kinds of sublime celestial food and drink, oceans of clouds of various kinds of sublime celestial garments, and oceans of light from various kinds of maṇi jewels.
Lamps and candles form an ocean of clouds; various banners, streamers, precious canopies, and jeweled parasols form an ocean of clouds;
and various sublime celestial music forms an ocean of clouds. Throughout all the assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, these constitute a truly vast and magnificent offering.
By forming mudrās and making offerings while reciting this dhāraṇī, one obtains an immeasurable mass of merit, as vast as space and without limit.
In every lifetime, one will always be born within the great assemblies of all Tathāgatas, arising by transformation from a lotus flower.
One will attain the five supernormal powers and manifest a hundred billion bodies, able to rescue and deliver suffering beings within defiled worlds.
May all living beings be brought to peace and happiness; they shall receive immeasurable rewards in this very life and attain rebirth in the Pure Land in the future.

(Regarding the collection of mantras and mudrās within these ritual manuals for the *dōjō*: in the Age of Dharma Decline (*paścimakāla*), practitioners who do not rely on secret mantras find it difficult to achieve protection and assistance; thus, they must accomplish their practice through contemplative visualization. Now, there are two gates of offering: first, the offering that accords with the fundamental source-nature;

second, the offering that relies upon the auxiliary conditions of the secret dharma. Within this [second gate], there are also two kinds: first, the offering of precious substances; second, the offering of mantras and mudrās. Both rely upon the secret dharma. Furthermore, the former [the first gate] is the offering of the nature-arising through contemplation.)

This is precisely the newly accomplished offering of dependent origination, as it encompasses all things; thus, it forms an ocean of offerings in which the nature of conditions is perfectly interfused. From this point downward, whether it be praising, prostrating, recollecting the Buddha, circumambulating, chanting sutras, or reciting mantras, everything is to be done in this same manner (the assembly should know this).
Having made these offerings, take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Second is the Praise of the Tathāgata (which has two sections).

[After having invited the Triple Gem, prostrate yourself fully on the ground, bowing at the Buddha’s feet. With body upright and dignified, stand attentively with a single mind, facing the Dharma seat. Burn incense and scatter flowers, while mentally contemplating the subtle and wondrous merits of the Triple Gem, gazing upon them without ceasing.]
Recite with these words:
(1) Praising the Buddha Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body with a Brahma-voice: His physical marks are inconceivable; those who behold him give rise to joy.
Reverently honoring and joyfully believing in the Dharma throughout the oceans of lands in the ten directions, all the infinite and boundless Buddhas,
in every single thought-moment, each manifest their spiritual powers. The Bodhisattvas of great wisdom,
having deeply entered the ocean of Dharma and sustained by the Buddha’s power, are able to understand these skillful means.
2. Direct Praise of the Buddha Praising the Buddha’s Virtues:
The Great Hero with Ten Powers is most unsurpassed; He is like space, without equal.
The scope of his realization is vast and immeasurable; His merit is foremost, transcending the world.
The merit of the Ten Powers is boundless, Beyond the reach of thought or mental calculation.
This single dharma-gate of the Lion among Men Cannot be known by sentient beings even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Even if the lands of the ten directions were ground into dust, and someone were to count them to know their number,
the measure of the merit of a single pore of the Tathāgata could not be told even in a thousand million billion kalpas;
it would be like a person holding a measuring rod attempting to measure empty space, or like one following behind to calculate its extent.
The limits of space cannot be apprehended; The realm of the Tathāgata is likewise so.

Should there be one who, in a single instant, Could fully know the minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, Even if they were to pass through eons as numerous as all those beings, They could not know the nature of a single thought-moment of the Buddha.
Just as the Dharma-realm pervades all, yet cannot be seen or grasped as "all," so too is the realm of the ten directions; it pervades all, yet is not "all.
(Praise of the Merits of the Dharma)

If one were to fully expound upon even a single phrase of the Dharma, it would not be exhausted for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), yet its words and meanings would each remain distinct; by means of this, the Bodhisattva first generates the mind [of enlightenment].
Within that light, Buddhas appear in unspeakable numbers, and the Dharma taught by those Buddhas is likewise unspeakable.
The wondrous verses within the Dharma are unspeakable; Hearing these verses and attaining liberation is unspeakably unspeakable.
In every moment of thought, one clearly realizes the True Reality, which is unspeakable;
Manifesting all Buddhas of the future, they constantly expound the Dharma without end.
Each and every Buddha-dharma is unspeakable; The various purities are unspeakable;
The production of sublime sounds is unspeakable; The turning of the wheel of the true Dharma is unspeakable.
Within each and every one of those wheels of Dharma, The expounding of the sūtras is unspeakable.
Within each and every sūtra, the distinct dharma-gates are unspeakable;
Within each and every dharma-gate, the various dharmas taught are likewise unspeakable;
Within each and every dharma, the taming of sentient beings is unspeakable.
Or again, within the space of a single hair-tip, they may dwell for unspeakable eons;
as it is with one hair-tip, so it is with all others—the number of eons they remain is always thus.
(Praise of the Merit of the Sangha)
The merits of the Bodhisattva are boundless; All sublime practices are fully perfected.

Even if immeasurable and infinite Buddhas Were to speak for immeasurable eons, they could not exhaust them— How much less so could the gods and humans of the world, Or all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?
Even if one were to praise and extol them for immeasurable and boundless eons,
The number of all sentient beings could be easily known, And the mental capacities of the three periods of time could likewise be known;
Yet the limits of the merit of such sons of the Buddhas, Samantabhadra, Can never be measured.
One could know the limit of space by measuring it with a single hair; One could count and know the number of atoms in all lands.
Yet the dwelling, conduct, and vows of these great sages and their disciples Cannot be measured.
Even if the lands of the ten directions were ground into atoms, Their number could not be known within a single thought-moment.
The measure of space at the tip of a hair can be known, but even if one were to proclaim it for billions of eons, it could never be exhausted.
We, this great assembly, during the first part of the day, having paid homage and praised these merits, dedicate the roots of goodness thus obtained to the ocean of all sentient beings.
May they all forever be free from the hindrances and obscurations, and may they accomplish the path of omniscience.

Therefore, in this sutra, after enumerating Buddhas as numerous as atoms, it further states: "I shall, with profound faith and understanding and through direct knowledge and vision, each employ a subtle tongue-root surpassing that of the goddess Sarasvatī, producing inexhaustible sounds and words."

In praising the ocean of the Tathāgata’s merits, one must know that this can only be attained through clear insight gained by means of contemplative wisdom; for both the one who praises and that which is praised are like the ocean—profound, vast, and inexhaustible.
Having finished the praise, take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Third, pay respectful homage to all Buddhas.

(Once the praise is concluded, one should, with a single mind and upright posture, pay homage to the Buddhas in succession. Regarding the method for paying homage to the Buddhas: one must, in accordance with each Buddha being honored, sincerely recollect that this Buddha’s true body is like empty space, appearing according to the capacity of sentient beings.)

The forms [of the Buddhas] are like the moon in water, distinct and clear as if facing one before their eyes, receiving my prostrations. Toward each and every Buddha, one should apply the mind in this manner, invoking the essence by its name to pay homage. One must not allow the mind to become distracted. Furthermore, one must know for oneself that body and mind are empty and still, such that there is no actual form of prostration;

it is a reflection seen through the conditions of obstruction. Within the dharma-realm, there are Buddhas present before one at every single point. This physical act of bowing the head and face with total reverence follows the "Contemplation Gate of Prostrating to the Buddha" (Lǐfó Guānmén) by Tripitaka Master Ratnamati, which distinguishes seven levels of quality. The first is the prostration of pride (*māna*).

2. The Reciprocal Salutation (*saṃgīti-vaṃdana*): These two [preceding types] are not the proper ritual. 3. The Reverential Salutation (*satkṛtya-vaṃdana*): Respect arises from the mind and is manifested through body and speech; one places the five wheels (*pañca-cakra*) upon the ground. 4. The Signless Salutation (*animitta-vaṃdana*): One enters deeply into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), free from the characteristics of subject and object.

5. The Salutation of Manifesting Function (*viniyoga-vaṃdana*): One contemplates that both oneself and the Buddha arise from conditions, like illusions and shadows; universally mobilizing body and mind, one pays homage to all. 6. The Salutation of Inner Contemplation (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā-vaṃdana*): One pays homage only to the true Buddha of the *dharmakāya* within one's own body, without taking other Buddhas as an object. 7. The Salutation of True Reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-vaṃdana*): Whether internal or external, [one perceives all as such].

Whether ordinary beings or Buddhas, they share the same true reality (*dharmatā*). To see the Buddha as one who is worthy of veneration is itself a false view; likewise, to contemplate the true reality of one's own body and to contemplate the Buddha in that same way is called "equal veneration. Thus, Mañjuśrī said: "Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, I pay homage to that which has nothing to be observed," and so forth. Subsequently, these four modes of veneration all belong to contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*): 1.

The fourth is the veneration of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), because the Buddha of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) enters the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). 2. The fifth is the veneration of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), because the Buddha of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) arises from the essence in the form of function. 3.

The sixth is the veneration of the Middle Way contemplation (*madhyamaka-vipaśyanā*), because the Buddha of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-satya*) does not calculate emptiness or form, but directly perceives the true nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). 4. The seventh is the veneration of the single mind through the three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā-ekacitta-vandanā*); since the three truths are a single realm, the Buddha does not grasp at the real or discard the provisional, but remains in a state of total cessation beyond reliance. Now, regarding the scriptural text for these seven modes of veneration: since...

This pertains to the section on the "conforming characteristics" (suixiangmen), specifically the third and fifth [practices]. Because one honors the mind with the mind, one contemplates the body and contemplates the Buddha in every thought-moment. Since these arise from nature following conditions like illusions or shadows, other practices such as "formless worship" (wuxiangli) represent the meaning of contemplating mindfulness by detaching from characteristics at a lower level.

Therefore, although the three examples are perfectly clear, it is only while performing acts of physical and verbal reverence and worship that one should cultivate this contemplative wisdom. This does not mean that one should never perform physical or verbal worship and praise; rather, one simply employs formlessness and so forth to serve as the actual worship of the Buddha. One must reflect upon this well.

If one uses contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), it is already called "paying homage to the Buddha," and there is no need for physical prostration. In the third case as well, one should simply regard reverence as paying homage to the Buddha; it is not appropriate to involve the body or speech. Since the principle is thus, how could this not be correct? Question:

In the Mahāyāna school, if a transgression arises from the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), it is immediately termed a breach of the precepts (*dauḥśīlya*). What prevents us from applying this same principle here, whereby mental prostration would constitute the accumulation of merit? Answer: In that case, one forms a thought within the mind specifically intending to carry out actions of body and speech. Once such thoughts of killing, stealing, and so forth have been fully realized and there is no intention of regret, it is termed a breach of the precepts.

In the present instance, one merely intends to perform the bodily act of prostration and the verbal act of praise; the resolve of the mind is determined and free from hesitation. Even if one has not yet succeeded in purifying the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), during the act of prostration, merit is clearly and certainly generated.

Virtue. If there is no intention to direct the body or speech, there is fundamentally no merit. This is like when one originally has no intention to kill and so forth; likewise, there is fundamentally no transgression. However, once contemplative wisdom is established, the object of contemplation is constantly perceived. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, the practice of worship is uninterrupted.

Provided that the contemplating mind does not regress, it will naturally flow on continuously. This is like a person who has taken up an evil vow (duskrta-vrata); their intent to kill and so forth flows on from moment to moment, even if they are not actually killing or stealing at that very instant. One who takes up an evil vow engages in such activities as butchery, hunting, or banditry.

Question: In the fifth prostration, it is said that both subject and object are like reflections. Since a reflection has no mind, how can the meaning of worship be established? Answer: The mind of reverence from moment to moment is also like a reflection. In the world, things such as mirrors only reveal—

One cannot see the reflection of sound, odor, taste, touch, or the mind within the reflection of form; yet this Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, like the realm of space, perceives forms, sounds, and so forth, as well as the mind and mental factors. When performing this contemplation, one first contemplates the body and mind of oneself.

This is the momentum of ignorance, arising from defiled conditions. Now, by means of right wisdom, one contemplates that the entirety of emptiness and lack of self-nature is precisely the One True Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Thereafter, one contemplates this Dharma-realm as not abiding in its own nature, yet constantly able to arise in accordance with conditions.

Consequently, one performs prostrations and pays homage, single-mindedly surrendering oneself and entrusting oneself to the pure conditions of the Buddhas and the meaning of the Dharma. This gives rise to the body-mind and the Buddha; following these pure conditions, they arise as the body-mind and the Buddha, like a reflection appearing in a mirror.

Having realized that one’s own body-mind is without self-nature and is in union with the Dharma-realm—and since the Dharma-realm is all-pervasive—one’s own body-mind, following the Dharma-realm upon which it relies, is likewise all-pervasive and there is nowhere it does not prostrate. Therefore, it is said: "The entire body pervades all. As stated in the sixth [chapter]:

Regarding the True Buddha within one’s own body: it is like a great scripture within a speck of dust, like pure gold wrapped in tattered cloth, like a Buddha image within a scorched mold, or like the sound of a bell within a vessel. Since there is thus a correspondence between the true and the false, and the internal and the external, this is not a matter of unilaterally eradicating all marks;

rather, it should be understood as occurring within the midst of mindfulness. According to the Huayan school, there is furthermore a ritual of the mutual integration of self and others, which is complete in four propositions: First, bowing with one body to many Buddhas. That sutra says:

"With each and every body, one universally bows to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. It further states: "Bodhisattvas should know that within their own minds, at every moment of thought, there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment. All sentient beings are likewise so; in every moment of thought, they all possess a Buddha."

1. Attaining Perfect Enlightenment. Second, many bodies prostrating before a single Buddha. As the sutra says: "Before each and every Buddha, one manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields. It further states:

"When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, within his own body he universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment. Third, a single body prostrating before a single Buddha. Fourth, many bodies prostrating before many Buddhas. That sutra says: "When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he enters the Samādhi of the Wisdom of Excellent Awakening and perceives that bodies equal in number to all sentient beings abide within his body, even within a single pore.

There are bodies equal in number to all sentient beings pervading the entire Dharma-realm; it is likewise for every single pore. There is not the slightest space where there is no Buddha-body. Explanation:

It is said: Simply by taking any single body and confronting it with the Buddha, or taking any single Buddha and confronting him with the body, and then correlating these with the words and their meanings, one forms four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Yet, in reality, the number of bodies and so forth are all inexhaustible. Question: Why is it that the bodies of practitioners are thus one and the same as the inexhaustible Buddhas?

Answer: Because the causes and conditions are complete. That sutra says: "By the power of my Samantabhadra vows and practices. This refers to the power of the Dharma, which is the condition (*pratyaya*). It further says: "Arouse deep faith and understanding as if [the Buddha] were before one's eyes.

This refers to one's own power, which is the cause (*hetu*). "Deep understanding" is precisely "superior understanding" (*adhimukti*). Superior understanding means definitive confirmation and retention (*niścita-dhāraṇa*). That is to say, through the power of Samantabhadra’s Dharma, one perceives all objects as being the realm of the Buddha; and through the power of the wisdom of deep understanding, one confirms and encompasses them.

Maintain it. As described above, let the realm of the Buddha dwell within the mind as if it were before one's eyes. This means that regarding the objective realm, do not grasp at fixed characteristics such as arising and ceasing, unity or multiplicity; this is the integration with the realm of the Buddha. When the mind relies upon wisdom rather than consciousness, then every moment of mind is a mind that beholds the Buddha.

Therefore, that sutra says: "All phenomena are without birth; all phenomena are without cessation. If one can understand them thus, the Buddhas are ever present. Thus, that sutra concludes its prostration to the Buddha by saying:

"When the realm of empty space is exhausted, when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, when the karma of sentient beings is exhausted, and when the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted, my prostrations would then be exhausted. Because the realm of empty space, the realm of sentient beings, and so forth are inexhaustible, these prostrations of mine are without end. Moment after moment they continue in succession without interruption, through body, speech, and..."

The mental karma is free from weariness; thus, making offerings and offering praise—each of the ten types of practice and vows is exactly like this. To summarize: one should know that if one does not rely on the power of the practices of Samantabhadra’s contemplation, how could one achieve uninterrupted continuity in every thought-moment?
The wise should carefully reflect upon these words: do not perform acts such as prostration, praise, and offering with a mind of arising and ceasing or by grasping at signs.

Furthermore, even if one has committed transgressions equivalent to ten Buddha-fields and entered the Avīci Hell to suffer for the full duration of a kalpa, and is reborn thereafter—if they [then] recite..."

After the end of life, one will certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and attain the highest grade of birth in the presence of Amitābha Buddha.

before the Dharma seat, with body upright and dignified, respectfully kneeling, the right knee touching the ground, burning incense and scattering flowers, one should visualize the Three Jewels filling the void of space, together with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and his immeasurable adornments and retinue).

Surrounding [the assembly], act as the presiding master of the confession. Visualize each [deity] as if they were right before your eyes. With single-minded devotion and profound sincerity, give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, openly confessing and repenting for all evil karma created through the six sense faculties and three modes of action throughout immeasurable kalpas.

I sever the continuity of the mind; from this moment until the end of the future, I shall never again create [karmic actions]. Why is this? Although the nature of karma is empty, its retribution is not lost. If one commits evil and does not repent, although it is a cause and condition of falsehood and perversion, [the result will still follow].
One will then receive false and illusory retributions. (The words of repentance are mostly drawn from the scriptures and treatises of the Great Canon.

Disciple Bhikṣu [Name], on behalf of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, universally prays to sever all karmic obstructions. I take refuge and repent.

Next is the Repentance for the Retribution of the Ten Evil Karmas. (Now, one who wishes to repent must first understand the causes and conditions through which [karma] arises in succession. From beginningless time, due to non-awakening, greed, hatred, and delusion arise; these incite the body, speech, and mind to create all karma—namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the immovable.

If one focuses on the internal examination of the mind, both wholesome and unwholesome deeds are repented, because at the time of delusion, both wholesome and unwholesome karmas are produced by the heart of greedy attachment. However, if one proceeds according to the specific offenses committed, one repents only the evil karma, because from the moment of awakening until the attainment of Buddhahood, one ultimately never abandons wholesome conduct. Wholesome [karma].

This is because it accords with principle. When one is deluded, one seeks retribution by grasping at signs; thus, the faults of the body are formed. After awakening, one merely leaves behind that illness without eliminating wholesome dharmas; therefore, there is no need for repentance. Evil karma runs counter to principle and invites suffering;

it must be severed entirely, and thus one performs universal repentance. Within this repentance, there are again two kinds. First, if one commits a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense), one must first perform the ritual repentance according to the teachings. A prohibited offense is not inherently poisonous or evil, but is simply forbidden by the Buddha’s precepts as a restriction; thus, it is improper [to commit it].

To perform [an act] constitutes an offense as soon as it is performed. If one commits a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), one must further undertake the practice of repentance. A natural offense refers to the ten unwholesome actions, such as killing and stealing; their essential nature is evil. Even before the Buddha appeared in the world and there were yet no prohibitions established by precepts, committing them was inherently sinful by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*).

This is because one would otherwise fall into the three miserable realms (*trāya*). Regarding the "arising of practice," there are two types: first, ritual repentance (*sāṃkheya-pratikramaṇa*); second, principle repentance (*tattva-pratikramaṇa*). Ritual repentance is as described in such texts as the *Vaipulya-buddhanāma-sūtra*, which also prescribes the performance of formal rites while simultaneously arising in practice. Specifically, that *Vaipulya* sūtra instructs that one should first purify the *maṇḍala*:

smear the ground with fragrant mud, construct a circular altar within the room, decorate it with paintings and hang five-colored banners, burn coastal incense, light lamps of clarified butter, arrange a high seat, and invite twenty-four images of the Buddhas—though having more is not forbidden—and provide offerings of delicacies.

Regarding the meal: exert all one’s heart and strength to prepare it fresh and pure. As for clothing and footwear, there must be nothing old or unwashed; when entering or exiting, wearing or removing them, ensure they do not become intermingled. Observe the seven-day fast, bathing three times each day. On the first day, make offerings to the Sangha according to one’s means.

Separately invite a person who clearly understands both the internal and external Vinaya to serve as a preceptor. Receive the twenty-four precepts and the *dhāraṇī*, and confess one’s transgressions before the preceptor. One should set the period from the eighth to the fifteenth day, taking the seventh day as the primary limit; this cannot be shortened. If one is able...

Proceed further as you see fit and according to your capacity; ten people may return, but no more than this. Laypeople may also do so, provided they prepare their three robes with single-layered seams and equip themselves according to the Buddhist rites.

They should circumambulate one hundred and twenty times, then sit back and engage in contemplation, as described extensively in the sutras. Furthermore, within that text, it instructs one to arouse seven kinds of mental states as a preliminary means: first, shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*); second, fear; third, weary detachment (*nirveda*); fourth, the arousal of the bodhicitta; fifth, equanimity toward enemies and kin;

sixth, mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness; and seventh, contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses. Having aroused these seven mental states, one should visualize the Buddhas and sages of the ten directions, raising the joined palms (*añjali*) and confessing with utmost sincerity, expressing shame, reforming oneself, and so forth. If one follows the *Tiantai Zhiguan*...

Contemplation: Sudatta contemplates the ten minds in both their forward and reverse orders. First, he recognizes the ten types of minds that accord with birth and death as the objects to be remedied: first, the false discrimination of self and person, which gives rise to the view of a self-entity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); second, when internal afflictions are present and external adverse conditions are encountered, the mind of self increases and flourishes.

Third, having already possessed both internal and external [conditions], one suppresses thoughts of goodness and does not rejoice in the virtues of others. Fourth, one gives rein to the three karmas, committing every kind of evil. Fifth, although one’s actions may not be extensive, an evil mind is pervasive throughout. Sixth, the evil mind continues in succession, uninterrupted day and night. Seventh, one conceals and denies one’s faults, unwilling to let others know of them.

Eighth, one acts with arrogance and insolence, showing no fear of the evil realms. Ninth, lacking shame and remorse, one has no dread of either ordinary beings or sages. Tenth, one repudiates cause and effect, becoming an icchantika. From beginningless time, whether in oneself or in others, [these ten characteristics have persisted].

There is nothing that is not thus. Next, one should give rise to a mind that turns against the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), overturning and destroying it from the back [of the stream]. 1. Clearly understand cause and effect. 2. Feel shame and remorse, reproaching oneself; conceal one's offenses with shame before the heavens and manifest one's offenses with remorse before others.

3. Fear the evil realms (*apāya*); this overturns obstinacy and insolence. 4. Do not conceal one’s flaws; this overturns the habit of hiding them. 5. Sever the mind of continuity; this is like having committed a crime against the royal law and then regurgitating what was already swallowed. 6. Generate the Bodhicitta; let the mind be equal to space, overturning the former pervasiveness of evil. 7. Cultivate merit to compensate for transgressions; this overturns...

First, one previously committed evil. Eighth, protecting the True Dharma, which reverses the aforementioned destruction of goodness. Ninth, mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions, which reverses adverse conditions. Tenth, contemplating that the nature of sin is empty and seeing non-self. If one possesses these [ten], there is no sin that will not be extinguished; if one does not understand them, [there is no liberation].

Always, at dawn, midday, sunset, evening, midnight, and the hour of cockcrow, one should wash and rinse the mouth, adjust one’s robes, and with palms joined, pay homage to the ten directions. From wherever one is facing, one should confess one's transgressions, saying:

Whether it be an offense committed by body, an offense committed by speech, an offense committed by mind, or an offense committed by intention—such as harming the Buddha with one’s intent, being jealous of and hating the sutras and the Way, fighting with the Saṃgha of bhikṣus, killing an arhat, or committing suicide.
Parents, [commit] three types of bodily and four types of verbal misconduct of the mind. Regarding the three [bodily acts]: they kill living beings themselves; they incite others to kill;

seeing others deceiving, they rejoice in it with their bodies. They engage in double-tongued speech themselves; they incite others to double-tongued speech...

Tongue. Seeing others engage in divisive speech, one rejoices in their bodies on their behalf; one reviles oneself and teaches others to revile. Seeing others reviling, one rejoices in their bodies on their behalf;
one speaks falsehoods oneself and teaches others to speak falsehoods. Seeing others speaking falsehoods, one rejoices in their bodies on their behalf;
one is envious oneself and teaches others to be envious. Seeing others being envious, one rejoices in their bodies on their behalf; one is greedy for bait oneself and teaches others to be greedy.

Bait. Seeing others covet bait, he rejoices in their bodies on their behalf; yet he himself lacks faith, and he teaches others not to have faith. Seeing others lack faith, he rejoices in their bodies on their behalf; yet he himself lacks faith.
He believes that performing good deeds brings good results and performing evil deeds brings evil results, yet he teaches others to commit evil.
Seeing others commit evil, he rejoices in their bodies on their behalf; yet he himself steals the property of Buddhist temples, or steals the property of the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*.

Regarding material things and teachings: when one sees others committing theft, one rejoices in their actions with one’s own body; when one uses small measures and short rulers to deceive others, or heavy weights, large measures, and long rulers to exploit others;
when one teaches others to exploit others, or sees others exploiting others and rejoices in those acts with one’s own body;
when one commits robbery oneself, teaches others to commit robbery, or sees others committing robbery and rejoices in those acts with one’s own body—one is committing evil.
Rebellion. Teaching others to commit evil rebellion. Seeing others commit evil rebellion, one rejoices in their deeds with one’s own body.

This refers to the transgressions and evils committed since beginningless time while the body was born in the five states of existence—while dwelling in the hells, while dwelling among birds and beasts, while dwelling among the *preta*s, and while dwelling among humans.
At the time of birth within these five realms, one failed to be filial toward one's parents and did not obey them.

They do not respect their teachers; they do not respect their virtuous friends; they do not respect śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way; they do not respect their elders; they treat their parents with contempt;
they treat their teachers with contempt; and they treat those who seek the path of arhatship and those who seek the path of pratyekabuddhahood with contempt.
If we have slandered or been envious; if we saw the Buddha-way and called it wrong, or saw the evil paths and called them right;

if we saw what was correct and called it incorrect, or saw what was incorrect and called it correct—whatever transgressions and evils we have committed, we pray that the Buddhas of the ten directions will compassionately accept our repentance.

The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "If there are good sons or good daughters whose minds do not wish to enter into *nirvāṇa*..."
Those who have been ploughed through as animals or reborn among the *preta* (hungry ghosts) must repent for all their transgressions and not dare to conceal them.

After receiving the precepts, one must not commit evil again. Those who do not wish to be born in borderlands—places where there is no Buddha, no sutras, no community of bhikṣus, no righteous principles, and no distinction between good and evil—all must repent and must not conceal [their faults].

Concealment. Those who do not wish to be born ignorant, deaf, blind, or mute; those who do not wish to be born as butchers, fishermen, hunters, prison officials, or into impoverished households—all should repent their transgressions and must not conceal them. Women who seek to obtain a male body should all repent their transgressions.
Those who desire to attain the stage of *srotāpanna* and no longer enter the hells or the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) should all repent their transgressions.
Those who wish to attain the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, to be reborn as humans in the heavens above; those who wish to attain the stage of *anāgāmin* in the two upper heavens of the form realm;
those who wish to attain the state of *arhat* and enter *nirvāṇa*; those who wish to attain the path of *arhat* within this world;
those who wish to attain the path of a *pratyekabuddha*; and those who wish to know the matters of the past and future—all must repent their transgressions and not dare [to commit them again].

[Regarding] concealment: The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "If there are sons or daughters of good family who, three times each day and night, prostrate themselves and pay homage to all the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions;

and furthermore, for all transgressions committed since beginningless time—such as violating the precepts, breaking the rules of training, overstepping the laws and regulations, engaging in false conceptualization and discrimination, and being attached to a self and persons—they shall [confess] all such karmic obstacles."
May they be extinguished. May the turbid minds of confusion, obstacles, and interruptions be entirely purified.

May those with restless bodies and minds, sorrow, and the feverish afflictions of distress all attain liberation. May anger, agitation, frowning countenances, displeasure, reproaches, and harm be entirely purified.
May mutual vexation, strife, discord, legal disputes, verbal quarrels, contentious debates, anxieties, and transgressions be likewise cleansed.

May all karma be extinguished. May those lacking virtue transmit the precepts; may those lacking talent act as teachers; may those with meager learning seek to benefit others; may they preach the Dharma with impurity and consume the offerings of the faithful in vain;
and may all whose mental conduct is stained by desire be completely extinguished.

We were shrouded by ignorance and did not recognize the causes and retributions of the ten non-virtuous karmas. Now, having encountered this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), we are finally able to awaken to this knowledge.
We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy and holy ones.
Burning incense and scattering flowers, we openly confess and repent for all our bitter retributions; we dare not conceal them. By virtue of these causes and conditions, I and...
May all karmic retributions of the ocean of sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* be entirely purified.
Next is the mudrā and mantra for repentance and the eradication of transgressions:
Form the *vajrabandha* with both hands; bend the second joints of the thumbs and forefingers; and press the ring fingers and little fingers together.
Recite the mantra of confession: Oṃ sarvapāpāni me kṣayaṃ gacchantu svāhā (recite three times).
Sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas are instantly swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose entirely from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
Whatever has arisen from my body, speech, and mind, I now confess it all.
Having confessed, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Fifth, rejoicing in merit:
I rejoice in all the merit of every sentient being throughout the ten directions, of those of the two vehicles—
both those in training and those beyond training— and of all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas.
Having rejoiced, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Sixth, I entreat you to turn the wheel of Dharma:
O Lamp of the World in all ten directions, you who first accomplished enlightenment—
I now exhort all [the Buddhas] to turn the unsurpassed, wondrous wheel of Dharma;
having requested them to turn it, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Seventh, the Entreaty for the Buddhas to Remain in the World:
If any of the Buddhas should wish to manifest parinirvāṇa, I shall entreat them all with utmost sincerity:
"May you remain for as many eons as there are motes of dust in a world-system, for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings."
Having requested them to remain, take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Eighth, constantly following the Buddhas in their training:
I follow the training of all Tathāgatas and cultivate the perfect conduct of Samantabhadra.

I make offerings to all the Tathāgatas of the past, As well as the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present, And all the Teachers of Gods and Humans in the future; May all my aspirations be perfectly fulfilled.
I vow to follow and train throughout the three times, And swiftly attain the realization of Great Bodhi.
Having studied [this] accordingly, take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Ninth: May all the lands throughout the ten directions, vast, pure, and wondrously adorned, always accord with the needs of sentient beings.
May the assemblies surrounding all Tathāgatas, seated beneath the king of Bodhi trees,
cause all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to be free from suffering and affliction, to dwell in constant peace and happiness,
to obtain the benefits of the profound and true Dharma, and to extinguish their afflictions without remainder.
Having thus constantly complied, with a sincere heart take refuge and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha. Tenth,
universally dedicate all acts of prostration,
praise, and offerings to the Buddhas, entreating the Buddhas to remain in the world and turn the wheel of Dharma.
Rejoicing in and repenting of all roots of goodness, I dedicate them to sentient beings and the path of the Buddha.
Having thus dedicated them, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
We, the disciple-monks [Name] and others, for the sake of all sentient beings, make this vow with a sincere heart:
When I am on the verge of death, May all obstacles be completely removed;
May I behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, And immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Once I have been reborn in that land, may these great vows be manifested before me,
fully perfected without exception, bringing benefit and happiness to the entire realm of sentient beings;
when that Buddha’s assembly is entirely pure, may I then be born from a supreme lotus flower.
I beheld the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Light, who bestowed upon me the prophecy of enlightenment in his very presence.
Having received that prophecy from the Tathāgata, I manifested countless hundreds of koṭis of transformation bodies;
with vast power and wisdom pervading the ten directions, I universally benefit the realms of all sentient beings.
Until the realm of empty space is exhausted, And until sentient beings, karma, and afflictions are all exhausted—
As long as all such things remain inexhaustible, May my vows likewise endure eternally without end.
Having made this vow, with a sincere heart, I take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.

(The following is for the recitation of impermanence. However, this rite of repentance involves extensive principles and phenomena (*dharma*), making it difficult to fixate upon within the six periods of the day. Therefore, I shall now write out in full, during this first period, the texts to be used for the remaining six periods.

Those who examine the original text and chant it must first master it thoroughly; each should employ it according to its respective time. As for the verses on impermanence, they will be written separately for each subsequent period. Regarding the verses on impermanence found in the sutras and śāstras, these are universally applicable across all six periods, though one may also choose to recite other specific ones according to one’s own inclination.)

Furthermore, if there is leisure time, one should recite the *One Hundred Verses on Exhorting the World* (*Ārya-śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra-śataśloka*) and may also employ the exhortation on impermanence. Herein, beginning with the hour of the tiger (*yínshí*), the [recitations for] all six periods of the day are fully recorded.
(Recitation: May the assembly listen to the Verse on Impermanence for the Early Morning:
Those who seek the bliss of nirvāṇa Should train in the Dharma of the śramaṇas. Regarding food, clothing, and the preservation of life, Whether coarse or fine, follow the example of the community.
May all members of the assembly, at the early morning hour, Purely recite the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).
Furthermore, each should recite the Verse on Impermanence (which must necessarily be used at the beginning of every session):
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; They are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, Cessation is bliss.
The Tathāgata has realized nirvāṇa, Forever severing the cycle of birth and death. If one can listen with a sincere heart, One will always obtain immeasurable bliss.
(The Verse for Noon)
If one does not apply diligence in this life, it is like a tree without roots.
Even if one gathers flowers and places them in the sun, for how long can they remain fresh? The flowers will not stay fresh for long, nor will their color remain beautiful.
Human life is like a mere instant; it cannot be preserved even for a moment. Therefore, I exhort all sentient beings.
Diligently Cultivating the Unsurpassed Path:
A Verse for Sunset In the West, the sun has already set; Defilements and worldly toil remain undispelled; The time of old age, sickness, and death has arrived.
We meet for but a brief time; every thought hastens the passage of years.
Like fish in a dwindling pool of water, I exhort the assembly who pay homage to the Buddha to practice and study until nothing remains.
Furthermore, each person should recite this verse:
This day has already passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly; like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be?
(O assembly,) you should apply yourselves with diligence, as if your hair were on fire, contemplating only impermanence; be careful not to be heedless.
The verses for the first watch of the night:
The afflictions are deep and bottomless; The ocean of birth and death is boundless. Since the boat for crossing over suffering has not yet been established, how can you delight in sleep?
Awaken from your slumber! Gather your mind and remain constantly in meditative concentration.
Valiant and diligent in effort, The path to enlightenment is naturally [attained].
O Bhikṣu, rise, rise! Why do you cling to sleep? What benefit is there in sleep?
When one is ill, how can one sleep? When sharp thorns pierce the body, how can one find sleep?
Now that you have renounced the household life, this is the time for the aspiration of liberation; you should, according to that original vow, apply yourself with diligent effort day by day.
In the latter part of the night, the divine light of the verses shifted and flowed, continuing until the beginning of the fifth watch.
Impermanence arrives moment by moment, ever coexisting with birth and death; I exhort all who practice the Way to cultivate and study until nothing remains.
Furthermore, there is one verse applicable at all six times:
The world is not solid, Like foam, bubbles, and flames; You all should swiftly give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
I prostrate to the Worthy and Holy Ones;
I look up to the Ten-Body Pervasive Illumination Buddha, To all the Tathāgatas of the Flower Treasury World,
and to the Honored Śākyamuni, the Original Teacher of this Sahā World, And to Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and all the foremost leaders.
The assembly of noble ones throughout the oceans of lands and their retinues, the sublime beings gathered in the Flower Treasury Assembly,
the hosts of Śakra, Brahmā, and the various classes of devas and spirits, and all those who have attained the divine eye of knowing others' minds—
may you all, not forsaking the power of your compassion, bear witness to us two people.
For the sake of practicing the dharani-gate of vows, at this time [I], with a sincere mind, together perform this rite of worship and repentance.

May the merit thus produced be used entirely to adorn the ocean of lands within the Dharma-realm. May all sentient beings aspire that celestial beings do not fall, and that they realize that worldly pleasures are impermanent.
May the land be peaceful and tranquil; may those who recognize the True Vehicle be superior to their peers, and may they dwell forever therein.

May all those who hold official rank rejoice in the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle; may the people enjoy eternal peace and security, and may they all cultivate the Way of Awakening and Illumination.
May the masters, monks, and parents be bathed in a vast ocean of blessings and joy. May the donors and patrons fulfill the ten thousand practices;

may those in the three miserable realms simultaneously leave suffering behind, and may the eight difficulties be entirely eliminated. May the cauldron of boiling water transform into a cool, refreshing pond, and the iron bed turn into a lotus flower.
Upon the flower-throne, the sounds of lamentation ceased and were replaced by the voices of reciting the Buddha’s name. Every person possessed the mind to return to the source;

each was endowed with the illumination that restores one to the origin. May they constantly give rise to their present vows and future aspirations, and together perfect their non-regressive resolve through contemplative practice.
To realize together in the ocean-like assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is the supreme and auspicious condition:
the Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha, the Perfect Sambhogakāya Rocana Buddha,
and the thousand billion Nirmāṇakāya Śākyamuni Buddhas.
The Twelve Supreme Vows of the Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-rāja;
the Forty-eight Vows of Amitābha Buddha;
the Great Holy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra; and the Great Holy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī.
The Dharani of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra: The Great Holy Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
the Great Holy Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, and the Great Holy Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Pervading the Dharmadhātu.

namasamanta-mukha-durnivāra-tejodhana oṃ kīṭi kīṭi tattvātman vaśaṅkara durnivāra-udbhūta-māta-māta-tattvātman-ātman namasamanta-mukha-durnivāra-tejodhana oṃ kīṭi kīṭi tattvātman vaśaṅkara durnivāra-udbhūta-māta-māta-tattvātman-ātman.
If one recites this mantra once— OṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ—
the merit obtained is equal to that of reading the entire Avataṃsaka Sūtra in its entirety.
The Vairocana Consecration Light Mantra: Oṃ āḥ maḥ me laṃ khaṇḍe maheśvara-maṇi-paṇ-ma-cakra-pravartaya hūṃ.
The Sūtra states: "If there should be a person who, throughout kalpas as numerous as the dust motes of the Buddha-fields of the ten directions,
commits the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and other such sins, and by virtue of these heavy transgressions falls directly into the Avīci Hell—
if another person holds and recites this mantra of Vairocana Buddha and scatters it upon the corpse, the name tablet, or other remains of that deceased person at their burial site," and so forth.
Recite [the mantra] over flowers, rice, and so forth twenty-one times, or one hundred and eight times, and scatter them upon that person’s remains.
By the power of Vairocana’s original vow, he emits great radiance that shines upon the bodies of those sinful beings, whereby all karmic obstructions are completely extinguished.
Through this light, they are gathered and led to the Lotus [Palace] in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Born by transformation;
the ten-fold adornment is now complete. Recite the verse for concluding the session:
Abiding in the world like empty space, Like a lotus flower unsullied by water.
With a mind pure and transcending that [previous state], prostrate to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Circumambulate clockwise while reciting;

(having already performed repentance and made vows, one should with single-mindedness maintain upright posture and dignified deportment. Circumambulate the Dharma-seat to the right, burning incense and scattering flowers. Walking slowly and with composure, call to mind the subtle and wondrous merits of the Triple Gem, reciting them aloud.)
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the Dharma-realm. Homage to the Dharmas of the ten directions throughout the Dharma-realm.
Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions throughout the Dharma-realm. Homage to Vairocana Buddha.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha. Homage to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya.
Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Homage to the Great Bodhisattvas of the Dharma Assembly. Homage to Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha Bodhisattva.
Homage to Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva. Homage to Vajragarbha Bodhisattva.
Homage to the fifty-five holy ones, beginning with Mañjuśrī. Homage to the Bodhisattva Sudhana.
Homage to the assembly of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in the oceans of lands throughout the Dharma-realm.

This is the realization of sound: its nature is empty, and body and mind are like clouds and shadows. With every step raised and every step set down, the mind finds nothing to grasp; one does not dwell upon the characteristics of walking. The illusory reflection is itself emptiness, for it is the true Dharma-nature. Thus, this shadow-body of mine—

Manifesting throughout the ten directions, filling the Dharma-realm, there is nowhere they do not appear universally. They circumambulate all Buddhas three times, and so on up to twenty-one, seven hundred, or seven thousand times; there is no fixed number, and one should determine this for oneself.

When the practice of walking the path is nearly finished, return to reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha as before: "Namo Amitābha Buddha! Namo Amitābha Buddha! Burn incense with right mindfulness until the end of the practice, then take refuge in the Triple Gem with single-minded right mindfulness, chanting these words aloud yourself: )
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all sentient beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all beings preside over great assemblies without any hindrance;
may they pay homage to the noble multitude and sit in contemplative reflection.

The ten preceding sections concern the expedient means of practical cultivation; each should be understood according to the text as the manifestation of the Dharma. One must not become mired in the literal words while losing sight of the underlying meaning;

rather, one must ensure that the reality of the principle is fully clarified. When this is realized within one's own mind, one may immediately enter into contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) to establish it as the object of focus for long-term cultivation.

Restraining the thoughts and controlling the mind, close the eyes, straighten the body, and sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). With a sincere heart, contemplate clearly and without distraction.
Before every single Buddha and Bodhisattva throughout the oceans of peripheral lands and across the three periods of time, one should reverently pay homage and circumambulate with earnest devotion.
Furthermore, one should offer clouds and oceans of various kinds of ritual implements to all such holy assemblies.

Having made these extensive offerings, one should contemplate that one’s own mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, spontaneously perfected by its very nature, and radiating universal light.

Illumination is like empty space. Furthermore, I deeply give rise to compassionate thoughts, feeling pity for sentient beings who do not realize their own minds and thus wander through the various realms of existence;

I shall transform and deliver them all, causing them to attain awakening and understanding. Moreover, I contemplate that my own mind, the minds of all sentient beings, and the minds of all Buddhas are fundamentally without distinction—equal and of a single characteristic. Thus, I bring forth the Great Bodhicitta, which is luminously penetrating and pure, vast and expansive.
It is vast, pervasive, perfectly pure, and white, forming a great lunar disc equal in measure to space, without limit or boundary.
Upon that lunar disc, one visualizes a golden syllable *A*, emitting immeasurable light that pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
Within each ray of light are immeasurable Buddha-fields; within each Buddha-field are immeasurable Buddhas; and within each Buddha...

Surrounded by bodhisattvas, he attains perfect enlightenment. His wisdom enters the three periods of time, his body pervades the ten directions, and he turns the great wheel of Dharma to rescue sentient beings from suffering.
Having completed the attainment of Buddhahood, one should contemplate with clarity the self-nature of the syllable *A*, the truth of non-arising, wherein all conceptualizations are empty;
one abides in reliance upon this self-nature. When weary, recite the short syllable *A* twenty-one times.
Based on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, this is the first section: the Gate of Briefly Determining the Three Verses (transmitted by the Great Master Qizhen).
The first is the Gate of Briefly Determining the Infusion of Seeds upon Hearing the Name, from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Section Two: The Three Contemplations as Remedies for Cultivating the Mind (divided into three parts) First:
The Contemplation of True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics;
the Dharma-nature is Primordially Empty and Quiescent. There is neither grasping nor seeing; the emptiness of nature is itself the Buddha.
The contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena is beyond conceptualization.
If one wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm.
All is created solely by the mind;
through the three cycles of pervasive, harmonious contemplation,
one understands the infinite within the one, the one within the infinite, and realizes their mutual arising.
The Verses on the Three Contemplations composed by the First Patriarch of the Avataṃsaka, the Great Master Dushun:
If one wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, The True Suchness within the body pervades all that is external.
Sentient and insentient beings share a single body; everywhere they are identical with the true Dharma-realm.
By employing a single thought to contemplate a single object, all objects are simultaneously realized within that one object.
Within all-encompassing wisdom, there are all Dharma-realms.
A single thought-moment illuminates and enters into many eons;
within each thought-moment and eon, all times and places are gathered, manifesting in layered patterns like a celestial net.
This unimpeded penetration of all-knowledge is called "The Three Verses on the One Name. Whether one contemplates or recites them, they become the indestructible, adamantine seed of awakening.
Now, regarding those who perform this *Avataṃsaka* Liturgy and Repentance Ritual for seven days or twenty-one days:

all shall first enter the altar. At noon, they receive the instructions; after the midday meal, the invocation is performed; at evening, the food offerings are released; lamps are lit and the Way is practiced while reciting the Seven-Branch Verse.
One should turn the Wheel of Dharma. On the following day at dawn (the *yīn* hour), the Seven-Branch Practice is performed, and the assembly stands in formation.

Regarding the ritual: the breaking of the fast occurs at the third watch (寅時). On the first day, one should perform worship during the six periods—noon, evening, the first watch of the night, the middle watch, and the last watch—which corresponds to the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night prescribed in various sutras.

Furthermore, regarding the first two sessions and the final *Jingtu hui* (Pure Land Assembly), one should follow the sequence of the text and perform the worship of the third session, which consists of the worship of the Tathāgata’s ten bodies.
When this is concluded, the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) stands at the Dharma seat and announces the sutras and the names of the Buddhas for the assembly to hear and receive.

The assembly kneels and prostrates. From the third session (*śam*) through the thirty-ninth session, when they have finished the thirteen prostrations and are seated, the procedure for announcing the sutras, the names of the Buddhas, and the ritual of prostration is to be understood as being identical to what preceded. All other ritual procedures are to be adopted accordingly.
This is the Ritual for the Avataṃsaka Maṇḍala. I respectfully compose this record of the ritual text for the Avataṃsaka Maṇḍala to honor the Great Teaching of the Avataṃsaka.
This Great Teaching of the Avataṃsaka is the fundamental wheel of the Dharma of the Tathāgata; all Buddhist scriptures flow forth from within it. To use an analogy:

It is as if the heavens cover, the earth supports, the ocean contains, and spring nurtures. For the most part, this is because one cultivates the causes of Samantabhadra in order to realize the fruit of Vairocana.
This is the profound essence of the treatises of the Elder Li and the commentaries of National Preceptor Guan.

Profound! It reveals what is obscure and hidden. Yet, the ritual texts of Master Xingxiang are so attuned to human sentiment and so well-timed to the opportunities of the moment that they may truly be called a guide for spiritual practice.
