To all the ocean-like assemblies... [as above].
Homage to all the assemblies in the oceans of bodhimaṇḍas of all the Buddhas throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
I take refuge in them all from the ten directions. May my transgressions be extinguished, may my pure faith increase, and may I be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean.
In the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss,
following the repentance for the three realms and five destinies,
I take refuge in the inexhaustible Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha jewels of the Indra’s Net, Vairocana Tathāgata, Samantabhadra, and Mañjuśrī.

The assembly of noble ones gathered like the ocean, and the world-transcending and worldly deities, by virtue of their compassionate original vows, radiate great light that illuminates this Dharma assembly.
May they bear witness, protect, and keep us in mind; may they look upon us with pity and grant their acceptance. I pray that for myself and the ocean of all sentient beings, from time immemorial...

Up until this very moment, the ocean of karma has been inexhaustible, with its Indra-nets of worlds layering upon one another. All karmic offenses and retributions within the three realms and five destinies are now fully disclosed and repented.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "What is called the 'world' is of two kinds: first, the world of sentient beings; second, the world of the vessel (the physical environment).
As for the world of sentient beings, it refers to the sentient beings of the five destinies: devas, humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings;
these are termed the world of sentient beings of the five destinies. As for the world of the vessel, within the desire realm there are two [kinds]..."

There are ten locations in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and four in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); these forty types are called the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), the dwelling place of sentient beings.
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are twenty locations; the first refers to the eight great hells.
Each of these hells has sixteen subsidiary compartments on its four sides as its retinue, surrounding it on all sides.
Observing them therein, one gives rise to the thought of dissatisfaction. What are the names of the eight great hells? The first is named the Hell of Alternating Death and Revival;
the second is named the Black Rope Hell; the third is named the Hell of Crushing Multitudes; the fourth is named the Hell of Wailing.
The hells: fifth is the Hell of Great Wailing; sixth is the Hot Hell; seventh is the Greatly Hot Hell; eighth is the Avīci Hell.

If there are sentient beings in the past, future, or present who, by means of their own body, speech, and mind, have committed various evil karmas, they will consequently be born within those great hells and remain there for immeasurable kalpas. [They shall] fully...

They undergo hundreds of thousands of various kinds of suffering and affliction. Even if they should behold exquisite forms within that hell, because their minds are so oppressed, they do not give rise to the perception of pleasure.
Because they lack the perception of pleasure due to these causal conditions, great suffering arises once more.
Thus, passing from one hell to another, they experience the most extreme of sufferings, which are unbearable and beyond description. If...
The ear hears sounds and the nose smells odors; the tongue tastes flavors, the body perceives tactile sensations, and the mind conditions mental phenomena—all are likewise thus.
All those states of mind are neither loved nor enjoyed; they are never met with joy. All are unpleasant, and not a single one is agreeable.
Their bodies are constantly ablaze, eating hot iron balls and drinking molten copper; at every point of contact, it is all...
All are fire; they are unbearable and constitute extreme painful sensations. Because those sentient beings have not yet exhausted their evil karma, they do not die in this manner.
As long as the retribution for all [karma] has not been fully experienced, they are reborn therein.
Furthermore, because they committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind while among humans, they likewise experience the results there. One must repent for these karmic offenses.
Now, the various distinctions within the hells are so numerous that they cannot be fully recounted. As for the lords and sovereigns of these hells:

there are all the sinful beings, as well as the Son of Heaven, Yama; the thirty great kings, the thirty-three kings, the nine ranks and twenty-four bureaus, the ten great hell-emperors, the thirty hell-kings, the thirty-six kings, and the eighteen hell-dwellers. There are also the Ox-head Ābhangas and the Horse-head Rākṣasas.

The Lords of the *kṣetra*, the Lords of Life who govern and restrain; the Poisonless King of Ghosts; the assistant minor ministers; the leaders of the various departments; the Lord of the Staff; the Lord of Purity;
the Lord of Water; the Lord of Iron; the Lord of Earth; the celestial boys of good and evil; all the *gōngcáo* (merit-officials) and jailers; the confession of karmic retribution for offenses.
Furthermore, the Six Fasting Days and the Eight Kings; the thirty-two ministers of forbearance; the four great kings of forbearance; and the five paths.
Great Deity, repentance for the retribution of sins: ○ Furthermore, repentance for the retribution of sins in the eight cold and eight hot hells beneath the earth, and in the neighboring hells;
○ Furthermore, repentance for the retribution of sins in all hells within burial mounds, amidst waters, within mountain palaces, in wildernesses, and in the air;
○ Furthermore, repentance for all cold hells and all hot hells existing among the four continents of the human realm.
Hell: Repentance for the Retribution of Sins. Furthermore, within Mount Cakravāḍa there are eight great hells;
each of these hells has sixteen subsidiary hells. Repentance for the Retribution of Sins. Moreover, among those are ten hells, and there are also five great hells.
Within the Iron Ring Mountains of the south lies the City of King Yama, with sevenfold walls on both the east and west sides.
First, one is born in the hells; repentance for the retribution of these sins. Furthermore, there are thirty-two hells, sixty-four hells, and one hundred and eight hells.
Within Mount Cakravāḍa in the east, there are immeasurable hells; repentance for the retribution of these sins.
Moreover, there are thirty-two śramaṇa hells. Furthermore, near the Avīci Hell, there are eighteen minor hells.

The Hells: Repentance for Karmic Retribution. Within those minor hells, there are eighteen cold hells, eighteen hot hells, eighteen dark hells, eighteen minor hot hells, eighteen sword-wheel hells, eighteen forest-of-swords hells, eighteen wheel-of-swords hells, and eighteen chariot-fire hells. Ten...
The Hell of Boiling Excrement; the eighteen Hells of Cauldron Soup; the eighteen Hells of the Ash River. Confession for these karmic retributions.
Furthermore, five hundred billion Hells of Sword Forests; five hundred billion Hells of Thorny Forests;
five hundred billion Hells of Copper Pillars; five hundred billion Hells of Iron Ash; and five hundred billion Hells of Iron Nets. Karmic retributions for these.
Repentance: Furthermore, there are the eighteen Iron Cavern Hells; the eighteen Iron Pellet Hells; the eighteen Stone Spike Hells;
and the eighteen Copper-Drinking Hells. Repentance for these karmic retributions.
Moreover, due to immeasurable karma, there are distinct minor hells, numbering up to eighty-four thousand hells, all of which are unspeakable in number.
This suffering is neither to be heard nor to be described; there is no one capable of speaking it, and no one capable of hearing it.
Should anyone attempt to speak of it, that person would vomit hot blood and die. This is the confession for the retribution of such transgressions.

The second [realm] inhabited is that of animals (*tiryagyoni*). Just as there are differences in body size among animals, there are some sentient beings whose bodies are so small that they are like a hundredth part of a single hair split apart;
there are those with such inconceivably minute bodies. Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose bodies are like motes of dust drifting in a window, and again, there are sentient beings...
They are born with bodies ten thousand *yojanas* in height. Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose lifespan lasts for a single *muhūrta*;

others whose lifespan lasts for seven *muhūrtas*; and still others whose lifespan lasts for one *kalpa*, up to a hundred *kalpas*, or even hundreds of thousands, ten millions, and billions of *kalpas*.
Due to their evil karma, they are born there; they take no delight in wholesome dharmas, do not plant roots of goodness, and lack...
There are those who practice the Dharma yet lack wisdom; they are without shame or remorse, and devoid of a heart of compassion.
They constantly experience suffering and affliction, giving rise to great fear. Each harbors a mind of mutual harm toward others and remains far removed from all wholesome dharmas.

Constantly practicing what is unwholesome, they dwell in the darkness of ignorance within the perilous and evil paths, creating karma for the hells and giving rise to a mind of anger and resentment. Not...

Delighting in merit and virtue is the time when retribution ripens. One undergoes inferior bodies and inferior states of mind within the evil realms, being born in such places where one constantly suffers various forms of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat;
being beaten, ridden, and burdened with heavy loads until one is exhausted; with the skin on one's neck pierced and the flesh on one's spine broken;
and being greedily bitten and eaten by mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects. Such afflictions are immeasurable and boundless. [I now repent of these karmic retributions for my sins.]
Furthermore, among the animals, there are those dwelling in the oceans, in the waters, on the land, in the fires, and in the air;

there are the species of snakes, shrimp, fish, horses, and elephants—thirty-six billion such classes. Each and every one of them undergoes immeasurable suffering. [I now] repent of these retributions for my transgressions.
The third place of residence is the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Among the hungry ghosts, there are differences in body size:
some hungry ghosts are one foot tall; some are the size of a human being; and some have bodies as large as a thousand *yojana*.
Furthermore, there are some ghosts whose bodies are like the Snow Mountains. Those hungry ghosts are naked and without clothing; their hair is disheveled and entangles them.
They are black, emaciated, and gaunt, with skin that merely covers their bones, devoid of all flesh and blood. Their bodies are coarse and rough, like withered trees.
They suffer from hunger and thirst constantly, longing for food and drink but never obtaining it. Fire burns within their mouths, with flames issuing forth externally.
Their minds are perpetually filled with anger and resentment, devoid of compassion. Tormented by heat and agitation, they seek coolness but find none.
Furthermore, driven by the urgency of hunger and thirst, they drink molten copper and eat glowing iron balls, as well as other hot, foul, putrid, and festering pus and blood.
Hot excrement and hot urine; hot parched grain and hot gruel; as well as various hot winds or hot rains—all grasses, trees, rivers, seas, mountain streams, and ponds;
leaves, flowers, fruits, and all things consumed—these are extremely difficult to find and can never be obtained.
Even if one were to obtain it, it might last for a thousand years, or perhaps a hundred thousand years; with such a lifespan, one constantly undergoes suffering and affliction.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one remains in darkness and ignorance. [This concludes] the Repentance for the Retribution of Sins. Now, within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), there are three categories.
The nine classes, the ten classes, the thirty-six classes, the ten classes of solitary ghosts, and the *saṃsāra*-like hungry ghosts endure immeasurable suffering.
One should repent for these karmic retributions of transgression.
Fourth, regarding the dwelling places of human beings: a person of wisdom next contemplates that among humans, all possess various kinds of suffering.

That is to say: the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death; the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*);
the suffering of hunger, the suffering of thirst, the suffering of greed, the suffering of hatred, and the suffering of jealousy.
The suffering of falsehood, frivolous speech, and double-tongued talk; the suffering of harsh words, abuse, and slander; the suffering of cold and heat;
the suffering of evil winds, torrential rains, epidemics, and locusts; the suffering of being harmed by venomous birds and beasts;
the suffering of evil times, wicked kings, and imprisonment; and the suffering of poverty, low status, and short life. Having contemplated these sufferings, one gives rise once more to...
Heavy suffering. Conditioned by suffering, suffering arises, and one further creates the causes of suffering; thus, in future bodies, one again undergoes the retribution of suffering.

In this manner, revolving and turning, one undergoes immeasurable and boundless hardships and pains without end. [The Repentance for Karmic Retribution of Sins] Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
Within these four continents, there are eighty dwelling places of devas and sixty dwelling places of nāgas. Four...
There are dwellings of asuras; four dwellings of garuḍas; fifty-two dwellings of kiṃnaras;
forty-six dwellings of mahoragas; eight dwellings of kumbhāṇḍas; thirty dwellings of pūtanas;
and thirty dwellings of piśācas. Furthermore, within eighty-four thousand cities, there are six thousand four hundred [dwellings].
Categorizing the abodes of persons and compiling them together, there are these ten classes of people. In this manner, all such [beings] repent for their retribution for transgressions.
Fifth, regarding the places of birth among the gods of the Desire Realm where they dwell: a person of wisdom contemplates that within the first Desire Realm, there are six heavens.
Among these sentient beings, they constantly delight in sensual desires and are entangled by craving for desire. The karmic fruits they receive differ and are not equal;
they give rise to painful sensations, or else the fruits are superior or inferior, being either high or low. As for those lower fruits:
Seeing the superior karmic retribution [of others], they feel shame, remorse, and humiliation, constantly giving rise to painful sensations.

Or, those who have come here due to merit cultivated in the past, now find their birth ending and their merit about to be exhausted; when they reflect in this way, they give rise to painful sensations.
Furthermore, due to various activities performed with diligent toil and hardship, one gives rise to painful sensations;
or, because beloved people and cherished objects are divided and scattered, one gives rise to painful sensations; or, when all the fruits and rewards of merit are completely exhausted.
Seeing a pleasant place, the mind gives rise to attachment and delight; yet being unable to go there, one experiences great suffering.

Furthermore, knowing that through such karmic actions one will swiftly fall into the evil realms among animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings, for this reason, one experiences even greater suffering.
Thus, regarding these various and boundless sufferings, one should repent for the retribution of one's transgressions.

As for the sixth realm, the heavens of the tainted form-realm (*rūpadhātu*), a person of wisdom who does not give rise to a mind of attachment and delight therein contemplates those sixteen abodes of the form-realm.
All the devas there have practiced worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) to attain birth in those places; since their causes [were thus conditioned],...
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are tainted dharmas (*sāsrava*). Because suffering has not yet been exhausted, one cannot attain the bliss of mental tranquility or the various other superior joys;

therefore, they are painful sensations. Furthermore, because one has not yet reached the further shore of happiness, one remains within this flow of suffering and does not know the path leading out of it.
For this reason, one has not yet attained [liberation] within the three evil destinies.
Liberation. Therefore, regarding the painful sensations [experienced] as the retribution for transgressions, one performs repentance.
Seventh, one further contemplates those sentient beings in the untainted (anāsrava) realm of form. Because they have thus cultivated untainted dhyāna, they dwell in that celestial realm;
yet, because they have not fully perfected the Eightfold Noble Path, they experience painful sensations. This is for the sake of desiring the Eightfold Noble Path.
Because they are not yet fully satisfied, they apply themselves with diligent skillful means; therefore, they experience painful sensations.

Because they have not yet attained the minds of all the stages of samādhi belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they give rise to painful sensations. Because those pratyekabuddhas have not yet attained mastery over the various dhāraṇīs, they give rise to painful sensations.
Regarding the objects of the three times of the Tathāgatas, because they have not yet attained mastery over them, they give rise to painful sensations. First.

The realm of all sentient beings is entirely suffering. Thus, within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), if sentient beings desire to enter parinirvāṇa with two heads, they will fully experience the various sufferings as described above. [This is] for the sake of repenting for karmic retribution.
Eighth, one contemplates that the gods of the formless realm do not give rise to the perception of pleasure. A person of wisdom contemplates the four types of celestial abodes in the formless realm;
because they are able to cultivate tainted (*sāsrava*) samādhi, they are born there. Since they have not yet attained liberation from all taints, suffering arises.
Furthermore, because they have not attained mastery over all stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), [suffering arises].

Birth is suffering. Because one is unable to hear the True Dharma of the Buddhas, birth is suffering. Because all cravings have not been utterly severed, one lacks mastery within the cycle of transmigration;
therefore, birth is suffering. Having ended one's life there, one fails to attain a superior rebirth and is instead born with wrong views;
such is great suffering. One has not yet [abandoned] all the afflictions and paths of action of the three evil realms.
To eternally sever such suffering of birth, which has not yet been transcended within all three evil realms—such is the suffering of birth.
We repent for these karmic retributions of sin.
Enshrouded by ignorance, we did not recognize the causes of sin within the three realms and five destinies; now that we have encountered this site of enlightenment, we [realize it].
Being able to awaken to this, I take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy and holy ones.
I burn incense and scatter flowers, confessing and repenting for my heavy karmic offenses without daring to conceal them.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, may the heavy karmic offenses of myself and the ocean of sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm be entirely purified.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for repentance and the eradication of sins: Oṃ sarvapāpam me kṣayaṃ kuru svāhā.
(Recite three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred eons are entirely swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose solely from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
I now repent of everything produced by my body, speech, and mind.
Having repented, I take refuge with all sincerity and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Proclamation: Listen, all you people, to these verses on impermanence from the Sūtras:
Within the span of a single human life, one harbors delusions for ten thousand years. At the gathering of the evening breaths, the heart is seized;
at midnight, the life-force is exhausted. Relatives and kin all abandon one and depart; wealth and possessions are taken by others as they please.
Relying solely upon one’s own roots of goodness as provisions for the perilous path.

the first fifty of the hundred assemblies of the Buddha’s congregation, presided over by the hundred seas of beings.
With all reverence, we pay homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
All members of this assembly kneel with their right knees on the ground and, holding incense and flowers, make offerings according to the Dharma.
May this ocean-like cloud of offerings pervade the worlds of the ten directions, interlaced by a million vajras, and adorned with a million canopies of flowers and a million clouds of incense.
A million precious canopies covered it from above. A million flower canopies, garland canopies, incense canopies, and jewel canopies were arranged in rows all around.
A million rays of light shone forth in brilliance. A million kings of the Yāma heaven paid homage with reverent prostrations;
a million Brahmā kings leaped for joy; and a million bodhisattvas extolled and praised [the assembly]. A hundred...
The myriad celestial musicians each played a million kinds of Dharma-sounds, continuing without interruption.

A million kinds of flower-clouds, a million kinds of garland-clouds, a million kinds of cloud-like ornaments, and a million kinds of clothing-clouds completely covered and overspread the surroundings.
A million clouds of mani-jewels radiate brilliant light. With such various articles of offering, one constantly makes offerings.

May the ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages within the infinitely layered Indra-nets receive these clouds of offerings and transform them into luminous terraces, vast as boundless realms, immeasurable and inexhaustible, performing the work of the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, with all due reverence,
they next present the most excellent vast oceans of the nature of precious lattices and jewels, along with mountains of the seven treasures and other such sublime things.
I issue forth such clouds of offerings and present them to all the Buddhas. Oṃ sarva-tathāgata-arcana-pracarya-samaya-hṛdaya-hūṃ.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "There is a dhāraṇī called the 'Spell of Immeasurable Varieties,' which can accomplish all things and possesses great efficacy.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ sīmala sīmala maimada sigrāmaha liṅga hūṃ."
Next is the mudrā and mantra of Ākāśagarbha:
Oṃ a ma ā ba dzra ma ṇi pa ṇa ma ma hā ti ṭa ta tā me laṅ kye ḍṅ sa man da pra sa ra hūṃ.

The Brahma-voice praises that the Buddha’s form-body is not the Buddha, and that his voice is likewise so; yet one does not perceive the Buddha’s power of spiritual transformations apart from the form-body—
those of little wisdom cannot know this, for it is the true realm of all Buddhas.
Having long cultivated pure deeds, one is thus able to understand this: The state of the Perfectly Awakened Tathāgata neither comes nor goes;
His pure and wondrous form-body appears through the power of supernormal faculties.
(Thus) he spoke directly in praise of the Buddha.
If you wish to know the mind of the Buddhas, first contemplate the Buddha’s wisdom. The Buddha’s wisdom has no place of dependence;
like space, it has nothing upon which to rely. The various pleasures of sentient beings, as well as all the wisdoms of skillful means, all depend upon the Buddha’s wisdom.
The Buddha’s wisdom has no dependence, [far less] that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
And the liberations of all Buddhas All rely upon the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases;
The Buddha-wisdom is likewise so. It gives birth to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
Without increase and without decrease, Without arising and without exhaustion. Like water flowing secretly beneath the earth, One never fails to find it when sought.
Without thought and without exhaustion, His power pervades the ten directions.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise so, Universally present within the hearts of all sentient beings. If there are those who diligently practice, They will swiftly attain the radiance of wisdom.

In the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, next is the Repentance for Eating Meat:
I take refuge in the inexhaustible Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha like a celestial net; in Vairocana Tathāgata; and in Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.
The assembly of noble ones gathered like an ocean, and the mundane and supramundane deities, by virtue of their compassionate original vows, emit great radiance that illuminates this Dharma assembly.

May they bear witness, protect, and keep us in mind; may they look upon us with pity and grant their acceptance. I pray that for myself and the ocean of all sentient beings, from beginningless time...
Up until this very moment, the ocean of karma remains inexhaustible, with its Indra-net of interwoven layers. I now openly confess and repent for all karmic offenses of eating meat.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "O Mahāmati Bodhisattva, there are immeasurable causes and conditions regarding all meats; among these, the Bodhisattva..."
You should give rise to compassion and must not eat them. Mahāmati, I shall now describe to you a small portion of this:
all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been wandering incessantly through birth and death;

there has never been one who has not been your father, mother, brother, son, daughter, or relative, nor even a friend, a loved one, or a servant. As births change, they receive the forms of birds and beasts.
"Equal to one's own body. How could one take [flesh] from among them and eat it? Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all sentient beings as being the same as his own body;
mindful that flesh comes from the life of a living being, how could he eat it?
Mahāmati, even when rākṣasas and others hear me speak thus, they should still abstain from meat, let alone those who delight in the Dharma. Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva..."
O Mahāsattva, wherever you are born, you should contemplate all sentient beings as your own kin, even regarding them with loving-kindness as if they were your only child.
For this reason, you should not eat any meat whatsoever. Mahāmati, there are those who sell meat at crossroads and in marketplaces.
Or they may sell the flesh of dogs, horses, humans, oxen, and so forth for the sake of profit.
How can such impure things be eaten? Mahāmati, all meats are produced from semen, blood, and filth;
how can those who seek purity take them as food? Mahāmati, when sentient beings see those who eat meat, they are all struck with terror.
"O Mahāmati, how can one who cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) eat meat?
For example, Mahāmati, when hunters, *caṇḍālas*, fishermen, bird-catchers, and other such wicked people are seen by dogs, they bark in alarm; when seen by beasts, they flee in terror.

All sentient beings—whether flying in the air, moving on water, or dwelling on land—if they see such a person, will all think: 'The breath of this person is like that of a *rākṣasa*; he has now come here...'"
"Upon reaching this point, they will surely kill me. For the sake of protecting one's life, all flee and avoid it. Those who eat meat are likewise the same.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva practicing the conduct of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) should not eat meat. Mahāmati, as for those who eat meat..."
The body becomes foul-smelling and impure; one’s ill repute spreads abroad; and the wise and virtuous will not associate with or show intimacy toward such a person.
For these reasons, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, as for blood and flesh, they are discarded by the various sages and are not consumed by the assembly of holy ones.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva acts thus to protect the faith of sentient beings and to cause them to [enter] the Buddha-dharma.
One should not give rise to censure or slander, for out of compassion one ought not to eat meat.
Mahāmati, if my disciples were to consume meat, it would cause all people in the world to harbor censure and say:
"How can these śramaṇas, who practice pure conduct, abandon the flavors enjoyed by celestial beings and sages, yet wander about like wicked beasts with their bellies full of meat?"
In the world, this causes all sentient beings to harbor fear and terror, destroys pure conduct, and leads them to lose the path of the śramaṇa.

Therefore, you should know that within the Buddha-dharma there is no practice of such subjugation. Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Bodhisattva protects them so that they do not give rise to such thoughts;
thus, one should not eat meat. Mahāmati, it is like burning human flesh: its odor is foul and putrid.
It is no different from eating the remains of burnt meat; how, then, could there be a distinction between eating it and not eating it?

Therefore, those who delight in purity should not eat meat. Mahāmati, whether they are good men or women practicing in silence among graves, under trees, or in forest hermitages (araṇya)—whether they abide in a mind of loving-kindness, maintain incantations, seek liberation, or aspire [to the higher realms]—[they should refrain from meat].
In the Mahāyāna, because of eating meat, all obstacles arise and one cannot achieve accomplishment. Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to benefit both self and others should not eat meat.
Mahāmati, for one who eats meat, the mere sight of its form and color gives rise to a mind that craves its flavor.
How then can a bodhisattva, who regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were his own body, look upon such things?
and thus conceive the notion that it is food. For this reason, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, those who eat meat are shunned by the devas;
their breath is constantly foul; they experience unrest in sleep and dreams; upon waking, they are filled with anxiety and dread; yakṣas and evil spirits steal away their vital energy;
their minds are frequently seized by terror; they know no satiety in eating; they increase their illnesses and are prone to sores and scabs; they are perpetually...
They are being devoured by various worms, yet they are unable to develop a profound sense of revulsion toward their food.
Mahāmati, I have always said that whatever one eats and chews should be regarded as the flesh of one's own child; if this applies even to other foods, how could I permit my disciples to eat meat?
Mahāmati, meat is not wholesome; meat is impure. It gives rise to all manner of evils and destroys all merits. It is rejected by all the sages and holy ones;
how then could I permit my disciples to eat it? If anyone were to say that I permit its consumption, Mahāmati, such a person slanders me.
Mahāmati, you should know that pure and excellent food consists of non-glutinous rice, millet, large and small wheat, and beans.
Ghee, honey, rock sugar, and other such items as these were permitted by the Buddhas of the past and are what I proclaim.
Within my lineage, those sons and daughters of good family who harbor pure faith and have long planted roots of virtue, regarding their bodies, lives, and wealth—

They give rise to no greedy attachment and regard all beings with compassion as they do their own bodies; such food is fit for those people, not for those of evil habits whose nature is like that of tigers and wolves.
Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhaja who was addicted to the taste of meat and ate various kinds of flesh.
Not stopping at this, he eventually came to eat human beings, [causing distress] among his ministers and subjects.
Unable to endure it, they all rebelled and deserted him, causing him to lose his royal throne and undergo great suffering and distress.
Mahāmati, Śakra-devendra, while dwelling in the position of the Heavenly King, due to the residual habit of eating meat in the past, transformed himself into a hawk and pursued a pigeon.
At that time, I was a king named Śibi. Out of compassion for the pigeon, I cut flesh from my own body to save its life.
Mahāmati, if even Śakra’s residual habits still cause distress to sentient beings, how much more so for others who lack shame and constantly eat meat?
You should know that eating meat causes self-affliction and afflicts others; therefore, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, in the past there was a certain king...
While riding out on horseback for a hunt, his horse became startled and bolted, entering a perilous mountain wilderness.

Having no way to return and being far removed from human habitation, he encountered a female lion with whom he dwelt; he subsequently engaged in unseemly conduct with her and begot several offspring. The eldest among them—
His name was Pāda (Ban-zu). Later, he became king and ruled over seven hundred million households. Due to the residual habit of eating meat, he would not eat anything that was not flesh.
At first he ate birds and beasts; later, he even went so far as to eat humans. All the sons and daughters born to him were rākṣasas. After this body passed away, [he was reborn...]
Furthermore, they will be reborn among lions, jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, eagles, vultures, and the like;

though they may seek a human body, it can never be obtained, let alone the path to nirvāṇa that transcends birth and death. Mahāmati, for those who eat meat, there are such immeasurable faults as these.
By renouncing and abstaining from it, one attains great merit. Yet the ignorant and foolish do not understand such benefits and harms; therefore—
I shall now explain this for you: no meat whatsoever should be eaten. Mahāmati, those who kill living beings do so largely for human consumption;
if people did not eat it, there would be no killing. Therefore, eating meat is a crime equal to that of killing.
How strange it is that those in the world are so attached to the taste of flesh! They will even take the flesh from the bodies of human beings and eat it; how much more so for birds and beasts?
Because they are attached to its flavor, they employ extensive means, setting out nets and snares everywhere.
Whether moving through water, on land, or flying in the air, all are slaughtered. Even if they do not eat it themselves, they act in this way out of greed for its value.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are people in the world who lack compassion and are devoted solely to cruelty, like rākṣasas.
When they see sentient beings with flourishing bodies, they immediately conceive the thought of meat and say, "This is fit for craving.
Mahāmati, there is no meat in the world that is not killed by oneself, nor killed by another, nor where one does not suspect it was killed; yet such [meat] is eaten. For this reason...

Therefore, I permit the śrāvakas to eat such meat. Mahāmati, in future ages there will be foolish people who, having gone forth within my Dharma, will falsely expound the Vinaya, corrupt and disturb the True Dharma, and slander me by saying that I allow the eating of meat and have eaten it myself.
Mahāmati, if I had permitted the śrāvakas to eat meat, I would not be... [the Tathāgata].
For those who abide in a mind of loving-kindness, who practice contemplation, who observe the dhūta ascetic practices, and who are intent upon the Mahāyāna—
how should one exhort these sons and daughters of good family to conceive of all sentient beings as their only child and to abstain from all meat?

Mahāmati, when I have established prohibitions against ten kinds of meat in various places while permitting three kinds, this was intended as a gradual restriction for the purpose of bringing about total cessation.
Regarding this practice, within this very sutra, all meat—whether from animals that have died naturally or been killed by others—is entirely prohibited.
Mahāmati, I have never permitted my disciples to eat meat; I do not permit it now, nor shall I ever permit it.
Mahāmati, for any renunciant, the consumption of meat is entirely impure. Mahāmati, if there are deluded people who slander me by saying:
"Those who come to request permission to eat meat, or those who eat it themselves, should be known as persons entangled by evil karma;

they will certainly fall forever into states that are not beneficial. Mahāmati, even my noble disciples do not consume the coarse food of ordinary beings, much less the impure food of flesh and blood. Mahāmati, [this applies to] the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas..."
“Sāḥ. Even [bodhisattvas] still rely on the food of Dharma; how much more so the Tathāgata? Mahāmati, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not a body that consumes mixed food.
Mahāmati, I have severed all afflictions; I have washed away all habitual tendencies; I have skillfully discerned all mental wisdoms.
With great compassion that is impartial, I regard all sentient beings as if they were my only child. How could I [partake of ordinary food]?”
"It is impossible that I would permit my śrāvaka disciples to eat the flesh of their own children, let alone eat it themselves. For one to make such a claim is not possible.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
All have once been one's own kin; grown from manifold impurities, they terrify all sentient beings.
Therefore, one should not eat any meat or onions, leeks, garlic, or various liquors—such impure things as these the practitioner should avoid, and likewise always abstain from sesame oil.
And as for beds with many holes, because of those tiny insects within them, one should be greatly terrified.
When one becomes negligent regarding food and drink, negligence gives rise to wrong thoughts; from those thoughts, greed arises.
Therefore, one should not eat. Because wrong thoughts give rise to greed, the mind becomes intoxicated by greed.
With hearts intoxicated by long-standing desire, one is not liberated from birth and death.
To kill sentient beings for profit and to take their flesh for wealth—both are evil karmas. Upon death, one falls into the Raurava Hell.
If one neither contemplates, teaches, nor seeks [meat], these three types are called "pure. In this world, such meat does not exist.
I condemn those who eat [flesh], who devour one another; upon death they fall among the foul-smelling and crazed beasts of prey. Therefore, one should not eat it.
Those born into such lineages as hunters, caṇḍālas, butchers, and rākṣasas—all these are the retribution for eating meat.
In the *Hastikakṣya*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Aṅgulimālīya*, as well as in this *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, I have strictly prohibited the eating of meat.
Those who eat it without shame or remorse will be perpetually insane throughout their successive lives.
It is something loathed by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; I have previously declared that meat is forbidden on account of what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Having already abandoned all meat because of its evil habituation, the fool engages in false discrimination;
just as craving obstructs liberation, so too do meat and the like.
Those who consume it cannot enter the Noble Path; in future ages, sentient beings will speak of meat with delusion.
Regarding this purity and lack of fault, the Buddha permitted us to eat such meat. Even pure meat should be regarded like medicine or like the flesh of one's own child.
Therefore, the practitioner who knows moderation in begging and dwells in a mind of loving-kindness—I say that such a person is always free from aversion toward lions, tigers, and wolves.
One should dwell and travel together [with the Sangha]; eating meat is contrary to liberation.
Furthermore, it violates the outward signs of a noble one and causes living beings to feel fear; therefore, one should not eat it.
If one abstains from all things such as alcohol and meat, one will surely be born among the worthy and holy, possessing abundant wealth and wisdom.
Furthermore, the *Ārya-māṃsabhakṣaṇa-vivarjana-sūtra* states:
"It would be better to burn oneself or gouge out one's own eyes than to take the life of another to eat their flesh.
The Buddhas have expounded the Dharma of compassion; within that Dharma, it is taught that one who practices loving-kindness [must refrain from meat]."
It is permissible to extract the brain and strike the bones, but one should not eat the flesh of those sentient beings.
If one violates the Buddha-dharma by eating meat, that person’s cultivation of loving-kindness will not be perfected;
they will constantly suffer from short lifespans and many illnesses, sinking into the cycle of birth and death without attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: Bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, why does the Tathāgata not permit the eating of meat?
The Buddha said, "Those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion. Kāśyapa spoke again, "For what reason did the Tathāgata previously permit bhikṣus to eat the three kinds of pure meat?
The Buddha said, "These three kinds of pure meat were permitted according to specific circumstances."
[The Buddha] gradually established the prohibitions. Furthermore, for what causes and conditions did he not permit the eating of the ten kinds of impure meat?
As for the "ten kinds," they are: human, snake, elephant, horse, donkey, dog, lion, pig, fox, and monkey.
Moreover, for what reason were even nine kinds of pure meat not permitted? The Buddha said: Those were also [prohibited] because of matters that had to be addressed gradually.

Next, I shall establish the regulations. All the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata each have a distinct underlying intention. Because of these distinct intentions, I permitted the consumption of the three kinds of pure meat;
because of a different intention, I prohibited ten kinds of meat; and because of yet another intention, I prohibited all meat whatsoever, including that from animals that died naturally.
From this day forward, I decree for my disciples that they must no longer consume any meat at all. O virtuous sons...
My son, such pure food as this, even a bodhisattva would not eat; how much less, then, should one eat meat?

Regarding the repentance for the retribution of transgressions, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* further states: "After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Dharma-ending age, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish."

"In the world, some say that by eating meat one attains the path to Bodhi. Ānanda, when I permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat, those meats were all produced through my supernatural power;
they originally possessed no life-force. You, O brāhmaṇa, live in a land where the ground is largely damp and humid."

Furthermore, it is covered with sand and gravel where grass and weeds do not grow. It is through the empowerment of my great compassionate supernatural power, and by virtue of my great kindness and pity, that these are provisionally called "flesh" so that you may obtain their flavor.

How can it be that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings yet call themselves sons of the Śākya, widely practicing greed and defilement while devouring meat, act as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and cause all sentient beings to fall into the views of craving?
We have fallen into a pit and lost the path to Bodhi. We repent for this karmic retribution of our sins.
Enveloped by ignorance, we failed to recognize the sinful causes of eating meat; only now, having encountered this place of practice, do we finally awaken to this truth.
We take refuge in Vairocana Tathāgata and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy and holy ones. We burn incense and scatter flowers.

I openly confess and repent for the karmic offenses of eating meat, not daring to conceal them. By this cause and condition, may the grave sins of eating meat committed by myself and the ocean of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm be entirely purified.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for repentance and the eradication of transgressions: Oṃ sarva-pāpa-m-ucchedana-dahana-vināśaya svāhā.
(Recite three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred eons are entirely swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
I now confess all that has arisen from my body, speech, and mind.
Having confessed, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Proclamation: Listen, all of you, to these verses on impermanence from the Sūtras:

The unsurpassed World-Honored Ones, The Pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas— Since they constantly relinquish their impermanent bodies, How much more so must ordinary people? Parents, wives, and children, Brothers, and kinsmen as well.
Contemplating the separation between birth and death, how could one not feel sorrow and lamentation?

The Sixteenth Session of the Tiantai Practitioner of Teaching and Contemplation, the Śramaṇa Zhengzhi, for the Purpose of Stabilizing the Mind:
With all reverence, I pay homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
All these people knelt with their right knees on the ground and, holding fragrant flowers, made offerings according to the Dharma. They made this aspiration:

"May this ocean-like cloud of offerings pervade the worlds of the ten directions—incalculable flowers, incalculable incenses, incalculable garlands, incalculable ointments and powdered incenses, robes and precious jewels, banners, pennants, and exquisite parasols, as well as all manner of ornaments, each in incalculable quantities."
I shall use these to make offerings. With such various articles of offering as these, I constantly perform worship.

May the ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages—their Indra-nets layered upon one another—receive these clouds of offerings and transform them into platforms of light, vast as boundless realms, immeasurable and inexhaustible, vowing to perform the work of the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, with all-encompassing reverence,
they next present the most supreme [offerings],
such as oceans of vast self-natures of precious lattices and jewel-gems, and mountains composed of the seven treasures.
I bring forth such clouds of offerings as these and present them to all the Buddhas. Oṃ sarvam-tathāgata-ākarṣaṇa-samāja-spharaṇa-samaye hūṃ.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "There is a dhāraṇī called the 'Spell of Immeasurable Varieties,' which can accomplish all things and possesses great power.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ sīmala sīmala mīmada sigrāmaha liṅga hūṃ."

Oṃ a ma ā bhuñja mane pade mama kīli kīlaya tathāgatamūrdhni saṃtrāsayāpaya sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ.
With Brahma-sounds they praise the Buddha’s body and all its marks; All infinite Buddhas appear therein,
universally entering every single atom Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field— Such are all those lands.
They are able to cause all lands and all miraculous deeds to appear within a single thought-moment, and within every single atom;
they manifest them all within one world-system. Such is the power of the Bodhisattvas—thus he directly praises the Buddha.
The World-Honored One sits at the site of enlightenment, Pure and of great radiance;
Like a thousand suns rising to shine universally upon the realm of space. After immeasurable billions of kalpas, A Guide has now appeared in the world;
He is honored and revered by all— Behold the radiance of the Buddha!
The emanated Buddhas are inconceivable; within all their palaces, they dwell in tranquil meditative absorption.
Behold the Buddha’s spiritual power: from his pores emerge clouds of flames that illuminate the world with inexhaustible radiance.
You should contemplate the Buddha’s body, its net of light being utterly pure.
Manifesting forms and all else, pervading the ten directions, Your wondrous voice fills the world;
all who hear it rejoice. In accordance with the languages of all sentient beings, You praise the virtues of the Buddha.
Wherever the World-Honored One’s light shines, All sentient beings find peace and happiness; All suffering is completely extinguished.
Their hearts gave rise to great joy as they beheld the assembly of bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions.
They all released clouds of maṇi jewels and, appearing before the Buddha, offered praise. From the site of enlightenment, wondrous sounds emerged;
these sounds were exceedingly deep and far-reaching, capable of extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings through the Buddha’s spiritual power.
All paid him homage with reverence, their hearts filled with great joy; together they gazed upon the World-Honored One before them, looking up to the Dharma King.

To Vairocana Buddha,

throughout the ten directions, I take refuge; may my transgressions be extinguished and my pure faith increase, and may I be born within the ocean of the Flower Treasury and the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Next, for the confession of the Four Noble Truths:
I take refuge in the inexhaustible Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha jewels of the Indra-net; Vairocana Tathāgata;

and the assembly of holy beings in the ocean-like gathering of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, as well as all mundane and supramundane deities. By the power of your compassionate original vows, may you emit great radiance to illuminate this dharma assembly.
May you bear witness and protect us with your mindful attention; may you compassionately embrace us.

I pray that I and the ocean of all sentient beings, from beginningless time until this very moment, shall confess and repent for all offenses committed through delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths.
As for the Four Noble Truths, the four teachings—Zang (Tripitaka), Tong (Shared), Bie (Distinct), and Yuan (Perfect)—all take the Four Noble Truths as their foundation.

Even the Shared and Distinct Teachings all expound upon the Four Noble Truths; however, here we specifically designate the Perfect Teaching to clarify the Four Noble Truths, which thereby encompasses the other teachings as well.
As the Sūtra says: "O Bodhisattva, this is the Noble Truth of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering; this is..."

The Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. This is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering. He thoroughly knows the conventional truth; he thoroughly knows the ultimate truth;
he thoroughly knows the truth of characteristics; he thoroughly knows the truth of establishment; he thoroughly knows the truth of phenomena; he thoroughly knows the truth of arising;

he thoroughly knows the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising; he thoroughly knows the truth of the knowledge of entering the path; and he thoroughly knows the sequence of all the bodhisattva stages.
He accomplishes the truths, up to and including the truth of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

This bodhisattva knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) because he brings joy to sentient beings according to their mental inclinations; he knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) because he penetrates all true marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

One knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*) because one awakens to the specific and general characteristics of phenomena; one knows the truth of differentiation (*viśeṣasatya*) because one understands the distinctions between the various states of all phenomena;

one knows the truth of establishment (*siddhisatya*) because one skillfully discriminates the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; one knows the truth of things (*vastusatya*) because one awakens to the suffering and affliction of body and mind;

one knows the truth of birth (*janmasatya*) because one awakens to the continuity of rebirth in the various realms of existence; and [one knows the truth of cessation] because all feverish afflictions are ultimately extinguished.

He knows the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, because it gives rise to non-duality. He knows the truth of the knowledge of entering the path, because he has perfectly awakened to all modes of activity (*ākāra*).
He skillfully knows the successive continuity and accomplishment of all the stages of a bodhisattva, up to the truth of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
He knows what is not so by the power of wisdom through faith and understanding; he knows such truths by the power of ultimate wisdom.
Having discerned and known as they truly are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)— which are false, deceptive, and delusive toward the foolish— the Bodhisattva, at that time,
increases his great compassion for all sentient beings and gives rise to the light of great loving-kindness. Attaining such power of wisdom,
he does not abandon any sentient being but constantly seeks the Buddha-wisdom, observing all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are.
Regarding the future limit, one knows that it arises from ignorance and craving in the past, resulting in the cycle of birth and death.

Within the dwelling of the aggregates, one is unable to move beyond or emerge; thus the mass of suffering increases. There is no self, no life-principle, no nourisher, and no further appropriator of a body in future states of existence.
Being free from "I" and "mine," one knows that the past and future limits are likewise thus—all are without [intrinsic reality].
There is false attachment; its exhaustion is liberation. Whether things exist or do not exist, one knows them all as they truly are.
We ordinary persons are foolish and ignorant, and are most pitiable. Countless bodies have already perished, are currently perishing, and will perish;
though they are thus utterly extinguished, we cannot conceive of weariness toward the body, but instead further increase the mechanical affairs of suffering. Following [this cycle]...

In the stream of birth and death, they are unable to turn back from the house of the aggregates; they do not seek liberation. They do not recognize the fear and sorrow of the four great poisonous serpents.
They cannot extract the arrows of pride and views. They cannot extinguish the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion.
They cannot shatter the darkness of ignorance. They cannot dry up the great ocean of craving and desire. They do not seek the Great [Vehicle] of the Ten Powers.

O Holy Teacher, we sentient beings have not emerged from the dense forest of Māra’s intent; within the ocean of birth and death, we are adrift and drowned by the waves of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
We undergo such suffering, solitary, destitute, and oppressed by hardship;
without rescue, without reliance, without an island, without shelter, without a guide, and without eyes; shrouded by ignorance and enveloped in the darkness of cataracts.
We have been shrouded by ignorance; we were unable to realize or know the profound meaning of the Noble Truths. Now, having encountered this site of enlightenment, we have finally awakened to it.
We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy sages.

Burning incense and scattering flowers, we openly confess and repent for our immeasurable karmic offenses arising from our failure to understand the Noble Truths, not daring to conceal them. By virtue of this...
Through these causes and conditions, may all the sinful karma of myself and the ocean of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm be entirely purified.
Next is the mantra for the seal of repentance that extinguishes sin: Oṃ sarvapa-pame-spu-ta-na-ha-da-ma-dra-ya svāhā.

The Brahma-voice praises the Tathāgata’s great majestic power, Accomplished through the vows of Samantabhadra; Throughout all lands,
his wondrous voice reaches everywhere, Throughout countless billions of kalpas, And within every atom-sized world-system.
The deeds performed in the past are all fully expounded by his wondrous voice; throughout the lands as numerous as atoms in the ten directions, networks of light pervade everywhere.
Within every ray of light there is a Buddha, universally transforming all living beings as he directly praises the Buddha with straightforward words.
Just as the realm of the mind is immeasurable, so too is the realm of all Buddhas;
just as the realm of the mind arises from the intellect, one should observe the Buddha-realm in this same way.
Just as a dragon does not leave its original place, yet pours down great rain through the power of its mind, so too should one contemplate the Buddha-realm.
Although the rain has no place from which it comes or to which it goes, it fills and saturates all according to the mind of the dragon;
so too is the Muni of Ten Powers: coming from nowhere and going nowhere, yet if one possesses a pure mind, one beholds his body, equal in measure to the Dharma-realm, entering into every pore.
Just as the ocean’s rare treasures are immeasurable, so too are sentient beings and the great earth.
The nature of water is of a single flavor, equal and without distinction; yet among sentient beings, each receives benefit.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: all that exists therein is immeasurable.

Slaves, and even various necessities for life. At that time, if there is a precept-breaking bhikṣu who accepts what others have discarded—even a single flower or a single fruit—that evil bhikṣu, due to his ignorance, receives the various items offered by those with pure hearts and will incur a great evil retribution.
In this present life, he shall receive four kinds of evil retributions. What are the four? First—
First, their evil reputation will spread far and wide, circulating throughout the ten directions.

Second, their parents, teachers, elders, brothers, kinsmen, servants, and relatives will all be scattered and separated from them. Third, they will contract a grave illness and lie amidst filth and excrement;
as the signs of their retribution manifest, they will die in agony. Fourth, their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and all their possessions will be taken by the five families.
This is called the fourfold evil retribution. In future lives, one will further incur four kinds of great and evil karmic results. What are these four?
First, when the body disintegrates and life ends, one falls into the great hells. Second, within the hells, one undergoes diligent suffering for a long time;
once the hellish existence has ended, one is reborn among animals or in the realm of hungry ghosts, where one is born without hands.
As retribution, they dwell in desolate wildernesses devoid of water for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, undergoing all manner of suffering and hardship.
Third, when their lives there end, they are born among venomous snakes; receiving the retribution of being sightless, they pass through immeasurable ages, eating nothing but earth.
Fourth, when their lives there end, they are born among humans, yet fall into the world of the five turbidities and do not encounter any Buddhas. Regarding...
In that world, although they obtain a human body, they are perpetually without eyes, nor do they have hands or feet.
They dwell in the wilderness, subsisting only on the filthy food discarded by humans, which is never sufficient. They cannot share their dwelling with other people.
When their lives there end, they fall again into hell; it is difficult for them to escape from the three evil realms. Why is this? Because of that [lack of] merit...
If a man or a woman of good family, with a pure mind, gives away fields, houses, gardens, forests, clothing, medicinal decoctions, and various other things,

desiring only to make offerings to bhikṣus who live according to the Dharma, yet a precept-breaker receives these gifts from others solely for his own bodily sustenance and does not give them to a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts in accordance with the Dharma—
for this reason, he incurs such a transgression. Furthermore, regarding the breaking of the precepts...
Such a person has long dwelt in birth and death, fully experiencing all manner of suffering. Although they have obtained a human body, they do not encounter the era of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are inconceivable and difficult to encounter. Those who break the precepts sever the mother of the Dharma;
they take no pleasure in diligence and do not seek to see or hear the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. For these reasons, they do not encounter a Buddha.
World-Honored One, those evil bhikṣus will, in a future age, receive such great and evil retributions as these; we now repent of them all.
Furthermore, if there are kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, or śūdras who, out of lack of faith, seize what has been given by others.
Furthermore, that foolish person shall obtain twenty kinds of great evil retributions within their present body. What are these twenty?
First, all the devas and benevolent spirits will completely abandon them. Second, they will have a great evil reputation spread throughout the ten directions.
Third, one's kinsmen and acquaintances will turn against and alienate oneself. Fourth, hateful and malicious people will gather together.
Fifth, all of one's wealth and possessions will be completely lost. Sixth, the mind will become deranged and deluded, constantly filled with agitation and turmoil.
Seventh, the sense faculties are incomplete. Eighth, one sleeps in unrest. Ninth, one is constantly hungry and thirsty.
Tenth, whatever food is consumed is like poison. Eleventh, all those one loves are separated from one.
Twelfth, those with whom one works together are frequently engaged in strife and contention. Thirteenth, parents, brothers, wives, and children, as well as servants...
13. Her female servants do not believe her words. 14. All her secret and concealed matters are made public by her acquaintances and close friends.
15. All her wealth and possessions are dispersed among the five families. 16.
She constantly encounters serious illness, with no one to look after her. 17. The necessities for her livelihood are never to her satisfaction. 18. [The eighteenth...]
Their physical forms are withered and emaciated. Nineteenth, they endure toil and suffering for a long time, finding it difficult to escape.
Twentieth, they constantly dwell amidst filth and impurity until the end of their lives. Such foolish people obtain these twenty kinds of evil retributions within their present bodies.
After their lives end, they fall into the Avīci Hell, where they suffer for one kalpa, eating [only] hunger.
They swallow iron balls and drink molten copper; they use hot iron sheets as clothing.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, everything they encounter is a mass of fire. Blazing flames from the six directions interpenetrate one another.
Those sinners undergo all such various sufferings within the Avīci Hell. When their lives there end, they are reborn in the Maghācarada preta realm.
Among the hungry ghosts, they dwell in desolate wildernesses where there is no water. From birth, they are without eyes and lack both hands and feet.
Hot winds blow from the four directions, striking their bodies with a pain as agonizing as knives and swords. They writhe upon the ground, undergoing great suffering and distress.
Their fat, marrow, and grease flow out as if they were being placed in a hot cauldron. Their spirits are frantic and disordered, emitting terrible cries as they endure all these torments.

Undergoing such hundreds of thousands of kinds of suffering for immeasurable years, they eventually die and are reborn within the great ocean, receiving a body of flesh that is vast in size, measuring a full hundred yojanas.

Yet, at a distance of one yojana from the exterior of their bodies, the place where those sinners dwell is filled with hot water resembling molten copper. There they suffer for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years.
Such various kinds of suffering and affliction are no different from those in the hells.
When their lives there come to an end, they suddenly manifest a transformation-body in the wilderness marshes of Jambudvīpa; its form is like a mass of flesh, resembling a great mountain.
Hot winds blow from the four directions, burning its body, while birds and beasts compete to devour it for immeasurable years. Thus it is said.
Then their life ends, and they fall back into hell. Again, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, they undergo all manner of sufferings.
Only after their life there ends are they born among the hungry ghosts (preta), even with bodies such as mere lumps of flesh, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years.

Wandering through the cycle of rebirth, they fully experience all sufferings. When their transgressions gradually diminish, they emerge to become human beings, yet are born in a land where no Buddha resides.
In this turbid kalpa, they were blind from birth, their faculties incomplete, their physical forms ugly and loathsome, such that people took no pleasure in seeing them;
now they all repent.
The Buddha said to King Bimbisāra: "Great King, such sinners as these shall, in a future world, obtain [such results]..."

Such are the great evil karmic retributions. Why is this? Because those bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma practice according to the Dharma, while those with faith provide them with all manner of abundant resources;
yet these [faithful] give such things to wicked bhikṣus and foolish people, who seize them for their own use.
Consequently, they obtain these various evil retributions. We now repent of all of this.
We have been shrouded by ignorance and failed to recognize the causes of our transgressions. Now that we have encountered this site of enlightenment, we are finally able to awaken to this knowledge.

We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy sages. Burning incense and scattering flowers, we openly confess and repent for the karmic offenses committed by the monastic and lay communities;
we dare not conceal them. By virtue of these causes and conditions, may I and the entire dharma-realm...
May the ocean of sentient beings be purified of all transgressions and grave offenses against the Dharma.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for repentance and the eradication of sins: Oṃ sarvapa pame svadana dharaya svāhā.
(One should recite this three times:
The sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas Are all swept away in a single thought-moment, Just as fire burns dry grass until nothing remains.
All the evil karma I have created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion,
Produced by my body, speech, and mind— I now repent it all. Having repented,
I take refuge with a sincere heart in the essence of the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Announcement: May the assembly listen to these verses on impermanence from the Sūtra:
Whatever worldly pleasures there may be, And whatever pleasure born of desire, Do not equal even one-sixteenth part Of the internal bliss of dhyāna.
The bliss of dhyāna is supreme; The pure Dharma brings liberation from birth and death.
The exhaustion of craving is the foremost bliss; it is the ultimate bliss from which there is no falling back.
For one who practices with contentment and is free from fear, there is no seeking; such is the bliss of meditative concentration.
There is no other bliss that can compare to it. One who is not bound by craving and harbors no doubt will cross over the ocean of existence.

following the "Chapter on the Names of Buddhas," concerning the Buddha-assemblies of the ten realms beyond the Sahā world.
With all reverence, we pay homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
May all these members of the assembly kneel with their right knees on the ground, solemnly holding incense and flowers, making offerings according to the Dharma.

May this ocean-like cloud of offerings pervade the worlds of the ten directions, adorned with every kind of incense, adorned with every kind of garland, and adorned with every kind of powdered incense.
Adorned with all manner of jewel ornaments, all manner of banner ornaments, all manner of precious silk streamer ornaments,
and all manner of balustrade ornaments— constantly making offerings with such decorative implements in infinite, overlapping layers like Indra’s net.

May all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the entire ocean-like assembly accept this offering. May these clouds serve as luminous altars, extending beyond boundless realms, immeasurable and inexhaustible, and may they perform the work of the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, they paid all homage.
Next, they presented the most excellent vast oceans of the nature of precious lattices and jewels, along with mountains of the seven treasures and other such supreme things.
I bring forth such clouds of offerings as these and present them to all the Buddhas. Oṃ sarva-tathāgata-arcanābhyudgate samantāvalokite svāhā hūṃ.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "There is a dhāraṇī called the 'Spell of Immeasurable Varieties,' which can accomplish all things and possesses great efficacy.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ sīmala sīmala mīmada sigrāmaha liṅkva hūṃ."

The Brahma-voice praises the Tathāgata as supreme and peerless, Profound and ineffable, transcending the path of language,
pure as space. Behold the Lion among Men and his power of sovereign spiritual transformations!
Having already transcended conceptualization, yet causing it to be seen through conceptualization, the Teacher has expounded the profound and subtle Dharma.
For this reason, he manifests this peerless body; I speak these direct words in praise of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is a great ocean of wisdom. He possesses four kinds of great jewels of wisdom, fully endowed with immeasurable majesty, virtue, and radiance.
The light of these jewels of wisdom touches all bodhisattvas, even causing them to attain the great wisdom of a Tathāgata.
What are these four? They are: the great jewel of wisdom that extinguishes all waves of distracted wholesome states; [the second is] the removal of one...
The great wisdom-treasure of detachment from all dharmas; the great wisdom-treasure of the universally illuminating light of wisdom;

the great wisdom-treasure of boundless merit equal to that of the Tathāgata. O Bodhisattvas, when practicing and accumulating all factors conducive to enlightenment, they give rise to immeasurable waves of dispersed goodness that cannot be destroyed by any in the world, including devas, humans, or asuras. Just as...
Next, with the great wisdom-jewel radiance that extinguishes all waves of distracted virtue,
he touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to abandon all waves of distracted virtue, to hold their minds in a single object, and to abide in samādhi. Furthermore,
with the great wisdom-jewel radiance that removes all craving for dharmas, he touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to relinquish attachment to the flavor of samādhi.

They give rise to vast and great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, with the light of wisdom that universally illumines the radiance of the jewel of great wisdom, they touch those bodhisattvas, causing them to relinquish the vast and great supernormal powers they have produced and to abide in the practice of the function of great illumination.
Moreover, with the light of the jewel of great wisdom that is equal to the Tathāgata’s—boundless and effortless—they touch those bodhisattvas, causing them to relinquish...
One gives rise to the practice of great luminosity without effort (*anābhoga*), until one attains the stage of equality of the Tathāgata, where all effort is stilled so that nothing remains.

If there were no touch of the great light of these four jewels of wisdom of the Tathāgata, it would be impossible for even a single bodhisattva to attain the stage of the Tathāgata. This is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s mind.
