Homage to the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Wholesome Dharmas, the Ninth Practice of the Dharmadhātu;
Homage to the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Reality, the Tenth Practice of the Dharmadhātu.
I take refuge throughout the ten directions; May my sins be extinguished and my pure faith increase, And may I be born in the Flower Treasury Ocean.
From the remainder of the "Chapter on the Ten Practices" in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, it says:
"At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, in each of the ten directions... [up to] they praise and extol [the Buddha] until reaching the ultimate."
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean, within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Next, the Dharma-realm Yāma-Realized-Dharma Buddha:
Homage to the Buddhas numbering as many as the atoms in one hundred thousand Buddha-fields beyond lands as numerous as the atoms in one hundred thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions.
To the Bodhisattva Sarvavyūpagaṇitadhvaja, who attained realization next after the Buddha Sarvavyūpaguṇa in the world-system Dhūlisaṃkhyāguṇadhvaja; and to all such Buddhas,
as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand buddha-fields that are unspeakable, incomparable, and immeasurable— homage to them!
In the world-system Gaṇaguṇadhvaja, throughout the ten directions, there are the ocean-like assemblies of all the Bodhisattvas of the Guṇakānanarāja;
next, within the section on auspicious signs, there are the ocean-like assemblies of all the devas.
Homage to all these [Bodhisattvas] of unspeakably many Buddha-fields as numerous as atoms of dust, and to the infinite sounds of all thundering voices.
To all the celestial hosts of the oceans, the Dharma-realm, and the Yāma Heaven; to the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices;
and to the Bodhisattvas who practice with Joy within the lands as numerous as the atoms in all the voids of the ten directions and the three periods of time—homage to you!
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of Beneficial Conduct throughout the entirety of the realms of space and the lands as numerous as atoms within the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of Non-Contrary Conduct throughout all lands as numerous as the atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of Unyielding Conduct throughout all lands as numerous as the atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Sama-sa-ma-sa-ta.

Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who practice free from delusion and confusion throughout the dust-mote lands of the ten directions and three periods of time, as far as the limits of empty space.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of Perfect Manifestation throughout all lands as numerous as atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of Non-Attachment throughout all lands as numerous as atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time.
Homage to the Mahāsattvas,

the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who practice the difficult-to-attain path within all the lands as numerous as the atoms of the entirety of empty space throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of Wholesome Dharma Practice throughout all lands as numerous as atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of True Practice throughout all lands as numerous as atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time.
The Mahāsattva,
with a sincere heart, takes refuge and pays homage to the Bhagavān Vairocana, the Honored One of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean within the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Homage to the assembly of all oceans of beings at the *bodhimaṇḍa* of the Tathāgata Vairocana, whose ten bodies are unimpeded.
Homage to the Dharma-gate of the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya*.
Throughout the ten directions, we take refuge; may our transgressions be extinguished, our pure faith increase, and may we be born in the ocean of the Flower Treasury (*Gandavyūha*).
The twenty-second scripture, the "Twenty-Two Treasuries of the Ten Inexhaustibles" within the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, states:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇakara... (up to) all attained the ultimate, inexhaustible great treasury."
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean, within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the World-Ocean of the Flower Treasury of the Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
and to the Honored One Vairocana Buddha.
Next is the repentance for the offense of disrespecting one's teacher.
I pray that the inexhaustible Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as vast as a celestial net; Vairocana Tathāgata; the assembly of holy beings including Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī;
and all mundane and supramundane deities, by the power of your compassionate original vows, may emit great radiance to illuminate this dharma assembly.
May you bear witness, protect, and remember us; may you compassionately take us into your care.

I pray that for myself and the ocean of all sentient beings, from beginningless time until this very moment, having been shrouded by the veil of ignorance, we have failed to recognize your kindness and virtue and have been unable to repay it—may all such karmic obstacles be purified.
Confess and repent.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:

"Good sons, in the past, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, you left the household life to pursue the Way. Relying on your own extensive learning, you maintained the pure precepts, yet you constantly harbored..."

With a mind of arrogance, pride, and self-indulgence, he further practiced *dhūta* austerities while remaining content with few desires; yet, at that time, he again gave rise to attachment toward his meritorious qualities.
At that moment, there were two Dharma-preaching bhikṣus who had many friends and were renowned for their gains and offerings.
Toward these men, you spoke false words out of a heart of stinginess and jealousy, slandering them by claiming they committed acts of sexual misconduct. At that time, the Dharma-master’s friends—
"Relatives! Because of your divisive speech, you have spoken of their family's faults and caused them all to fall into doubt, so that they no longer develop faith or acceptance.
Those sentient beings, toward this Dharma-master, have harbored no compliant mind and have severed all roots of goodness.
Therefore, by virtue of this evil karma, you have already been born in the Avīci Hell for sixty hundred thousand years; as the remaining karma is not yet exhausted, [you shall continue to suffer]."
For four million years, he was born in the Saṃjīva Hell; as his residual karma was not yet exhausted, he was further born in the Kālasūtra Hell for two million years;
as that residual karma was still not exhausted, he was born in the Tapana Hell for one million years.
After passing away from there, he again attained human birth, but for five hundred lifetimes, he was born blind.

They are blind due to their residual karma. In every place where they are born, they are always dull-witted and obtuse; they lose right mindfulness, and their roots of goodness are obscured and covered over.
Their merit and virtue are meager, their physical form is ugly and deformed, and people do not take pleasure in seeing them. They are slandered, despised, mocked, deceived, and detested.
They constantly dwell in border regions, impoverished and lowly, losing their wealth and treasures, and finding it difficult to sustain their livelihoods. They are not... [respected].

Respected and beloved by all, after passing away from this life, during the final five hundred years of the latter age when the Dharma is about to perish, they will again be born into lowly families in the borderlands.
Deprived of resources, suffering from hunger and cold, they will be slandered by others, lose their right mindfulness, and fail to cultivate wholesome dharmas.
Even if they wish to practice, they will encounter many obstacles; though they may briefly give rise to wisdom, it will not endure.

The light, due to the obstruction of their karma, immediately vanished again. After five hundred years from now, these karmic obstructions of yours shall be extinguished, and you will then be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
At that time, that Buddha shall bestow upon you the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, all the bodhisattvas...

When Śāriputra and the others heard what the Buddha had said, the hair on their bodies stood on end and they were filled with deep remorse. Shedding tears, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we now confess our faults and repent for our transgressions. We have constantly [spoken ill] toward those who belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle."
For all instances of contempt, envy, anger, and other karmic obstructions, I now repent before the Buddha as for my transgressions.

Furthermore, the *Sutra on Right Reverence* states: "If a bhikṣu is to cultivate a heart of respect and right reverence toward his ācārya, when he is reciting, chanting, or receiving and upholding the sūtras in the presence of that ācārya, he must not expose his teeth."
One may gaze at the teacher’s feet, but one must not move them, fold them, cross them, dangle them, or play with them.
One must not sit on a high seat. Unless the teacher asks a question, one must not speak. One must not disobey the teacher’s words.
One must not stare fixedly at the teacher’s face. Standing three cubits in front of the teacher, one should sit only when the teacher permits it; once permitted, one sits.
Having done so, one should arouse a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward the teacher. That reciter of the sūtras should first master the text through recitation.

Once it is mastered and he has finished reciting it, he should receive the sūtra from the teacher, in whatever amount is appropriate. Regarding any points within the various dharma-doors that may cause doubt, he should first inquire whether the teacher would permit him to ask.
If the teacher grants permission, only then should he question him. Having received the sūtra, he should place his right knee upon the ground.
On the ground, he should receive the teacher’s feet with both hands and pay homage. If the ground is uneven, he should retreat along whatever path leads to a level spot.
If the ground is already level, he should pay homage to the teacher’s feet and then proceed.
Having walked ten cubits (*hasta*), he should again pay homage and then follow the path. He should form this thought: "The Ācārya..."
The attendant shall follow behind me; I cannot remain far away from the ācārya. He should know the proper time and go to the ācārya’s location during the three periods of the day.
If he does not go, he should be dealt with according to the rule.
If he arrives but does not see the ācārya, he should make a mark using grass, wood, a staff, a clod of earth, or a stone. If...
If the ācārya is sitting in meditation within his room, one should circumambulate the room to pay respects and only then depart.
If there is anything to be done, one must not do it without asking the teacher, except for the acts of defecating or urinating.

One must not address the teacher with coarse, harsh, or evil speech. One must not sit in the same place as the teacher—whether on a rope-couch or a wooden bed—following too closely after the teacher's words.
None of them shall sit down. If that bed should become damaged, they must repair it. They should go there at dawn;
they should go at the proper time and not at an improper time. Having arrived, they should ask the ācārya:
"What is required? What should be done? Shall we enter the village? If he says, "Enter," then the ācārya’s robes and bedding should be washed by hand.
He should wipe his hands with his own robe. Having grasped the teacher’s robe with both hands, he should place it in a clean spot.
First, he should provide the teacher with pure water for washing the hands; then he should hand the robe to the teacher.

Afterward, he should offer him a *saṃghāṭī*, a whisk, or whatever other robes or requisites are needed, such as a body-covering robe or a rain-cloak. He should treat them with such respect; he must not act otherwise.

One must not spit or discharge nasal mucus before one's preceptor. Whether inside the monastery or in its eastern or western quarters, one must not fold the robes over the left or right shoulder, nor wrap them around the head.
One should sweep and sprinkle the area where the teacher dwells or where he practices walking meditation (caṅkrama) to keep it clean, fanning him three times each day.
He should bathe at the three times of day. At the three times of day, he should ask for water. He should beg for alms on behalf of his teacher.
If the teacher has any task to perform, the disciple should apply himself with effort to do it. When the meal is finished, he should request the bowl from the teacher and wash it.
If the teacher gives it to him, he should first wash the teacher’s bowl and then wash his own. If the teacher does not give it to him, he must not ask for it again. Why is this? Ānanda...
It is difficult. In the future, there will be monks who think to themselves: "The bowl of the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has no one to wash it.
Because they wish to emulate me, they will desire to wash it themselves. The Tathāgata permits such persons as these to take cool water in the summer and warm water in the winter;
whatever they require, they should be allowed to take. However, they must not chew a tooth-stick in the presence of their teacher.
One must not speak of the teacher as being either good or bad. If one sees the teacher from afar, one should rise to welcome him.
Ānanda, if one receives even a single four-line verse through reading, reciting, or requesting instruction, that person is called an ācārya;
therefore, one should show reverence to the ācārya. Ānanda, if one does not thus revere the ācārya, because of that lack of respect, one will abide in non-...
Regarding right practice: as for those who speak of the faults and evils of the Teacher, they do not say of me, "He is our World-Honored One.
Why is this? Ānanda, such persons do not revere the Buddha, do not honor the Dharma, and are not counted among the Saṅgha.
Why is this? Ānanda, such deluded people cannot be said to abide in right practice. This is the confession for the retribution of one's transgressions.
“Ānanda, it is for those who abide in right practice that I teach the Buddha-dharma. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda wept and shed tears, saying:

“World-Honored One, in future ages, if there are sentient beings who can abide in and practice such deeds as these, they will be most rare. World-Honored One, I am able to practice and abide in such things.”

"Yes, World-Honored One. If there is a bhikṣu who cannot show reverence toward his preceptor (upādhyāya), his teacher (ācārya), or those who speak of the Dharma, what kind of retribution will that person receive?

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If there is a bhikṣu who does not respect his preceptor, his teacher, or those who speak of the Dharma, I declare that person to be a foolish worldling (pṛthagjana). Why is this, Ānanda? Because he does not obtain..."
If one speaks ill of an *ācārya* when it is true, how much more so if one speaks falsely?

In this regard, Ānanda, if one does not show respect toward one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or *ācārya*, there is a pratyekabuddha hell named "Extinction" (*Nirvāṇa*). When that person dies, they are reborn in that hell.
Once born there, they immediately possess four heads, and fire blazes upon their bodies like glowing iron balls. Within this [hell]...
There are various worms called "iron dogs" that constantly devour the tongue-roots of those people.
When their lives end there, they are reborn among the animals as tigers, wolves, or jackals. All sentient beings who see them cry out, "This is a tiger, a wolf, or a jackal!
Those who behold them find no joy; because of their past transgressions of speech, they constantly consume filth and excrement. Once this retribution is exhausted, they pass away.
They are reborn among humans, yet always in border regions where the Buddha-dharma does not exist. Although born as humans, they are possessed of manifold evils and are far removed from merit.
Their physical appearance, complexion, and strength do not resemble those of ordinary human beings; the form of their bodies they have received does not even resemble that of their parents.
They will not be cherished or loved by their parents; they will constantly suffer malicious slander; they will remain far removed from all Buddhas;

in every birth they will be foolish, dull-witted, and devoid of wisdom; and they will swiftly fall into hell. Why is this? Because they did not respectfully honor those who teach and bestow the Dharma to rescue and deliver them from suffering.
Ānanda, such people as these repeatedly encounter the laws of suffering; they must repent for the retribution of their transgressions.
Ānanda, suppose one were to read, recite, receive, and uphold even a single four-line verse, or write out a sutra scroll and make offerings to it;
or for as many eons as there are characters in that text, one were to carry that teacher upon one's head, shoulders, or back, and provide him with all manner of articles of pleasure.
Ānanda, even after making such offerings, one still could not repay the kindness of the ācārya.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "In future ages, there will be such evil bhikṣus who, having obtained this sūtra, do not show reverence toward their ācāryas and upādhyāyas.
Because they lack proper conduct, they will speak of the faults of their ācāryas and upādhyāyas.
I now declare that such foolish bhikṣus shall fall into the various hells and undergo great suffering."
“Ānanda, I now inform you and issue this formal command to you: The Tathāgata has already explained the conduct of the paths of good and evil.
According to the good or evil deeds performed by those sentient beings, they receive such retributions. One must repent for the retribution of transgressions.”

Furthermore, a sūtra falsely attributed to the Buddha states: "At that time, because that son of a householder spoke ill of that bhikṣu for violating the pure precepts, as retribution for that evil karma, he fell into the great hells for ninety thousand years.

For five hundred lifetimes, although born among humans, he received the body of a eunuch; he was born among the Mlecchas and into families of wrong views; and for six hundred lifetimes, he was blind from birth."
They shall be tongueless. Although they may go forth as monastics for seven hundred lifetimes, they will be unable to attain *dhāraṇī*.
Why is this? Because of the obstruction of their evil karma from past lives. Good son, you should understand this Dharma-gate well.
I have now finished speaking. Having heard this, if you see a Dharma teacher who is actually breaking the precepts, you must not give rise to anger;
you should not even speak of it, let alone speak of it after merely hearing of it with your ears.

Son of good family, if there were a mass of evil karma resulting from gouging out the eyes of all sentient beings, the evil karma of one who looks upon a Dharma teacher with a mind of anger would exceed that.

As for that mass of evil: if one were to commit the mass of evil resulting from taking the lives of all living beings, or the mass of evil incurred by conceiving an evil mind toward a Dharma-preacher for even the duration of a moment’s turning away of the face—that former mass of evil does not equal even one hundredth part of this latter mass of evil;
it does not equal even one thousandth part, nor even one hundred-thousandth part.
Whether in terms of a *saṃkhyeya* portion, a *kalā* portion, or a numerical portion, they do not equal even one part;
even in terms of a metaphorical portion, up to an *upaniṣad* portion, they do not equal even one part. Why is this? To slander a Dharma teacher is to slander the Buddha;
[one must perform] repentance for the retribution of such a sin.
"Good son, if there is anyone who wishes to make offerings to the Buddha, that person should instead make offerings to the Dharma Master.
If there is anyone who wishes to provide for the Buddha, that person should instead provide for the Dharma Master.
If there is anyone who wishes to pay homage to the Buddha, that person should instead pay homage to the Dharma Master. Why is this? Because from the Bodhisattva, one [Buddha] is born."
Omniscience [is attained], for it is from the Bodhisattvas that all Buddhas arise. Furthermore, a verse from the *Yogamahārāja-tantra* states:
"If a person should step upon the shadow of the Guru, That person commits no different sin than destroying a stūpa;
Whatever they do or seek shall not be accomplished, And all Buddhas and noble sages will not grant their approval."
Do not cause disparagement of the ācārya, even in your dreams you must not do so.
If there is a fool who slanders the ācārya, he will be constantly terrified by the arrival of various māras.
Such a person of evil karma and delusion should always be avoided by the wise.
The hells spoken of, such as Avīci and the rest, where one falls and there is no time of escape—these are the fruits obtained by slandering an ācārya.
Therefore, with a sincere heart, seek bodhi and serve and attend upon the ācārya; revere and honor them, always remaining filial and obedient.
He is able to bestow the inconceivable, supreme fruit; the disciple should practice filial piety and repay the ācārya by making him joyful. If the teacher is joyful, the Dharma will be accomplished;
beyond this, there is no one more venerable in the world.

We were shrouded by ignorance and did not recognize the karmic cause of slandering the Teacher. Now that we have encountered this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), we have only just begun to realize it.
We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all holy sages; we burn incense and scatter flowers.

I confess and repent for the sin of disrespecting my teachers; I do not dare to conceal it. By these causes and conditions, may the sins of disrespecting teachers committed by myself and the ocean-like assembly of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm all be purified.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for repentance and the eradication of offenses: Oṃ sarvapa-pame-si-put-na-ha-da-mitra-ya svāhā.
(Recite three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred eons are entirely swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
Whatever has arisen from my body, speech, and mind, I now confess it all.
Having confessed, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Proclamation: Listen, all you members of the assembly, to these verses on impermanence from the sutras:
The fundamental nature of both ordinary beings and sages is equally eternal; Yet ordinary beings cling to appearances and pursue the impermanent.
Their bodies are oppressed by the six realms and three miserable paths; Life after life, birth after birth, they endure old age, sickness, and death.
This old age, sickness, and death are universally loathed; their physical forms are so hideous and foul as to be utterly repulsive.
The countenance of youth lasts but a moment; before long, all shall see it withered and frail.
Even if one’s lifespan should reach a full hundred years, in the end one cannot escape the onset of impermanence.
The sufferings of old age, sickness, and death constantly follow one; they perpetually bring no benefit to sentient beings.
One should draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) and diligently cultivate, moment by moment, the causes for the permanent state.
Abandoning impermanent form, protect the permanent form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.

The Twenty-second Session, Part Five:
The Assembly in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace; The Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Giving Rise to Understanding.
With all reverence, I pay homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
All these people knelt on their right knees, solemnly holding incense and flowers, making offerings according to the Dharma. They made this vow:
"May this ocean-like cloud of offerings fill the worlds of the ten directions. May immeasurable clouds of jewel-light radiate, each ray of light manifesting all lights.
Furthermore, may there be immeasurable jewel-lights and the light of pure wisdom that illuminates and clarifies all dharmas. Furthermore, there was another...
The *saṃghī* (monastic) unimpeded jewel radiance; each individual ray of light pervades the *asaṃkhyeya* jewel-places throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
All these jewels are fully endowed with *asaṃkhyeya* jewel-treasuries, revealing all the jewel-treasuries of the true Dharma.
*Asaṃkhyeya* jewel-banners, bearing the marks of the Tathāgata’s banner, rise up loftily and preeminently. *Asaṃkhyeya* jewel-virtuous ones...
The Wisdom-Virtue Image is fully endowed with purity. It gives rise to the bliss of various samādhis within incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel gardens.

With such various articles of offering, one constantly makes offerings. The ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages, arranged in the infinite layers of Indra’s net, receive these clouds of offerings and take them as luminous pedestals, surpassing the boundless realms in their immeasurability.
[May it be] exhausted. May [this] perform the work of a Buddha.
Having made offerings, all pay homage with reverence.
Next, they present the jeweled lattice.
Clouds of offerings such as these— vast oceans of the intrinsic nature of precious jewels, the most excellent emergence of the seven-jeweled mountains,
and so forth— I offer to all the Buddhas and others. Oṃ sarva-tathāgata-arcana-pratīccha-samaya-hūṃ.
*Phraṇatsamaing Hūṃ*. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"There is a dhāraṇī named 'The Mantra of Immeasurable Varieties,' which can accomplish all things and possesses great efficacy. The dhāraṇī says:
Oṃ smara smara me manaḥ siddharamate hūṃ. Next, offer the dhāraṇī: Namaḥ ratnatrayāya namaḥ maitreyāya. Ṭaṃ ma.
Jra-sarabramaṭtra-tattadatyāḍḍhaṃ samayakṣama-nayātattada oṃ mañjara mañjara mahāmañjara mahāḍaṃcamañjrimaha.
(Bhr̥kuṭī-mañjumaheśvara-tāmañjrimaheśvara-mānastambhabhañjana-karmanayamañjiri-rasmi-makara-avartana-bhr̥ṅgānanamañji)
*Svāhā*. With Brahma-sounds, they praise the Buddha’s body and its radiance;
its form and characteristics are inconceivable for those sentient beings who have faith and joy.
According to their needs, they cause all to see, within the body of a single Buddha, manifesting as infinite Buddhas;
their thunderous voice pervades all lands, expounding the Dharma as deep as the ocean.
From every single pore, nets of light pervade the ten directions, emitting the wondrous sounds of the Buddha to subdue those who are difficult to tame.
Speaking directly, he praised the Buddha, the unequaled Honored One throughout the ten directions: "Never for a single thought-moment has he given rise to a mind of pride;
according to the karmic deeds of merit he has cultivated, he likewise shows reverence and gives rise to respect."
Throughout all worlds in Tuṣita, the Lion among Men, self-awakened, possesses vast, pure, and peerless merit;
he can perceive his entire physical form as it truly is.
Sometimes he manifests his descent into a mother’s womb, displaying immeasurable, sovereign, and great supernormal transformations.
Having attained Buddhahood, he preached the Dharma and manifested parinirvāṇa, pervading the world without a moment’s rest.
When the Lion among Men was first born, all those of supreme wisdom paid him homage;
the various devas, Śakras, and Brahmās, there were none who did not reverently attend upon him.
Throughout the ten directions, without exception, within the immeasurable and boundless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
which is without beginning or end and neither near nor far, the Tathāgata manifests his sovereign power;
the Honored One among Men, having manifested birth, takes seven steps in each direction.
Desiring to awaken all sentient beings through the sublime Dharma, the Tathāgata surveys them all;
seeing that all beings are submerged in the ocean of desire and shrouded by blindness, darkness, and ignorance,

who abide in the stage of firm dedication that accords with all roots of goodness;
homage to those dwelling within the lands as numerous as the atoms of the entirety of space throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, who abide in accordance with equality.
Homage to all the ocean-like assemblies of Bodhisattvas at the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) among all sentient beings;

homage to the ocean-like assemblies of all Bodhisattvas at the stage of dedication who abide within the true-mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) throughout the dust-mote lands of the ten directions and three periods of time, as far as the limits of empty space.
Homage to all the ocean-like assemblies of Bodhisattvas dwelling within the dust-mote lands throughout the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time,
who abide in the stage of liberation through the dedication of being unbound and unattached;
homage to those who enter into the immeasurable dharmas within the dust-mote lands throughout the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time.
All the ocean-like assemblies of Bodhisattvas in the stage of dedication of realms,
with sincere hearts, take refuge and pay homage to the World-Honored One Vairocana, the Honored One of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean within the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Throughout the ten directions, all take refuge; Sins are extinguished and pure faith increases. May they be reborn in the Flower Treasury Sea and the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Next is the Repentance for the Karmic Retribution of Solitary Spirits Who Died Prematurely Throughout the Dharma Realm.
I pray that the inexhaustible Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as vast as a celestial net; Vairocana Tathāgata;

and the assembly of holy ones of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī—those who have transcended the world and manifested their divine powers—will, through their compassionate original vows, radiate great light to illuminate this Dharma assembly.
I pray that you will bear witness to my protection and mindfulness, and out of compassion, grant me your acceptance.

May I and the ocean of all sentient beings, from the beginningless past until this very moment, though our oceans of karma are inexhaustible and their Indra-nets are layered upon one another throughout the vast expanse of heaven and earth across the three realms and four quarters—[may we be liberated].

This is the most extreme suffering among all sufferings; there is no rescue and no refuge, something never before seen or heard. Regarding the karmic retribution of wandering ghosts who met with untimely death, I now openly confess and repent.
Concerning those who die an untimely death, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "There are three kinds of death: first, death due to breaking the precepts; second, death due to..."
Death by negligence; death when the three life-forces are exhausted. There are nine kinds of untimely deaths. As the Sūtra says:

The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "There are nine classes and nine causes and conditions by which one’s life is cut short and one dies prematurely before its time has expired. First, eating food that should not be eaten.
Second, not measuring one's food. Third, not being accustomed to the food. Fourth, not having digested previous food. Fifth, becoming feverish."
Sixth, failing to uphold the five precepts; seventh, associating with evil friends; eighth, entering villages at improper times and conducting oneself contrary to the Dharma;
ninth, avoiding the retribution for offenses while failing to avoid the causes of death, yet repenting only for the retribution.
Furthermore, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* states: At that time, Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Raktavimocana, "Virtuous son, how can a life that has already reached its end be extended?
The Bodhisattva Raktavimocana replied, "Great Virtue, have you not heard the Tathāgata speak of the nine types of untimely death?
For this reason, I urge the creation of banners and lamps for the prolongation of life, and the cultivation of various merits."
Because they have cultivated merit, throughout their entire lifespans they shall not undergo suffering or affliction. Ānanda asked, "What are the nine untimely deaths?
The Bodhisattva Tārāvara replied, "If there are sentient beings who fall ill, even if the illness is slight, yet they lack medicine and a caregiver."
Furthermore, even if they encounter a physician, the physician may prescribe what is not medicine; though they truly ought not to die, they instead meet with an untimely death.

Moreover, they place their faith in worldly masters of demons, heterodox paths, and malevolent spirits who falsely proclaim calamities and blessings, thereby becoming terrified and agitated, so that their minds are no longer upright.
They consult diviners to seek out calamity; they kill various kinds of sentient beings to offer sacrifices to the gods and spirits;

they summon various *māraṅgas* (sprites) to beg for blessings and long life, yet in the end they cannot attain it. Foolish and deluded, they believe in heterodox and inverted views, which ultimately causes them to die an untimely death and enter hell from which there is no time of escape.
This is called the first form of untimely death. Second, those who are suddenly struck down by the laws of the king.
First, they are executed by the sword. Second, they are killed by poison or by the fangs of venomous serpents.

Third, while engaged in hunting, sporting, indulging in lust, or addicted to wine, they become dissolute and immoderate, whereby non-human spirits (*amanuṣya*) recklessly seize their vital essence. Fourth, they are recklessly consumed by fire. Fifth, they are recklessly drowned by water.
Sixth, they are recklessly devoured by various kinds of predatory beasts. Seventh, they recklessly fall from mountain precipices. Eighth, they are recklessly struck by poisons or spells (*abhicāra*).

They are harmed by curses, incantations, and the raising of *vetāla* (reanimated corpses). Ninth, being tormented by hunger and thirst, they fail to obtain food or drink and thus meet an untimely death.
These, O Tathāgata, are the nine kinds of untimely deaths briefly explained; furthermore, there are immeasurable other untimely calamities that are difficult to describe in detail.
[This concludes] the confession of karmic retribution for these offenses.

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "There are three kinds of death: namely, through the exhaustion of lifespan, through the exhaustion of merit, and through failing to avoid uneven conditions.
It should be understood that these are deaths at the proper time or at an improper time, occurring either with a virtuous mind or a non-virtuous mind."

Or it may be with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*). What is death due to the exhaustion of the life-span? It is like someone who dies because the full measure of their allotted lifespan has been completed;
this is called timely death (*kāla-mṛtyu*). What is death due to the exhaustion of merit (*puṇya*)? It is like someone who dies because of a deficiency in the necessities of life.
What is death due to not avoiding the uneven? As the Blessed One said, there are nine causes and nine conditions for [the exhaustion of the life-span] before it is fully spent.
One dies at the end of one's lifespan. What are the nine? They are: eating without moderation; eating at an improper time; eating again before what was previously eaten has been digested;
vomiting up what has been produced [as waste]; retaining what has been digested; not resorting to medicine; being ignorant of what is harmful or beneficial to oneself;
engaging in unchaste conduct at the wrong time or in excessive measure. This is called untimely death. How does one die with a virtuous mind? A person...
When life is about to end, one may either recall the wholesome dharmas previously practiced by oneself, or do so through being reminded by another;
by means of these causes and conditions, at that time, wholesome dharmas such as faith manifest within the mind. This is what is called death with a wholesome mind.

What is death with an indeterminate mind? It is when a person who has previously practiced wholesome dharmas is unable to recollect them at the time of death, nor is there anyone else to remind them; this is death with an indeterminate mind. What is death with an unwholesome mind?
It is when a person’s life is about to end and they personally recollect the unwholesome dharmas they habitually practiced in the past, or are reminded of them by another.
At that time, various unwholesome states such as greed, hatred, and delusion manifest in his mind, and even coarse and subtle perceptions appear before him;
this is death with an unwholesome mind. Furthermore, when one dies with a wholesome mind, one dies in peace and happiness.
When one dies with a malevolent mind, the body is oppressed by various sufferings, and one dies in a state of anguish.

Furthermore, those who die with a virtuous mind do not perceive disordered forms; those who die with a non-virtuous mind perceive disordered forms; and those who die with a neutral mind are dazed and unconscious.
Although they do not die in anguish, they likewise do not die in peace. This is the repentance for the retribution of transgressions.
Furthermore, there is a method for the realm of the King of Ghosts, who presides over the multitude of *pīlī* ghosts numbering as many as the sands of ten billion Ganges Rivers.

These are not within my own sight or hearing; they are of countless species, both named and nameless, among the human race. They dwell upon trees and grasses, or attach themselves to city deities (*chéngxiáng*).
Clutching their resentful spirits and consciousness, they are the essences of all things that have been self-mutilated or brought to their end, left without support or refuge, their remains exposed.

Bones [of the deceased] lack offerings and their spirits are famished; there are also *chimei* and *wangliang* ghosts. Furthermore, there are all the souls of the three treasures and nine grades who repent for their karmic retributions.
O sons of the Buddha: though shrouded by ignorance, you do not recognize the causes of your transgressions; only now, having encountered this place of practice (*daochang*), are you able to awaken.
I acknowledge this. I take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy and holy ones.

I confess and repent for the karmic offenses committed by the spirits of those who died a premature death, scattering flowers and burning incense; I dare not conceal them. By virtue of these causes and conditions, [may they be purified].
May the ocean of sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*, all those with spirits of premature death and every retribution for their transgressions, be entirely purified.
Next is the Seal and Mantra for Repentance and the Eradication of Transgressions: *Oṃ sarvapa-pame svapadane dharaya svāhā*.
(One should recite this three times:
The sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas Are all swept away in a single thought-moment; Like fire consuming dry grass, they are utterly extinguished without remainder.
All evil karma that I have created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion,
Produced by my body, speech, and mind— I now confess it all. Having confessed,
I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.

From the highest realm of Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana down to the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), Though the seven treasures always accompany him and a thousand sons constantly surround him, When his lifespan comes to an end, he cannot remain for even a moment longer.
Returning once more to drift upon the ocean of birth and death, one undergoes manifold sufferings according to conditions.

The Twenty-third Session, Part Six: The Assembly in the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; The Section on Cultivating Understanding by Accordance with the Cause and Realization of the Fruit, as practiced by the Śramaṇas of Tiantai through Teaching and Contemplation, titled "Correct Stopping and Stabilizing the Mind."
With all reverence, we pay homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
May these members of the assembly each kneel on their right knees and, holding incense and flowers, make offerings according to the Dharma.
May this ocean-like cloud of offerings pervade the worlds of the ten directions. May the Tathāgata A-saṃkhyeya-ratna-ghoṣa’s wondrous voice universally manifest throughout the world. A...
There were asaṃkhyeya jewel-forms, each of which emitted immeasurable rays of light of the sublime Dharma.
There were asaṃkhyeya jewel-marks, each of which transcended all other marks. There were asaṃkhyeya jewel-dignities, upon seeing which all gave rise to the joy and delight of a bodhisattva.
There were asaṃkhyeya jewel-heaps, upon seeing which all gave rise to the heap of the treasure of wisdom. There were asaṃkhyeya jewels...
Those who behold them dwelling in peace all give rise to the precious mind of secure abiding.
Those who wear the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) precious robes give rise to the peerless samādhis of the bodhisattvas.

Those who wear the incalculable precious *kāṣāya* robes obtain, upon the mere initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment, the dhāraṇī-gate of complete vision. Those who see the incalculable precious practices...
Knowing that all jewels are the definitive purity of the fruits of karma, those who behold the unimpeded wisdom and vision of incalculable jewels attain the pure Dharma-eye that perceives all things.
Those who behold the treasury of light of incalculable jewels achieve the treasury of great wisdom. With such various articles of offering, they constantly perform [worship].

I make this offering. Within the infinitely nested Indra-nets, may the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the ocean-like assembly of worthy and holy ones receive these clouds of offerings and transform them into luminous altars, vast as the boundless realms, immeasurable and inexhaustible, performing the work of the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, with all due reverence,
they next present the most excellent Seven-Jeweled Mountains and the like, consisting of vast oceans of the nature of precious lattices and jewels.
I bring forth such clouds of offerings as these and present them to all the Buddhas. Oṃ sarvam-tathāgata-ārogya-bala-samudra-samaye hūṃ.
The *Ratnadhāraṇī-sūtra* states: There is a dhāraṇī called the "Innumerable Varieties of Mantras," which can accomplish all things and possesses great efficacy.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ sīmala sīmala maimada sigrāmaha liṅga ḍhak phaṭ hūṃ.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for offering with the mind (with the two hands in vajra-añjali,
placed upon the crown of the head, one should recite this mantra): Oṃ sṛ-mṛ-dha-me-ṅke ḍiṃ sphara-hīṃ āḥ āḥ nagaṇa svāhā.

Having praised the Buddha with Brahma-sounds, you have realized the wisdom of the Tathāgata; You illuminate the entire Dharma-realm equally, universally entering all oceans of lands within a single pore of the Buddha’s body.
Your body abides in all places, and all things are entirely equal.
With wisdom acting thus, one enters the realm of the Buddhas; In all Buddha-lands,
one beholds their supernatural powers, Manifesting various bodies and various names, Directly praising the Buddha with straightforward speech.
True Suchness is free from delusion and eternally quiescent; Without birth and without cessation, it is universally pervasive.
The realm of all Buddhas is likewise so; Its essential nature is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
The realm of the Guide is also thus: It pervades the three periods of time, yet is not "pervasive" [in a limited sense].
For example, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is not a limit; it is universally present throughout the three times, entirely unimpeded.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unconditioned and immutable, like space which is fundamentally pure.
The purity of the nature of all Buddhas is likewise so; this original nature is neither a "nature" nor a "non-nature," transcending both existence and non-existence.
The nature of phenomena does not reside in verbal discourse; it is beyond speech, free from expression, and eternally quiescent.
The nature of the realms of the ten directions is likewise so. No words or phrases can fully discern or describe it.
Knowing that the nature of all phenomena is quiescent is like a bird flying through the sky, leaving no trace behind.
By the power of his original vows, he manifests a form-body, Causing all to behold the Tathāgata’s great spiritual transformations.
If there are those who wish to know the Buddha’s realm, They should purify their minds like space,
Remaining far removed from false conceptualization and all grasping, So that wherever the mind turns, it encounters no obstruction.

The Asura King was this one; Puṣya Candra was the present Māra Pāpīyān; Puṣya Druma was you, Maitreya;

In the past, when I sought Bodhi, it was for the purpose of maturing Māra Pāpīyān.
For ten days, he performed such immeasurable acts of suffering, distress, and difficult practices that caused one's hair to stand on end and inspired terror.

Therefore, this Māra Pāpīyān, adorned with the two kinds of majesty—merit and wisdom—possesses such supernatural power and might that he now conceives a murderous intent toward me and an intent to topple the banner of the True Dharma. Regarding...
They give rise to a mind of destruction toward the Saṅgha-ratna; they give rise to a mind of eradication toward the Eightfold Noble Path;
they give rise to a mind of annihilation toward the lamp of the True Dharma; and they give rise to a mind of obscuration toward all wholesome dharmas of sentient beings.
They create obstacles, engender terror, lack compassion, and harbor a mind of transgression, causing sentient beings to retreat from and abandon the path of goodness and fall [into lower realms].

With a mind directed toward the evil realms, he gave rise to a sense of terror toward the hosts of nāgas, a desire for destruction toward the palaces of the asuras, and further, the intent to disrupt the great assembly. With such malicious thoughts, he sat there looking about.

If there were any sentient beings who, for the sake of creating obstacles, for the sake of harassing others, for the sake of subduing others, for the sake of insulting others, or for the sake of seeking renown...

For the sake of fame; for the sake of the pleasures of play and laughter based on the five desires; and for the sake of seeking wealth and status—they practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom not for the sake of liberation, nor for the sake of faith and reverence, nor for the sake of detachment and tranquility, but solely for the sake of the pleasures of the five desires for their own bodies.
Thus they practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Wisdom. Bound by such fetters as these and mixed with ignorance, one’s karmic fruit ripens within the desire realm as Māra Pāpīyān.
Devadatta was also like this. These four asuras and other asuras likewise, during the Dharma of Vipaśyin Tathāgata, were arrogant, self-exalting, and did not diligently practice.
They are at rest. Yet they again harbor doubts and are entangled in various afflictions, practicing mundane precepts.
Due to these causes and conditions, they are now born in the lower realms as suffering animals or asuras.

For this reason, they are not even able to give rise to mundane right view, let alone be able to give rise to unsurpassed roots of goodness. Because of this, myself and all sentient beings have such [defilements].
These are my transgressions; I now repent them all.
Furthermore, regarding Mahābrahmā, Maheśvara, and Viśva-karman who followed erroneous paths—concerning their past conditions, the *Maheśvara-caryā-bhūmi-sūtra* states:
"In a past age, eighty-four thousand kalpas ago, there was at that time a Buddha who attained [enlightenment]..."
A Samyaksaṃbuddha appeared in the world named Guṇasāgara. There was a great city also named Guṇasāgara.
There lived a brahmin named Śānta, who had two sons: the first was named Śaṅkha and the second was named Ruci.
He grew up gradually, becoming intelligent and possessed of great wisdom. Both he and his parents grew weary of the cycle of birth and death.

He paid obeisance to his parents and said to his father, "I wish to enter the mountains to cultivate the Way there. His parents would not grant his request, saying, "You must not go. He spoke to his father once more:
"I must go to cultivate the Way. Having thus petitioned three times, he departed from his parents and entered the mountain valleys.
He dwelt in a grass hut among the mountains. Ten paces outside the hut lived an elderly brahmin who practiced the methods of the rishis.
Furthermore, there was another person who also lived nearby and practiced his own discipline.
One day, on a festival day, the four of them gathered together and asked one another about the matters they each cherished and sought. Ruci asked the elderly brahmin:
"What practice do you cultivate? What fruit or reward do you seek? The old Brahmin replied, "That which I cultivate is to seek the body of Brahmā for a thousand years in the heavens.
He asked a neighboring practitioner, "What practice do you cultivate? What fruit or reward do you seek?
That one answered for himself, "I seek to be the Lord of the Three Realms for a thousand years in the heavens. Then the Great Seer Śaṅkha spoke to them himself:

He said, "I seek for a thousand years in the heavens the love and respect of the world. The seer Ruci, who possessed great wisdom, addressed him, saying, "What you seek shall be accomplished, and you shall obtain the worldly fruits thereof.
But that which I now seek concerns the saṃsāra of those in the worlds of form and formlessness—whether two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, or footless, and whether superior, middling, or inferior."
"May all sentient beings be brought to liberation. Later, at that time, those four former practitioners came to where the Buddha was.
Then the old brahmin offered white *śukla-śarīra* grass flowers to the Buddha, prostrated, circumambulated him, and made this aspiration:
"By virtue of this merit of mine, may I become the Lord of the Brahma-world, with five faces, dignified and handsome, and [accompanied] by countless..."

The aspirations of sentient beings were fulfilled. Next, a certain rishi offered a piece of iron to the Buddha and further anointed the Buddha’s feet with fragrant oil, making this vow: "By virtue of this merit, may I obtain the body of Nārāyaṇa."
He became the sovereign of the three realms. Next, the ṛṣi Śaṅkha lit three lamps and offered three needles, making his offering with a sincere heart and making this vow:
"By offering these three lamps and three needles, may I be endowed with the three eyes and obtain the trident."
Throughout successive births, he constantly practiced the vow of giving and became a sovereign of the world. He attained the eight masteries (*aṣṭavaśitā*) and fulfilled his desires;

his mind and consciousness were sharp and keen. At that time, Luṇḍika’s topknot was exquisite, with long, reddish hair. He then untied his topknot and spread it upon the road, addressing the Blessed One:
"I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will step over my hair. The Buddha’s two— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the full extent of the supplied passage.)

His feet were such that he attained what had never before been seen within the three realms. They possessed the marks of a thousand-spoked wheel with webbed fingers and toes, as well as the banners, pennants, and vajra-mudrās;
these seal-marks were like exquisite brocade paintings, wonderfully and beautifully adorned. The Buddha then stepped across them and made this vow:
"By means of this merit of mine, may I attain Buddhahood and rescue all sentient beings wandering in saṃsāra. Thus it was.
After the four individuals had each made their vows, the elder brāhmaṇa subsequently cultivated various roots of goodness and attained the body of a Brahmā King.
Possessing five heads and faces, he became the lord of the three realms; because he offered auspicious flowers as a gift, he was moved by this merit to hold a celestial fly-whisk in his hand.
As for the roots of goodness cultivated by the next practitioner, he obtained boundless merit and attained the body of Nārāyaṇa; because he gave iron as a gift...
Through making offerings, he was moved by the power of karma to receive a hand-held wheel-treasure named "Wondrous Manifestation" (Sudarśana), which is capable of destroying all asuras.
Because the third, the seer Śaṅkha, offered three lamps, he was moved to have three eyes appear upon his face. By offering three needles, he obtained a trident.
By circumambulating the World-Honored One clockwise, he attained the love and respect of the world, the eight kinds of mastery, and became their sovereign. He was able to...
In this world of arising and ceasing, the fourth Luṣi offered his hair as an act of worship.

Because of the power of his vow, he shall attain freedom from desire, transcend the three realms, and achieve the wisdom of all-knowledge, being titled the God among Gods. I now repent for all of this.
Furthermore, the Commentary states: "Those who create obstacles, though they are immeasurable in number, do not exceed four types: first, Māras; second, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas);
third, ghosts (pretas); and fourth, spirits (devas). These are called the four. As for what is meant by 'Māras,' there are the four great Māras and their retinues of thirty-two thousand māra-beings.
As for what is meant by 'non-Buddhists,' there are ninety-six kinds of great [non-Buddhist teachers]."
There were ninety-three thousand non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) and their retinues. Regarding those called "ghosts" (*preta*):
there were ten kinds of great ghosts and fifty-one thousand three hundred and two kinds of ghost-retinues. Regarding those called "deities" (*deva*):
there were fifteen great deities and fifty-one thousand three hundred and two kinds of deity-retinues. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there are eighty deities who [accompany]...

The world relies upon them as objects of veneration and respect. Even including all the devas of the three realms, the Four Heavenly Kings, the eight classes [of spirits], various miscellaneous deities, the spirits of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, and the spirits of mountains, trees, rivers, seas, food and drink, deserts, and vegetation—these and others serve as places for people to perform sacrifices, offer services, and seek refuge. Such are the malevolent spirits and heterodox practitioners.

All ghosts and spirits obstruct the True Dharma, leading sentient beings toward unwholesome paths. Before the Buddha appeared in the world, these beings used such teachings to delude sentient beings, who remained unaware and unconscious of their plight. Now, we repent for all of this.
From time immemorial, Maheśvara, Śuddhavastra Brahmā, Vairocana, Mahāpāpīyas, and others have encountered various Buddhas over many kalpas and resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.
They have extensively performed offerings and have previously cultivated immeasurable gateways of practice, such as the six perfections of giving, ethical discipline, and so forth.
Yet, because they have forgotten their original vows and because their cultivation has been intermingled with afflictions, they have not attained liberation.
I now repent for all of these.
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "All sentient beings, due to their deluded thoughts, cling to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.

Failing to understand the four marks [of existence], though they may practice the Way with diligent effort through many kalpas, it is merely called 'conditioned' and will ultimately never lead to accomplishment."
All the noble assembly, we now all repent.

Furthermore, the *Buddhapiṭaka-uṣṇīṣa-sūtra* states: "Due to the deluded attachment to the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—those who are deluded regarding these aggregates fall into fifty kinds of biased and heterodox views of Śamatha.
Because they do not conceive of them as the mind of a sage, they regard these as auspicious states."
If one gives rise to noble understanding while actually receiving various heterodox teachings, one will fall into the Avīci Hell due to being deluded and lacking awareness;
we now repent for all of this.

Furthermore, within the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras, there is failure to understand the three knowledges of what is to be known and the four types of preparatory application, as well as the one hundred and eight kinds of afflictions to be severed.
I now repent of all deluded thoughts, such as being entangled by the forty-six kinds of demonic activities that arise from them.

Furthermore, the *Heart-Instruction on Mind-Only* states: "If one does not awaken to the fundamental single mind, then even though one practices, one will cling to appearances and harbor biased views;
this is like a painting without glue, or like an unbaked earthen vessel, falling into one hundred and twenty kinds of errors. I now repent of all these.

We have been shrouded by ignorance; we did not recognize the causes of sin—the enmity of Māra, the heterodoxies of external paths, ghosts and spirits, and erroneous understandings based on false views.
Now that we have encountered this site of enlightenment, we are finally able to awaken to this knowledge. We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy sages.
We burn incense and scatter flowers, openly confessing and repenting our transgressions, daring not to conceal them. By virtue of these causes and conditions...

I, along with the ocean-like assembly of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, vow that all sinful karma resulting from being in opposition to the True Dharma and from biased attachment to false doctrines shall be entirely purified.
Next is the Seal and Mantra for Repentance and the Eradication of Sin.
Oṃ sarvapāpam me kṣayaṃ kuru svāhā. (Recite three times. Sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas Are entirely swept away in a single thought, Like fire consuming dry grass.
All the evil karmas I have created in the past, without exception, Arose from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion,
And were produced by means of body, speech, and mind; I now confess them all.
Having performed repentance, with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
(Announcement: May the assembly listen to these verses on impermanence from the sutra:
Sentient beings, deluded by attachment, Are made to pass through billions of kalpas; The foolish are unable to renounce them.
Ensnared by craving, sentient beings are deluded by craving; furthermore, dwelling within craving, these beings carry a heavy burden.
Like one who drinks salt water when thirsty—the thirst increases even more after drinking—they find no rest for even a moment.
Fools cannot reflect upon this; exhausted, they forget their suffering.

With all reverence, I pay homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
All these people knelt on their right knees and, holding incense and flowers with solemnity, made offerings according to the Dharma. They made this aspiration:

"May this ocean-like cloud of offerings pervade the worlds of the ten directions—clouds of hundreds of billions of various kinds of flowers, clouds of various kinds of garlands, clouds of various kinds of incense, clouds of various kinds of powdered incense, clouds of various kinds of canopies, clouds of various kinds of robes, and clouds of various kinds of ornaments."
Clouds of various kinds of precious jewels; clouds of various kinds of burning incense; clouds of various multicolored silks.
Furthermore, there were a hundred trillion *bhṛṅgāra* vessels made of jewels, capable of dispelling all evils; a hundred trillion golden treasuries woven with threads of gold;
a hundred trillion jeweled parasols with poles made of various gems, held aloft in rows; and a hundred trillion ornaments for adorning everything with gold.
The lattice-work was adorned with a variegated array; hundreds of billions of luminous jewels emitted various rays of light, illuminating everywhere.
There were also hundreds of billions of sun-treasury wheels and hundreds of billions of moon-treasury wheels, all composed of jewels of immeasurable colors.
With such various articles of offering as these, may one constantly perform offerings in a manner like Indra’s net, layer upon layer. May the ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and holy sages accept these clouds of offerings and transform them into platforms of light, vast as boundless realms, immeasurable and inexhaustible,
vowing to perform the work of the Buddha.

In Brahma-sounds they praise all Tathāgatas,
All of whom possess inexhaustible marks; Though they manifest immeasurable forms and appearances,
they are ultimately never exhausted, Appearing like reflections in all lands throughout the realms of all Tathāgatas.
Within all of those [realms], he manifests all manner of miraculous deeds; having purified the various practices and vows of Samantabhadra until they are bright and immaculate,
he is able to universally manifest the Buddha’s spiritual transformations in all lands,
directly praising the Buddha.
Just as there is a king of physicians skilled in medical arts, such that whoever sees him is healed of all illnesses—
even if their life has already come to an end, by applying medicine to their body, he enables them to perform all tasks just as before—
so too is the Supreme King of Physicians, who is fully endowed with skillful means and omniscience.
Through past sublime conduct, he manifests the body of a Buddha; Sentient beings who behold him have their afflictions extinguished.
Just as the king of jewels within the ocean Universally emits immeasurable rays of light, And those touched by it take on its color, So too are the eyes purified for whoever beholds him.
The Supreme King of Jewels is likewise: those who touch its light all become the same color;
those who behold it have their five eyes opened, destroying the darkness of all defilements and abiding on the Buddha-ground.
Like a wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel, whatever is sought is fully satisfied.
Sentient beings with little merit cannot see him; it is not that the King of Jewels has any discrimination.
The Sugata, the King of Jewels, is likewise thus: he completely fulfills all sought-after desires and pleasures.
Sentient beings without faith do not see the Buddha; it is not that the Sugata’s mind abandons them.

The *Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parivarta* states: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, when I was a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, I emitted a great light named Prabhā-ketu-rāja.
It illuminated worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields. Among those worlds, the sentient beings in the hells who encountered this light [were all...]"
Having rested from suffering, they attain ten kinds of purity. It is the same for the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
all give rise to joy, leaping for gladness and celebrating. When their lives there end, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. In that heaven there is a drum named "Extremely Delightful.
Once those devas have been born, this drum emits a sound and addresses them, saying: "O sons of the gods, by you..."
With a mind free from negligence, he planted various roots of goodness in the presence of the Tathāgata.
Having previously attended upon many spiritual friends and through the great majestic power of Vairocana, at the end of his life there, he was reborn in this heaven.
O Son of the Buddha, the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet is named King of Universal Radiance; it possesses an auspicious mark named King of Perfection, which is ever...

He emitted forty kinds of light rays. Among them was one ray named "Pure Merit," which was able to illuminate worlds as numerous as the atoms within a hundred billion nayutas of Buddha-fields, according to the various karmic actions and diverse inclinations of sentient beings.
They cause all to reach maturity. Those sentient beings in the Avīci Hell who encounter this light all have their lives end and are reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Once reborn there, they hear the sound of the celestial drum, which proclaims to them: "Excellent, excellent!"
"O sons of the gods, you should pay homage to the Bodhisattva Vairocana, who has entered the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement.
At that time, having heard the sound of the celestial drum thus exhorting them, all the sons of the gods conceived this thought: "How marvelous! How rare!
For what cause has this subtle and wondrous sound been uttered? Then the celestial drum addressed the sons of the gods, saying: "The sound I have produced..."
It is accomplished through the power of all roots of goodness. O sons of the gods, just as I speak of a "self" yet do not cling to a self or to what belongs to a self, so it is with all Buddhas:
they call themselves "Buddhas," yet they do not cling to a self or to what belongs to a self.
O sons of the gods, just as my voice does not come from the east, nor from the south, west, or north...
Coming from the four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir—attaining Buddhahood through karmic retribution is also like this;
it does not come from the ten directions. O sons of the gods, for example, when you were formerly in hell, neither the hell nor your body came from the ten directions;
they arose solely because you were bound by the delusions of inverted, evil karma and ignorance, giving rise to a body in hell. This has no fundamental basis and no place of origin.
"O sons of the gods, it is by the power of the majestic virtue of the Bodhisattva Vairocana that this great radiance is emitted.
Yet this radiance does not come from the ten directions. O sons of the gods, my Drum of the Celestial Sound is likewise;
it does not come from the ten directions, but is produced solely through the power of the roots of goodness of samādhi and the power of the majestic virtue of the Prajñāpāramitā."
With such pure sounds, he manifests these various kinds of mastery. O sons of the gods, you should go to where that bodhisattva dwells, attend upon him, and make offerings to him.
Do not again become greedily attached to the pleasures and requisites of the five desires; for attachment to the pleasures of the five desires obstructs all roots of goodness.
O sons of the gods, it is like the fire at the end of an eon that burns Mount Sumeru, utterly consuming it until nothing remains.
Nothing else can be found. It is the same with the mind enveloped by the fetter of sensual desire; it can never give rise to the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha.

O sons of the gods, you should recognize kindness and repay it. O sons of the gods, those sentient beings who do not know how to repay kindness will frequently meet with untimely deaths and be reborn in hell. O sons of the gods, formerly when you were in hell...

In the midst [of this], they were illumined by light that shone upon their bodies; thus they passed away from that realm and were born here. You all should now swiftly dedicate yourselves and increase your roots of goodness.

O sons of gods, just as my celestial drum is neither male nor female, yet can produce immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable things, so too it is with you, sons of gods and daughters of gods: you are neither male nor female, yet you are able to receive [these benefits].

"By means of various supreme and wondrous palaces and gardens, just as my celestial drum is neither born nor extinguished, so too are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—neither born nor extinguished.
If you can awaken to and understand this, you should know that you have entered the Samādhi of the Seal of Non-reliant Wisdom.
When the sons of the gods heard these sounds, they attained what they had never experienced before.

They immediately manifested ten thousand clouds of flowers, ten thousand clouds of incense, ten thousand clouds of music, ten thousand clouds of banners, ten thousand clouds of canopies, and ten thousand clouds of songs of praise.

Having performed these transformations, they proceeded together to the palace where the Bodhisattva Vairocana resided; there, with palms joined in reverence, they stood to one side, desiring to behold him.
Yet they were unable to see him. At that time, a certain son of heaven spoke these words:

"The Bodhisattva Vairocana has already passed away from here and been born among humans in the pure and brahminical royal house. He rides upon a sandalwood palanquin and dwells within the womb of Queen Māyā.
Then, all the sons of heaven, observing with their divine eyes, beheld the Bodhisattva’s body situated among humans in the palace of King Śuddhodana.
At home, the Brahmā and Kāmadhātu devas attended upon and made offerings to him. All the hosts of devaputras thought to themselves:
"If we do not go to the Bodhisattva’s abode to inquire after his well-being, and if we allow even a single thought of attachment to arise toward this celestial palace, it would be improper.
Then, each devaputra, accompanied by a retinue of ten nayutas, desired to descend to Jambudvīpa.
Jambudvīpa. At that time, a sound issued from the celestial drum, proclaiming: "O sons of the gods, it is not that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dies here and is reborn there;
rather, by means of his supernormal powers, he causes beings to see him according to what is appropriate for their minds.
O sons of the gods, just as I am now able to produce this sound without being seen by the eye, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
It is likewise with the Bodhisattva entering the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement: it is not something seen by the eye, yet he is able to manifest birth in various places;
free from discrimination, having eliminated pride, and without attachment.
I, the disciple [Name], because this nature of karma is empty and quiescent, and by virtue of hearing the gateway to the supreme and wondrous meaning,
have been inspired to resolve upon Bodhicitta by the celestial drum and the various devaputras. Through the samādhi of perfect penetration,

wherein principle and phenomena are non-obstructive, I now prostrate to the inexhaustible, eternally abiding Triple Gem of the Indra-net within the entirety of the realm of space throughout the ten directions.
O Jewel, repent with a sincere heart. We have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
We purify our minds and abide in virtuous deportment. We repent for and eliminate all karmic obstructions, afflictive obstructions, retributive obstructions, and obstructions to vision.

With bodies as numerous as the sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, with heads as numerous as the sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, and with... [the entirety of the text].
With tongues as numerous as the number of sentient beings in the realms, and through karmic actions as numerous as the number of sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm—
consisting of virtuous verbal karma and virtuous mental karma— they repent and eliminate all obstructive faults and evils, such that they are entirely purified.

(Recite three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas are entirely swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
Whatever has arisen from my body, speech, and mind, I now confess it all.
Having confessed, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Proclamation: May the assembly listen to these verses on impermanence from the Sūtra:
All who are born must return to death; Their countenances all fade and decay. The powerful are assailed by illness— None can escape this fate.
Even if it were Mount Sumeru, At the end of the kalpa, it would all be scattered and destroyed.
The great ocean, deep and bottomless, shall likewise be completely exhausted; the great earth, the sun, and the moon, when their time comes, all return to extinction.
Never has there been a single dharma that has not been swallowed by impermanence.
