May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss;
next, in the midst of the Śāla Forest of Adorned Banners, at the site of the Great Stūpa Temple, for the multitudes of those of various vehicles:
Homage to the Upāsaka of Great Wisdom; Homage to the Upāsaka Sudatta.
Homage to the upāsaka Vasudatta. Homage to the upāsaka Puṇyaprabha.
Homage to the upāsaka Yaśasvin. Homage to the upāsaka Dānayaśas.
Homage to the upāsaka Candravatsa. Homage to the upāsaka Sumati.
Homage to the Upāsaka Mahāmati; homage to the Upāsaka Bhadrapāla; homage to the Upāsaka Bhadraśrī;
homage to these and the five hundred other upāsakas throughout the ten directions who take refuge in them all.
May our sins be extinguished, may our pure faith increase, and may we be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean.
In the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī:
Homage to the Upāsikā Mahāprajñā; homage to the Upāsikā Suprabhā;
homage to the Upāsikā Suvapuṣā; homage to the Upāsikā Rucitakāyā.
Homage to the Upāsikā Bhadrā; homage to the Upāsikā Bhadraśrī;
homage to the Upāsikā Bhadraprabhā; homage to the Upāsikā Dhvajaprabhā;
homage to the Upāsikā Guṇaprabhā; homage to the Upāsikā Sunetra.
Homage to these five hundred *upāsikās* and all those throughout the ten directions;
we take refuge in them all. May our transgressions be extinguished and our pure faith increase, and may we be reborn within the Flower Treasury Ocean in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Homage to the youth Sudhana; homage to the youth Sucarita;
homage to the youth Suśīla; homage to the youth Susamudācāra;
homage to the youth Suvikrānta; homage to the youth Sucintita.
Homage to the youth Sudhi; homage to the youth Sujñāta;
homage to the youth Sunetra; homage to the youth Subhuja;
homage to the youth Suprabha; and homage to these five hundred youths such as these.
All in the ten directions take refuge; Sins are extinguished and pure faith increases. May they be born in the Ocean of Flower Treasury and the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Namo to the Girl Sudharmā; Namo to the Girl Mahāprajñā Upāsikā.
Homage to the maiden Bhadrasamudgata. Homage to the maiden Surūpā.
Homage to the maiden Bhadrā. Homage to the maiden Bhadraguṇā.
Homage to the maiden Guṇavatī. Homage to the maiden Brahmadattā.
Homage to the maiden Guṇaprabhā; homage to the maiden Suprabhā;
homage to these five hundred maidens and others;
homage to those who, like clouds, dwell in the great stūpas within the Śāla groves adorned with banners.
The infinite fourfold assembly and all the oceans of beings throughout the ten directions take refuge;
may their sins be extinguished and their pure faith increase, and may they be reborn within the Flower Treasury Ocean in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī... [preached] the Dharma according to their capacities, and then departed.
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean and within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Next, those of superior faculties follow Mañjughoṣa and join in his praise.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the youth Sudhana (through to) wept with compassion and, shedding tears, took his leave and traveled south" (these three phrases are combined with the preceding).
Next, the Repentance for the Hell of Solitude:
"I only pray that the inexhaustible Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Treasures of the Imperial Net, Vairocana Tathāgata, Samantabhadra, and Mañjuśrī..."

The assembly of noble ones gathered like an ocean, and the world-transcending and worldly deities, by virtue of your compassionate original vows, radiate great light that illuminates this Dharma assembly.
May you bear witness, protect, and sustain us; may you look upon us with pity and compassionately receive us.

I pray that for myself and the ocean of all sentient beings, from beginningless time until this very moment, regarding our inexhaustible oceans of karma—layered like Indra’s net—and all transgressions of laws and precepts, [may they be purified].
Confession and Repentance.
The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* states: At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita lost his companions and went alone. Before he had traveled far along the road, he heard the sound of a *gandī* (wooden gong).
Following the sound toward the monastery, he encountered a man on the way and immediately asked him: "For what reason and by what cause is the *gandī* being struck?"
There was the sound of a mallet striking. The man replied, "I am entering the warm bathhouse to bathe. Saṃgharakṣita thought to himself, "I have come from afar; I should bathe with the monks.
He immediately entered the monastic quarters and saw a group of people who appeared to be monks entering the warm bathhouse together.
He saw all the bathing implements—bathing robes, earthenware jars, ceramic vessels, and the bathhouse itself—all ablaze with fire. At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita...
He saw several bhikṣus entering a heated chamber together. Once inside, the fire blazed up; their flesh and sinews were completely consumed, and their bones were like charred wicks.
Saṃgharakṣita was struck with terror and asked the bhikṣus, "Who are you? The bhikṣus replied, "We are people from Jambudvīpa."
"His nature is such that he is difficult to convince. When you reach the Buddha’s presence, you may ask him about it; he will immediately become terrified, abandon the monastery, and flee.
Before you have traveled far on your way, you will encounter another monastery. That monastery is magnificent, vast, and exceptionally well-crafted.

You will again hear the sound of a *ghanṭā* being struck and see monks there. You should then ask them: 'For what reason and by what cause is the sound of the *ghanṭā* being struck? The monks will answer:"
He said, "The community of monks was eating rice. Then I thought to myself, 'I have come from afar and am very hungry; I too must eat.
Having entered the monastery, I saw the monks gathered together, and their eating vessels and bedding were all ablaze;
the people and the dwellings were entirely on fire, no different from before. Saṃgharakṣita asked, "Who are you? The man replied:
The words were no different from before. The bhikṣu was struck with terror and fled even more swiftly. Before he had traveled far along his path, he encountered another monastery.

The solemnity of that monastery was again no different from the previous one. He entered the monks' quarters and once more saw various bhikṣus sitting upon beds of fire, tearing at one another with their claws until the flesh was gone and the sinews exposed; their five viscera and marrow were like charred wicks. The bhikṣu...
Saṃgharakṣita asked, "Who are you? The bhikṣu replied, "I am a person from Jambudvīpa; we are by nature difficult to convince. When you reach the Buddha’s presence, you may ask the Buddha yourself.
Saṃgharakṣita was struck with alarm and fled in haste. Before he had traveled far along the road, he encountered another monastery.
As before, he entered the monastery and saw various beings sitting together and eating. The bhikṣus said to him: "You—"
"Now, go out! Saṃgharakṣita hesitated; before he had even gone outside, he saw that within the bowls of the bhikṣus there was only human excrement, boiling and bubbling over.
At that time, the bhikṣus were all devouring it; having eaten, fire blazed up, and their throats and five viscera were all turned to smoke and charcoal, passing straight through as they flowed down.
Having seen this, he was struck with terror and fled away in haste. Before he had gone far...
Traveling further, he again saw a monastery. Its solemn appearance was no different from the one before.

He immediately entered the monastic quarters and saw various bhikṣus holding iron mallets in their hands, striking one another until they were crushed to dust. Having seen this, he was struck with terror.
Continuing on his way, not far from there, he again saw a monastery. It was magnificent and beautiful, also no different from the previous ones. He immediately entered the monastery...
In the monastery, they heard the sound of the *ghanṭā* (gong). Saṃgharakṣita asked, "For what reason is the gong being struck?
The bhikṣus replied, "We wish to drink sweet syrup. Bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita then thought to himself, "I am now parched with thirst; I must drink some sweet syrup.
He immediately entered among the assembly and saw the various food vessels, beds, couches, and bedding. The bhikṣus were insulting one another regarding the food vessels.

In the center, molten copper was filled to the brim. All the bhikṣus together drank and ate from it; once they had finished eating, fire blazed up, turning their throats and five internal organs into glowing coals.
As it flowed straight through them, they were struck with terror upon seeing this and proceeded on their way.
Before they had gone far, they saw a great expanse of flesh. Its flames were fiercely blazing, and there were cries of wailing and agony so unbearable that they were terrified upon seeing it.
Terrified, he proceeded forward. Before he had gone far, he again saw the great earth, exactly as before without difference.
Proceeding further still, he saw a large cauldron of flesh, all ablaze with fire; the heat and pain were unbearable, exactly as before without difference.
Proceeding further still, he again saw a cauldron of flesh, all ablaze with fire, no different from before. Proceeding further still, he saw a single piece of flesh.
There is a jar; its flames are fiercely blazing, and the cries of wailing and suffering are unbearable in their poisonous pain.
Moving forward again, one sees a jar of flesh; its flames are fiercely blazing, no different from before. Moving forward yet again, one sees a great leather spring;

its flames are fiercely blazing, and the boiling, rotting leather emits cries of agony and bitter torment, no different from what was seen previously. Having seen this, one is struck with terror and moves forward once more.
Proceeding further, though not yet far along the way, he again saw a large vat of flesh, its flames blazing fiercely; the suffering there was as before.
Continuing forward once more, he saw a bhikṣu holding a sharp blade in his hand, who was cutting off his own nose. Once cut, it grew back; once grown, he cut it off again.
Thus it began and ended, repeating itself without rest. Continuing forward yet again, he saw another bhikṣu with his hand...
He seized an axe and cut his own tongue; having finished, he began again, no different from before.
Proceeding further, he saw a bhikṣu standing alone in water, crying out "Water! Water! incessantly, suffering bitter torment.
Proceeding yet further, he saw a bhikṣu in an iron thorn grove, standing upon iron thorns, wailing with cries of agony.
It was no different from before. Proceeding further, he saw a hall of flesh; its flames were blazing and the sounds of wailing in suffering were no different from those before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a stake of flesh shaped like an elephant tusk; its flames were blazing and the suffering was as before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a camel whose body was being scorched by fire, wailing with cries of pain. It was likewise.
It was no different from before. Moving forward again, he saw a horse whose body was being burned by fire; it wailed in agony, no different from before.
Moving forward again, he saw a white elephant whose body was being consumed by blazing flames; its suffering was no different from before.
Moving forward again, he saw a donkey whose body was being scorched by fierce fires; its suffering was no different from before. Moving forward again, he saw—

There was a single ram; its body was scorched by fierce flames, and its suffering was no different than before. Proceeding further, he saw a meat-altar, ablaze with great flames, and its suffering was no different than before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a meat-house; his body was scorched by fierce flames, and as he wailed aloud in pain, his suffering was no different than before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a meat-couch, wailing aloud in pain—his suffering... [was no different than before].
It was no different from before. He proceeded further and saw a bed of flesh, its body scorched by blazing flames; it was also no different from before.
Proceeding further still, he saw a scale of flesh, being stretched and contracted while burned by fire; the suffering was no different from before.

Proceeding further still, he saw a pair of flesh-tongs, being stretched and contracted while burned by fire; the suffering was no different from before. Proceeding further still, he saw a rope of flesh.
A bed; being burned by fire and suffering there is no different from before. Proceeding further, he sees a wall of flesh, burning and quivering; the suffering is no different from before.
Proceeding further still, he sees a rope of flesh, burning and stretching and contracting; the suffering is no different from before.
Proceeding further still, he sees a cesspool well, with excrement and urine surging and boiling; the suffering is no different from before. Proceeding further still...
He proceeded forward. He saw a high seat upon which sat a bhikṣu with his mind concentrated and sitting upright, being consumed by fierce flames;
his cries of suffering were as before. Proceeding further, he again saw a bhikṣu on a high seat undergoing suffering, no different from the one before.
Proceeding yet further, he saw a fleshly *gaṇḍī* being scorched by fire, its cries of suffering likewise no different from the previous ones. Proceeding further still, he saw a fleshly *brahmā*.
Qi-zhi (Vimalakīrti). His Sanskrit name is Kuśala. A fierce fire burns his body; he undergoes suffering as described before.

Proceeding further, he sees a fleshly kuśala, undergoing suffering as before. Proceeding further still, he sees a great mountain of flesh, scorched and rotted by fierce fires, quivering and shrieking;
the suffering is no different from before. Proceeding further still, he sees a sumanā flower tree, [consumed by] fire...
The suffering from being burned was no different than before. They proceeded further and saw *sumanā* flower trees; the sound produced by the fire burning them was also no different than before.
Proceeding further still, they saw flesh-flower trees; the sound produced by the fire burning them and the suffering were no different than before.
Proceeding further still, they saw flesh-fruit trees; the sound of suffering from the fire burning them was likewise no different than before. Again, proceeding further...
He moves forward and sees another tree; it is being burned by fire and suffering pain, no different from before. Moving forward again, he sees a pillar of flesh;
it is being burned by fire and suffering pain, no different from before. Moving forward again, he sees another pillar of flesh;
the hell-wardens hack at it with axes, and it suffers as before. Moving forward again, he sees a pillar of flesh; it is being burned by fire and suffering pain.
It was no different from before. Proceeding further still, he saw fourteen trees of flesh, where beings were suffering from being burned by fire; this too was no different from before.
Proceeding further still, he saw two bhikṣus striking each other with their fists, their heads split open and their brains crushed, as pus and blood flowed out.
Once extinguished, they are born again; as it ends, it begins once more. Suffering does not cease.

The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita advanced a short distance further and saw two śrāmaṇeras lying asleep, embracing one another, their bodies being consumed by fierce flames; their suffering did not cease. The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita—
Having seen this, he was struck with terror and asked the śrāmaṇera, "Who are you that undergoes such suffering? The śrāmaṇera replied, "I am a person from Jambudvīpa.
The people there are by nature difficult to convince; when you reach the World-Honored One, you may ask the Buddha yourself."
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the essentials of the Dharma for the great assembly.
Then, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, before the World-Honored One and amidst the great assembly, cried out in a loud voice, recounting the causes and conditions of the hells he had previously seen:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the fundamental causes and conditions for me. The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita: "As for the bhikṣu’s bathhouse that you previously saw..."
This is not a bhikṣu, nor is this a bathhouse; these are inhabitants of hell.

These sinful beings were, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, ordained bhikṣus who did not rely on the Vinaya but followed their own foolish inclinations. They used the monastic bathing implements and various utensils as they pleased.
Although the bhikṣus who upheld the Vinaya constantly instructed them in the proper rules, they did not follow those instructions. From the time of Kāśyapa...

Since the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, they have been undergoing the sufferings of hell without ceasing until now. The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita: "The monastery you first saw was not a monastic temple, nor were those there bhikṣus;
they were inhabitants of hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who failed to fulfill the five virtues.
Regarding the property of the Sangha from the four quarters, they did not strike the *ghanṭā* (bell), but used it in common while the assembly remained silent. Because of this cause..."
Because of these conditions, he suffered the agony of the flaming bed. Since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, he has endured the sufferings of hell without ceasing until now.
As for the second temple you see, it is neither a monastery of the Saṃgha nor does it belong to bhikṣus; it is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who lacked the five virtues. When various donors constructed a temple for him, [the four...]
The provisions were abundant. When the donor first established the monastery, he intended to strike the *ghanṭā* (gong) with the aim of providing relief to all.

However, these bhikṣus did not strike the *ghanṭā*, but instead accepted and consumed the offerings in silence. Consequently, when visiting bhikṣus arrived, they received no food or drink and departed with empty bowls.
Due to this karmic cause, they suffer the torment of being burned by fire; they claw at one another until their flesh and sinews are completely consumed, leaving only bones.
Like a scorched wick, since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have endured such suffering, which continues unabated until now.
As for what you see as the third temple, it is not a monastery of the Saṃgha, nor are those there bhikṣus; they are inhabitants of hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who lived together with many indolent bhikṣus, and they said to one another: "We, now..."
"You may invite a Vinaya-holding bhikṣu to perform the ritual together with us; thus it shall be in accordance with the Dharma.
They immediately searched for one and found a bhikṣu of pure conduct with whom they lived, ate, and stayed overnight.

This bhikṣu of pure conduct, in turn, sought out fellow practitioners. As the number of such practitioners of pure conduct increased, [the others] immediately pursued them and drove them outside the monastery.
At that time, those who had broken the precepts set fire to the monastery during the night and extinguished the bhikṣus.
Due to these causes and conditions, they now grasp iron hammers and destroy one another; since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have endured great suffering and affliction.
It continues thus without ceasing even to this day. As for the fourth temple you see, it is not a monastery for monks, nor are those there bhikṣus;
they are inhabitants of hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who resided permanently within that temple.

When various donors brought offerings of fat and meat, they should have been distributed in the presence of the community. At that time, visiting monks arrived, yet the resident bhikṣus, out of a heart of stinginess, waited—
The guest departed. Later, they were about to divide [the remains], but before they could do so, worms emerged and the flesh became putrid and rotten; it was discarded outside.
Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell to eat excrement and urine, suffering without respite since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha.
As for what you see as the fifth temple, it is not a monastery for the Saṃgha, nor are those there bhikṣus; it is a hell.
This person was a renunciant during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. At the time of the midday meal, he ate contrary to the Dharma and reviled one another with harsh speech.

Due to these causes and conditions, he has been undergoing the suffering of the iron bed; within all the food vessels, boiling fire surges forth, his flesh and sinews are completely consumed, and his bones are like charred wicks.
From the time of Kāśyapa Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until now, it has not ceased. You see this next...
As for these six monasteries, they are not monasteries of the Sangha, nor are there bhikṣus there; they are inhabitants of hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, these were renunciants who did not strike the *gandi* but instead drank the sweet gruel of the Sangha in silence, fearing that other monks might arrive.

Due to the causes and conditions of their stinginess, they have fallen into hell, where they drink and consume molten copper. They have been undergoing this suffering since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha.
The suffering continues to this day without ceasing. This is the confession for the retribution of one's sins.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita: "That which you see as the first ground is not the great earth;
it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who, within the fields belonging to the Saṃgha, cultivated crops for his own private use."
Regarding the payment of wages to the Saṃgha, a bhikṣu who maintained the Vinaya reprimanded him according to the precepts, saying, "Why do you now fail to pay the wages due to the Saṃgha?
At that time, relying on the power of the king, this man did not accept the instruction and replied to the bhikṣus, "I am your slave."

"If you had the power, why did you not plant for yourself? Because of these causes and conditions, you have been undergoing the sufferings of the Fire Hell since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha until now, without ceasing. As for what you see as the second earth, it is not actually the earth;
it is a sinner. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a layman who planted crops on monastic land but did not pay the monks their wages."
Because of these causes and conditions, they have fallen into hell and become a great mass of flesh, undergoing various sufferings that continue unabated to this day.
As for what you see as the first "meat jar," it is not actually a meat jar; it is a sinner.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was the senior monk (upādhyāya) of the Saṃgha, yet he was incapable of meditating or reciting the scriptures, nor did he understand the Vinaya. He merely ate his fill and slept soundly, doing nothing but engaging in idle talk.
Because he spoke useless words while serving exquisite delicacies as the first food and drink, due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a great vessel of flesh.
He has been suffering from being burned by fire until this day, without respite. Do you see that second vessel? Is it not a vessel?
It is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained monastic who lacked the five virtues and served the Saṃgha [with improper intent].
He was in charge of the kitchen. He would consume the soft, delicious offerings for himself first, while distributing the coarse, bitter, and inferior food to the Sangha.
Because of these causes and conditions, he has entered hell and been made into a great vessel of flesh, suffering as it is burned by fire, without ceasing even until now.
As for the third vessel you see, it is not actually a vessel; it is a person from the hells who, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, was a *śrāmaṇera* (monastic attendant) for the Sangha.
When preparing food and drink, if one first tastes and eats what is exquisite and fine, or gives it to one's wife and children, while setting aside what is coarse, bitter,
and poor to distribute among the Sangha, by reason of these causes and conditions, one will become a great vessel of flesh in hell, suffering the torments of being burned by fire.
It continues to this day without ceasing. This is the repentance for the retribution of one's sins.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita: "That which you see as the first jar is not a jar."
This person is a denizen of hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained monk who served as the kitchen steward for the Saṅgha.
He would set aside food intended for the morning meal until the following day, and food intended for the following day until the third day.

Because of these causes and conditions, he has entered hell and been made into a large vessel of flesh, suffering the torments of fire that continue unabated even to this day. As for the second vessel you see, it is not he.
"Is this a jar? This is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who resided permanently in a monastery.
There were several donors who presented jars of ghee as an offering to the assembly of monks present; it was to be divided among everyone. This man was the official in charge of the matter."
He saw a visiting monk who remained hidden behind him; only after the visitor had departed did he divide [the food].
Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and was made into a large vessel of flesh, suffering as it was scorched by fire without ceasing even until now.
The person you previously saw standing in the water was not a bhikṣu, but a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant. For...
The monk was in charge of the water. Seeing the monks using the water, he would supplement it only at his own discretion;

where it suited him, he would provide enough, but the remainder he did not give out. Because of these causes and conditions, he fell into hell. Standing alone amidst the water, he cries out, "Water! Water!
and undergoes great suffering that continues even now without ceasing. [I now] repent for this retribution of sin.

That which you see as a large jar is not a jar; it is a person from the hells. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monastic who served as the steward for the Sangha’s fruits and vegetables.
He would first eat for himself those that were fragrant, delicious, and beautiful, while giving the sour fruits and bitter vegetables to others according to his own whims.
Because he acted with such inequality, by reason of these causes and conditions, he has entered into the hells. Thus it was made.
In a great vat of flesh, they suffer being burned by fire, which continues without ceasing even to this day. This is the retribution for their sins; repent!
As for the bhikṣu you saw whose nose was cut off with a blade, he was not a bhikṣu; he was a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, [he...]
This was a renunciant who, while on the pure ground of the Buddha and the Sangha, defiled the earth with his mucus and saliva.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell, where his nose was sliced off with knives and he suffered being burned by fire; even until now, his suffering does not cease.
You see this bhikṣu holding an axe in his hand and cutting out his own tongue, but he is not a bhikṣu—he is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant śramaṇa...

Śrāmaṇera, while you were dividing the rock honey for the community of monks, you cut it into portions; however, a small amount of the honey clung to the edge of your axe, which you then licked and ate.
Because of this cause and condition, you have suffered the torment of having your tongue cut, which continues unabated to this day. We repent for this retribution of your transgression.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita: "That which you see as a spring is not a water spring;

it is a person from the hells. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained śrāmaṇera who served honey for the Saṃgha. He would first taste it himself before offering it to the community of monks.
Because he reduced the amount and did not distribute it equally, by this causal condition, he has entered the hells and become a great pool of flesh and fire."
They are scorched and boiled until they are ruined, undergoing great suffering and affliction that even now has not ceased. This is the retribution for their sins; I repent on their behalf.
As for the bhikṣu you see standing upon the spikes, he is not a bhikṣu; he is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, [he was a bhikṣu who...]
This person was a renunciant who, by means of harsh speech, reviled and cursed the bhikṣus.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and stands upon iron spikes, suffering as he is burned by fire, which continues unabated until now. What you see as a meat canopy is not a canopy;
it is a person from among those in hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who resided permanently in a monastery and possessed the five virtues.
He was not virtuous. As the kitchen supervisor for the Saṃgha, he would first eat the finest and most delicious food himself, or sometimes give it to laypeople to eat.

With a mind full of arrogance and partiality, he distributed [the remaining food] to the assembly of monks. Because of these causes and conditions, he has been undergoing the sufferings of hell until now, without ceasing.
That which you see as a meat stake is not actually a stake; it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was...

This renunciant lived as a permanent resident in a monastery. On the walls of the monastic quarters, he recklessly drove in various wooden stakes for no purpose other than to hang his own robes and alms bowl.
Due to these causes and conditions, he has entered hell and become a great stake of flesh, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now.
I repent for this karmic retribution.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita: "That which you see as a camel is not actually a camel; it is a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this being was a renunciant and served as the senior monk (upādhyāya) in a monastery. He habitually received his own portion of food, or even the portions belonging to one or two other people.
When a bhikṣu who upheld the Vinaya instructed him according to the Dharma, the senior monk [refused], saying: 'It is not the way of a senior monk...'"
Thus it was. At that time, the old bhikṣu replied to the Vinaya Master, saying: "You know nothing; your voice is like that of a camel.
Among the assembly, I am the Elder (sthavira). When I offer blessings, preach the Dharma, or occasionally perform chants (geya), you should consider my labor and grant me what is due.
Why do you always scold and reproach me? Because of these causes and conditions, I have entered hell and received the body of a camel, being burned by fire."
They wail, and even now it does not cease. As for the horse you see, it is not actually a horse; it is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he served as a monastery attendant (śrāmaṇera) and consumed an excessive amount of the monastic offerings.
He gave some to his relatives, acquaintances, laypeople, and other bhikṣus. When the bhikṣus rebuked him, saying, "You should not do this," that man spoke with evil words and reviled them.
"Monk, you are just like that horse who was never sated by its fodder.
Because I performed great labor for the Saṃgha and deserved the merit thereof, due to these causes and conditions, you entered hell and received the body of a horse.

Your body was burned by fire, and you have suffered great torment that continues unabated even until now. As for the elephant you saw—it was not a white elephant; it was a person from hell," said Kāśyapa.
At that time, there was a monk who served as the kitchen supervisor for the Sangha. Various donors brought offerings to the monastery to give to the monks;
some arrived after the meal had already begun. A donor said, "Venerable Sir, the sun has not yet set; please strike the *ghanṭā* to assemble the Sangha so they may receive this food.
The bhikṣu, speaking with harsh words, replied to the layperson, "The bhikṣus are just like white elephants."
"He did not eat his fill. Having finished eating the previous day, he remained idle until the following day.

Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and received the body of a white elephant, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even to this day. That which you see as a donkey is, in truth, not a donkey."
This person is a denizen of hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who served as the kitchen supervisor for the Saṃgha.

Not possessing the five virtues, he constantly took for himself two or three people’s portions of the monks’ food and drink. A bhikṣu learned in the Vinaya reprimanded him in accordance with the Dharma.
That person replied, "I am in charge of the monastery kitchen, as well as the orchards, fruits, and vegetables; I constantly manage the affairs of the Sangha with great toil and hardship.
Yet you bhikṣus do not recognize my kindness; you are like donkeys who care for nothing but your own bodies. Why do you not remain silent?"
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and has suffered in the body of a donkey until now, without ceasing. As for the ram you see, it is not actually a ram;
it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained monk who served as the administrator of a monastery.
While inside and outside the fields, he personally supervised every matter. He did not command his disciples or the junior bhikṣus to strike the gong or beat the drum according to the Dharma.
The various vinaya masters said to the monastery head, "Why do you not strike the mallet at the proper time to assemble the saṃgha?
The bhikṣu replied, "I must attend to the affairs of the saṃgha, which is extremely laborious and exhausting. You bhikṣus are just like rams, eating and grazing."

And so he remained. Why did he not strike himself? Because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and took the form of a ram, suffering the agonizing pain of being burned by fire, which continues unabated to this day. This is the retribution for his sin; may it be confessed.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita: "Do you see that meat-platform? It is not actually a platform;

it is a person from the hells. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who, while managing the bedding and furnishings of the monastic quarters, would lock the monastery doors and take the keys for himself as he traveled in all directions.
Consequently, the community of monks was subsequently deprived of both their bedding and their dwellings."
Because of these causes and conditions, they entered hell and were made into a great flesh altar, where they suffer being burned by fire, which has not ceased even until now.

As for the second great flesh altar you see, it is not actually an altar; it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who served as the administrator of a monastery.
He selected the best rooms for himself to enjoy and gave them to his acquaintances, failing to follow [the monastic rules].

Because the distribution of rooms according to the sequence of the precepts was unjust, for this reason they entered hell and became a great meat-platform, suffering myriad forms of torment that continue unabated to this day. That which you see as a room of flesh is not actually a room of flesh;
it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this one was an ordained monk who lived in a monastic cell and treated it as if it were his own. In the end...

Their bodies do not move. Because they did not follow the precepts in dividing the rooms in due order, as a result of these causes and conditions, they dwell in a great chamber of flesh where they suffer from being burned by fire, which continues without ceasing even to this day. This is their retribution for sin; may they repent.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita: "What you see as a rope-couch made of flesh is not actually a couch; it is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who took possession of the community's rope-couches as if they were his own.

He did not distribute the couches according to the sequence prescribed by the Vinaya. Because of these causes and conditions, he has entered hell and become a fleshly rope-couch, where he suffers being burned by fire."
They suffer, and even now their torment does not cease. As for the second rope bed you see, it is not actually a bed; it is a person from the hells.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who broke a monastic rope bed and used it to kindle a fire.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered the hells and became a flesh rope bed, suffering as it is scorched by flames, even now without respite. As for the flesh mat you see—

This is not actually a bedding; it is a person from the hells. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who used the monastery’s bedding as if it were his own, treading upon it with his feet and failing to follow the precepts.

Due to these causes and conditions, he has entered the hells and become a fleshly bed, being burned by fire and stretched and contracted, undergoing ten thousand kinds of suffering that continues unabated to this day. You see this flesh...
This "fleshly restraint" (kukṣepa) is, in truth, not a restraint; it is a person from the hells.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this individual was a renunciant who treated the Sangha’s restraints as his own private property. He did not rely on the Vinaya, but instead used or destroyed [the requisites].
Due to these causes and conditions, he has entered the hells and become a "fleshly restraint," suffering the torments of fire that continue unabated until now. You see this fleshly rope-bed.

This is not actually a bed; it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who relied upon the power of a king and appeared to possess the virtues of a sage.
Consequently, the fourfold assembly of disciples praised him with sincere hearts.

At that time, the bhikṣu silently accepted their praise and received fine rope beds and various excellent foods, accepting them as if he were a sage. Due to these causes and conditions, he has entered hell.

In this prison, they are made into flesh rope-beds and suffer being burned by fire; this has not ceased even until now. As for those you see as flesh walls, they are not actually walls at all, but are hell-beings.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who drove stakes into the walls of the Sangha’s quarters and broke through the walls to hang their robes and bowls.
Due to these causes and conditions, they have entered this hell and become great flesh walls of fire.
They suffer from being burned, and even now it does not cease. What you see as a meat-rope is not actually a rope; it is a person from the hells.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who took the communal property of the Saṃgha and used it for his own private purposes.

Because of these causes and conditions, he has fallen into hell and become a great meat-rope, suffering from being burned by fire, which continues unabated until now. What you see as a latrine well is, in reality...

This is not a latrine or a well; it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this individual was a renunciant who went to a bhikṣu monastery—a pure area for the Buddha and the Sangha—and relieved himself without regard for the location.
A bhikṣu who upheld the Vinaya reprimanded him according to the Dharma, but he refused to accept the instruction.
The foul stench of his excrement permeated all the monks. Due to these causes and conditions, he has entered into hell. He is...
The Flesh-Privy Well: suffering from being burned by fire, which continues without ceasing even to this day. To repent for this karmic retribution:

you who saw the Dharma Master on the high seat were not actually a Dharma Master; he was a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who did not understand the Vinaya-piṭaka.
He explained what is grave as light, and what is light as grave. Regarding those with roots of virtue, he spoke of their transgressions...

He has no roots of virtue. This man who lacks roots of virtue claims that he possesses them; he says he should repent when he ought not to repent, and he insists on repenting when he should not repent.
Because of these causes and conditions, he has entered hell and sits upon a high seat, suffering as he is burned by fire, which continues without ceasing even until now.
As for the second high seat you see, that is not actually a Dharma master; it is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this great Dharma master preached the Dharma through wrong livelihood. Where he obtained offerings and sustenance, he spoke according to the truth;
when there was no gain, he preached non-Dharma as Dharma and Dharma as non-Dharma. Due to these causes and conditions, he fell into hell.

They sit upon high iron seats, suffering from being burned by fire, which has not ceased even until now. As for those you see crying out with the sound of meat-drums (*mudgara*), they are not actually drums;

they are beings from the hells. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who used the property of the Triple Gem to strike drums unlawfully, feigning the performance of *karmavācanā* (formal monastic procedures). They seized the property of the Triple Gem for their own personal use. Because of these causes...
Due to these conditions, he entered hell and became a flesh *gaṇḍī* drum. He suffers there as it is burned by fire, and his torment has not ceased even until now.
What you see as a *kūśmāṇḍa* is not actually a *cīvara*; he is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was an ordained monk who served as the master of a monastery.
He used the food from the monastic kitchen to trade for goods, which he then used to make clothing for himself, thereby cutting off the offerings to the Sangha. Because of this—
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a "fleshly *kīṭika*. He suffers being burned by fire, and it has not ceased even until now.

You see that second *kūṣmāṇḍa*; it is not actually a *kīṭika*, but a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who served as the *vaiyyāvṛtyakara* (distributor) for the distribution of goods in the monastery.
He took items intended for the spring distribution and transferred them to the summer distribution; during the summer...
Regarding his clothing: during the middle of winter, because of these causes and conditions, he entered hell and became a *māṃsa-kūṣmāṇḍa* (flesh-demon).
He suffers there, burned by fire, without ceasing even until now. As for the mountain of flesh you see, it is not actually a mountain of flesh; it is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this being was a renunciant who served as the *karmadāna* (steward) for the Saṅgha. Lacking the five virtues and possessing a modicum of authority, he stole...

They misappropriated the property of the Sangha and destroyed the robes of the Sangha. Because of these causes and conditions, they fell into hell and became a great mountain of flesh, suffering as it was scorched by fire, which continues unabated even now. This is the confession of their karmic retribution.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita: "The *sumanā* pillar you first saw was not actually a pillar;
it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who served as a lay donor (*dānapati*) to the fourfold assembly within the Buddha-field."
He scattered *sumanā* flowers as an offering to the Buddha. Once the flowers had withered, a bhikṣu swept them up and sold them for his own use.
Because of this cause and condition, he entered hell and was made into a *sumanā* pillar, suffering as he is burned by fire, which has not ceased even until now.
Kāśyapa, that second *sumanā* pillar you see is not actually a pillar; it is a person from hell.
At that time, this renunciant was a monk who had received offerings from the fourfold assembly of donors for the sake of the Buddha.
He used *sumanā* flower oil to make offerings to the Buddha, but he then took some of it for his own personal use. Because of these causes and conditions, he fell into hell.
They were made into *sumana* pillars, and they suffer being burned by fire, which continues without ceasing even until now. As for the flowering trees you see, they are not actually trees;
they are inhabitants of hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were monastics who were in charge of the monastery’s orchard of fruits and vegetables.

Because there were fine flowers and fruits, they used them for their own private benefit or gave them to laypeople. Due to these causes and conditions, they have entered this hell and become great flowers.
This tree is one that suffers from being burned by fire, a state that has not ceased even until now. What you see as a flesh-fruit tree is not actually a fruit tree;

it is a person from the hells. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was a renunciant who, when presented with fragrant, delicious fruits intended for the Sangha, ate them privately or gave them to laypeople.
Because of these causes and conditions, he entered the hells and became a flesh-fruit tree, where he is burned by fire.
They suffer, and even now it does not cease. That which you see as a tree of flesh is not actually a tree; it is a person from the hells.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monastic who served as fuel for the Saṅgha. He used the Saṅgha’s firewood to kindle fires spontaneously within his quarters, or gave it to his acquaintances.
Due to these causes and conditions, he has entered the hells and become a great tree of flesh, suffering as it is burned by fire even until now.
[The suffering] does not cease. This is the confession for the retribution of one's sins.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita: "That which you see as the first pillar of flesh is not actually a pillar;
it is a person from hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monastic who resided permanently in a monastery and violated the Buddha-field."

A pillar. Because he used it for his own private purposes, by this cause and condition, he entered into hell and became a great pillar of flesh, suffering as it is burned by fire, which continues without ceasing even until now.
As for what you see as the second pillar of flesh, it is not actually a pillar; it is a person from hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this layperson scraped off the gold leaf from atop a statue with a knife. Due to this karmic cause, he fell into hell and was reborn as a great pillar of flesh.
There, the hell-wardens seized axes and hacked at his body as he endured suffering, while fierce flames scorched his person.
It continues thus without ceasing even to this day. As for the third pillar of flesh you see, it is not actually a pillar; it is a person from the hells.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a renunciant who served as an administrator for the Sangha. He misappropriated a beam or pillar belonging to the Sangha and gave it away to a layperson.
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered the hells and became a great pillar of flesh, suffering the torment of being burned by fire without ceasing even to this day. You...
He saw four trees of flesh, which were not actually trees, but were four sinful persons—beings from the hells. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who lacked the five virtues.
Serving as leaders of the great assembly, they adjudicated matters for the Saṅgha; yet, acting according to their own attachment, fear, hatred, and delusion, they rendered unjust judgments.
By this cause and condition, they entered the hells and became these four trees of flesh, where they undergo suffering while being burned by fire.
Suffering continues unabated even until now. Those whom you see as fourteen trees are not actually trees; they are inhabitants of hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who resided permanently in a monastery. They did not distribute bedding and seating according to the Vinaya, but instead took for themselves whatever was superior, or else acted with favoritism based on anger and attachment, discriminating between those they liked and those they disliked. Within the Buddha-dharma, there were bhikṣus as numerous as motes of dust in the sands... [who should have been...]

They received [the fruits] in succession because of their inequality. For this reason, these fourteen people fell into hell and became great trees of flesh, suffering from being burned by fire without ceasing even until now. As for those two bhikṣus you saw, they were not actually bhikṣus;
they were inhabitants of hell. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who, amidst the great assembly, engaged in strife and contention.

"Strike! Because of these causes and conditions, they have entered the hells, where their bodies are scorched by fire and they suffer the pain of being beaten, which continues without ceasing even until now.
As for those two novices you see, they are not actually novices; they are inhabitants of hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were ordained novices who slept together, embracing one another within a single blanket and bedding. Because of this cause and condition, they have entered the hells."
They are burned by fire within their bedding while embracing one another in suffering; this has not ceased even until now. This is the confession for the retribution of their sins.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita: "For this reason, I now tell you:
among those in the hells, the number of those who have gone forth is great, while those who remain as laypeople are few. Why is this? Because among those who have gone forth, there are many..."

They take pleasure in violating the prohibitions and precepts, do not comply with the Vinaya, and mutually oppress one another. They privately appropriate monastic property or divide food and drink without impartiality.
For this reason, I now reiterate my exhortation to you: you must diligently uphold the precepts and receive them upon the crown of your head in practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita: "I shall now tell you: these sinners, in past lives, left the household life but broke the precepts.
Although they were not diligent, the fourfold assembly of donors saw that these bhikṣus possessed a dignified demeanor resembling that of true monks."
By reverently making the fourfold offerings to the Sangha Jewel, one can still obtain great rewards that are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
I further tell you: it is like those offenders mentioned previously who, having gone forth in a former life, violated the property of the Sangha.
They shall fall into the great hells. Furthermore, in future ages, there will be laypeople who take the property of the Sangha;
their sin shall exceed that of the aforementioned monastics by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond measure. I speak this again to you.

If there is a single bhikṣu who conforms to the Vinaya and practices the Way according to the Dharma within the saṃghārāma, striking the gong at the proper time—if one makes offerings to such a person, the merit obtained is still vast and cannot be fully described; how much more so when making offerings to the Saṃgha of the four quarters!
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita: "If a renunciant is occupied with the affairs of the Saṅgha, it is difficult for them to maintain pure precepts.
When these bhikṣus first left the household life, they delighted in maintaining pure precepts and possessed the aspiration for nirvāṇa. [Yet now] the fourfold assembly of donors..."
When making offerings, these bhikṣus should accept such offerings while firmly upholding the pure precepts, so that no affliction arises later.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Observing the precepts is the greatest joy; The body does not undergo any afflictions. One sleeps in peace and, upon awakening, the mind is filled with gladness.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he further addressed Saṃgharakṣita: "There are nine kinds of people who dwell eternally in Avīci."
Within the great hells, what are the nine? First, consuming the property of the Sangha; second, consuming the property of the Buddha; third, killing one's father;
fourth, killing one's mother; fifth, killing an Arhat; sixth, causing a schism in the harmonious Sangha;
seventh, violating the pure precepts of a bhikṣu; eighth, violating a bhikṣuṇī of pure conduct; ninth, becoming an icchantika. These are the nine kinds of persons.
They dwell perpetually in hell. There are five kinds of persons who receive retribution in two places: first, in hell; second, as hungry ghosts.
As for those in hell, they are like the various hells you have seen. As for those who are hungry ghosts, their bodies are tall and large.
What are these five? First, to obstruct the giving of property to the Saṃgha; second, to obstruct the giving of food to the Saṃgha; third, to plunder the offerings given to the Saṃgha;
fourth, to cause those who ought to receive gifts not to receive them; and fifth, to preach what is Dharma as non-Dharma and preach what is non-Dharma as Dharma.
These five types of persons receive these two retributions; yet because their remaining karma is not exhausted, they undergo it within the five realms of existence. At that time...
World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, I speak these verses:
"Committing evil brings rebirth in hell; Practicing goodness receives celestial joy. If one can cultivate the concentration on emptiness, One will exhaust the outflows and realize nirvana."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Saṃgharakṣita: "The dragon king whom you saw in the ocean has received this dragon body with its tusks, claws, and scaly horns;
its form is terrifying, foul-smelling, and difficult to approach. Because of this state of being an animal, he is obstructed from the Dharma of renunciation."

It also obstructs the cultivation of dhyāna, and one lacks the fruit of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). Although one may attain a long life, one cannot escape being devoured by the King of the Garuḍas.
After the end of that life, one is reborn in Tuṣita Heaven; when one's lifespan there is exhausted, one receives a human body.
When Maitreya appears in the world, one becomes a great elder with wealth in the hundreds of millions, acting as a great donor (*mahādānapati*) to provide offerings and support.
They provided the World-Honored One Maitreya and the bhikṣus with the four requisites in full. These five hundred elders simultaneously left the household life and attained the fruit of arhatship;
their achievements were lofty and their fame far-reaching, such that they were well known to all.

If even these dragon kings were able to attain such merit and virtue, how much more so my disciples who leave the household life in accordance with the Dharma, practicing seated meditation and recitation?

Those born must return to death; Created by sin, they are oppressed by all manner of suffering.

His mind is unshakable, and so it is with respect to the Buddha’s body. When one is about to become a Noble Knower, if one realizes that the mind is equal toward all Buddha-dharmas, and the two [dualistic] thoughts do not appear before one, one shall tread upon the inconceivable stage.

Abiding nowhere and entering nowhere, one shall become a rare-to-be-meeting one. Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise without number;
if one possesses such wisdom, one shall become a Great Muni who sees both the mundane and the supramundane, transcending all while being able to skillfully know all phenomena.
One shall become a great radiance; if, regarding all-knowingness, one gives rise to the mind of dedication and perceives that the mind is unarisen, one shall obtain great renown.
Since sentient beings have no mind and likewise no destruction, if one attains such knowledge, one shall accomplish the unsurpassed path.
Within one, understand the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, understand the one. Realizing their mutual arising, one shall attain fearlessness.

Regarding sinful karma, one should confess and repent it openly.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas eliminate that which remains. There are three kinds of 'that which remains':
first, the remaining retribution of afflictions; second, remaining karma; and third, remaining existence (*bhava*). Good son, what is meant by the afflictions..."
The retribution for causing affliction to others: if there are sentient beings who habitually indulge in sensual desire, because this retribution ripens, they fall into hell.

Upon emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—namely, pigeons, sparrows, mandarin ducks, parrots, *kīra-kīra* birds, *śārika* birds, blue jays, fish, turtles, monkeys, gazelles, and deer. If they should obtain a human body, they take on the form of a eunuch or a woman.
If a person with two sexual organs, one without sexual organs, or a courtesan were to leave the household life, they would incur the first grave precept; this is called a residual retribution.

One must repent for the karmic retribution of such offenses. Furthermore, son of good family, if there are sentient beings who, with a mind of intense earnestness, habitually cultivate and draw near to anger, the retribution for that will ripen.
Therefore, they fall into hell. Emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals, namely venomous snakes endowed with four kinds of poison:
the poison of sight, the poison of touch, the poison of the bite, and the poison of the breath. They may also become lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, cats, weasels, hawks, or falcons.
If they obtain a human body, they are fully possessed of the sixteen types of evil non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). If they leave the household life as a monastic, they commit the second [offense].
The heavy precepts. This is called a residual retribution. One must repent for the retribution of one’s offenses.
Furthermore, son of good family, if there is a foolish person who practices [these transgressions], when that retribution ripens, they will fall into hell.
Upon emerging from hell, they will receive the body of an animal—namely, an elephant, a pig, an ox, a sheep, a buffalo, a flea, a louse, or a mosquito.

The forms of gadflies, ants, and the like; or, even if one obtains a human body, being deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired, crippled, maimed, or suffering from spinal sores, such that the sense faculties are incomplete and one cannot receive the Dharma;

or, even if one leaves the household life, having dull and obtuse faculties and frequently violating the grave precepts, up to the five *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses—these are called residual retributions (*avaśeṣa-vipāka*).
One should repent for these karmic retributions of sin.
Furthermore, good son, if there are those who practice pride, when that retribution ripens, they fall into hell.
Emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—namely, dung-worms, camels, donkeys, dogs, or horses.

If they are born among humans, they receive the bodies of slaves or servants, becoming impoverished beggars; or if they occasionally leave the household life, they are constantly held in contempt by sentient beings.
"Base. To violate the fourth precept is called a residual retribution (*avaśeṣa-vipāka*). Such as these are termed the residual retributions of afflictions.
Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to cultivate the Great *Nirvāṇa*, he completely eliminates them all. This is the repentance for karmic retribution.

What are residual karmas? They refer to the karma of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the karma of all *śrāvakas*, the karma of a *srotāpanna* for receiving seven more existences, the karma of a *sakṛdāgāmin* for receiving two more existences, and the karma of an *anāgāmin* for receiving existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
These are called residual karmas. Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*), he [transcends] such residual karmas.
All are completely severed. Having repented for the retribution of their sins, what remains?
Arhats attain the fruit of arhatship; pratyekabuddhas attain the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood.
Without karma and without fetters, yet they undergo the two fruits; this is called "remaining existence" (*avaśeṣa-bhava*).
The confession of karmic retribution—these three kinds of dharmas that have a remainder—are eliminated by a bodhisattva through the practice of the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s elimination of remaining existence and the confession of karmic retribution.
The *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "You should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks.

Originally, there were no worlds or sentient beings; it is due to delusion that birth exists, and due to birth that cessation exists. Birth and cessation are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called the True.
This is designated by the two titles of the Tathāgata’s Unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa, which are the two transformations of the basis. Ānanda!

If you now wish to cultivate the true samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of perversion regarding sentient beings and the world. When perversion does not arise, this is the true samādhi of the Tathāgata.

Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of sentient beings? Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the nature of the mind is perfectly full, one takes that luminosity as a basis to give rise to this nature.
From this, deluded vision arises; from that which is ultimately non-existent, there is established that which is ultimately existent. This existence is what they perceive as existing.
It is not the cause of causes, nor the abode of abodes; it is realized to be fundamentally without root. Relying upon this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established.
Being deluded regarding the original perfect luminosity, this gives rise to the false. The nature of the false has no substance and has nothing upon which it depends.

Desiring to return to the Real, one seeks the True; yet that which is sought as "True" is not the True Nature of Suchness. Seeking to restore what is not true results in the complete formation of non-characteristics.

These are neither arising nor abiding, neither mind nor dharmas; they arise from one another in succession. The power of this arising brings forth illumination, and through perfuming, karma is formed.
Karmas of the same kind respond to one another; because there is karmic response, they mutually extinguish and mutually produce. For this reason, sentient beings undergo perversion.
[Regarding] the repentance for the retribution of offenses:
Ānanda, what is meant by the "perversion of the world"? It is that which exists as having something; through this, false segments are produced. Because of this...
The realms are established. They are not caused by causes; they have no abiding place yet abide therein. Constantly shifting and never remaining still, through this the world is formed.
The three times and the four directions intermingle in harmony, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories. Therefore, in the world, sound arises from movement;
form arises from sound; fragrance arises from form; touch arises from fragrance; taste arises from touch; and [smell arises] from taste.
One who knows the Dharma understands that the six types of disordered deluded thoughts constitute the nature of karma; through these twelve divisions, one revolves in saṃsāra.
Therefore, the world’s sounds, smells, tastes, and touches undergo twelve transformations and return as a single cycle.

Because one rides upon this revolving wheel of inverted appearances, there exist worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth; those with form and those without form; and those with perception.
Neither non-perception; neither with form nor without form; neither with perception nor without perception. This is the repentance for the retribution of offenses.
Ānanda, because the world revolves through false delusions and the inversion of movement, the harmonious combination of these energies forms the eighty thousand [kinds of life].

Four thousand beings with chaotic thoughts of flying and sinking; because of this, there are those born from eggs and the *kalala* stage, who transmigrate through various lands as fish, birds, tortoises, and snakes, filling every category.
This is the retribution for their transgressions; now they repent.
Due to the inversion of desire within the world’s defiled cycle of saṃsāra, eighty-four thousand types of horizontal and vertical chaotic thoughts are formed through their conjunction and growth.
Thus, there exist the stages of the embryo—kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana—as beings transmigrate through various lands as humans, animals, nāgas, or seers.
These types fill the world. Regarding the repentance for the retribution of their offenses:
because they cling to the cycle of rebirth due to the inversion of the realms of existence, the combination of warmth gives rise to eighty-four thousand forms of inverted and chaotic thoughts.
Consequently, there are moist-phase *piśāca* spirits that transmigrate through lands, containing crawling and wriggling creatures.
These species fill the world. As for the repentance for karmic retribution:
due to the causes of the world’s shifting cycles and false inversions, the conjunction of sensory contact produces eighty-four thousand types of new and old chaotic thoughts.
Because of this, there arise the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of transformation, which circulate through various lands, undergoing metamorphosis and flying about.
These types fill the world. Regarding the repentance for karmic retribution:
due to the causes of worldly obstructions, the cycle of rebirth, and inverted views, they combine and adhere to form eighty-four thousand thoughts of chaotic radiance.
Consequently, there arise material forms and *kalala* (embryonic stages), which circulate through various lands as auspicious or calamitous spiritual essences.
Their kind fills [the world]. Regarding the repentance for karmic retribution:
because the causes of the world’s dissolution lead to the confusion and inversion of saṃsāra, the union of darkness forms eighty-four thousand obscure and chaotic conceptions.
Thus there exist formless kalala, which flow through the lands, dispersing into emptiness and sinking away.
These types are so numerous as to fill all space. Regarding the repentance for the retribution of their offenses:
because the world is characterized by illusory, revolving shadows and inversions, they combine with recollections to form eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts.
Consequently, there arise the *kalala* (embryonic stage) of conceptual signs, which flow and circulate through various lands as gods, ghosts, and spirits.
These types fill the world. Regarding the repentance for karmic retribution:
due to the causes of the world’s dullness, cyclic existence, delusion, and inversion, they combine with stubbornness to form eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts.
Because of this, there are non-perceptive kalala embryos that circulate through the lands, their spirits transformed.
Earth, wood, metal, and stone—these types fill the world. As for the repentance for karmic retribution:
because the world revolves through mutual dependence, falsehood, and inversion, they combine and form eighty-four thousand delusive thoughts based on causal conditions.
Thus, there arise non-material forms that take on material characteristics as *kalala* (embryonic stages), circulating through various lands.
The various jellyfish and similar creatures take shrimp for their eyes; such species fill the world. This is a karmic retribution for which one must repent.
Because the nature of cyclic existence is inverted by the mutual attraction of worldly phenomena, these beings combine through incantations to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning.
Thus, there exist those that are neither formless nor yet have the *kalala* stage of embryonic development, as they transmigrate through various lands.

Curses and spells arise; their kinds fill the world. This retribution for transgressions is repented through the cycle of delusion that joins the world together, due to the inversion of cause and effect. Through the harmonious blending of these differences, eighty-four thousand types of protective and chaotic discursive thoughts are formed.
Consequently, there exist the *kalala* (embryonic stage) characterized by non-existent perceptions and the formation of signs, which circulate throughout the lands.
Those such as the *pulu* (parasitic larvae) and others are formed from the transformation of different substances; their kind fills the world.

This retribution for sin is due to the repentance [of past deeds] and the inversion of killing within the cycle of enmity and harm in the world. Through the combination of strange conditions, they form eighty-four thousand types that harbor the notion of eating their own parents.
Thus, there exist these non-non-perceptive and non-perceptive *kalala* (embryonic stages), which circulate throughout the lands.
For example, the earth-owl and its kind take clods of earth as their offspring, and the "broken-mirror" bird takes the fruit of poisonous trees to raise as its young;
once the offspring have grown, both parents meet their end at the hands of those very children. Such species abound. This is the retribution for one's transgressions; now, one must repent.

These are called the twelve types of sentient beings. Ānanda, within each of these classes of sentient beings, there are likewise twelve kinds of inversions, just as flowers appear when one presses upon the eyes.
These inversions distort the wondrous, perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind, resulting in such fully developed false and chaotic conceptions. [This concludes] the repentance for karmic retribution.
As you now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, you must establish three gradual stages to eliminate the fundamental causes of your original deluded thoughts.
It is like removing poisonous honey from a clean vessel by using various hot waters mixed with ashes and incense.
One cleanses the vessel so that it may later hold nectar. What are the three stages of gradual progression? First, through cultivation, one eliminates their auxiliary causes.
Second, through true cultivation, one hollows out their fundamental nature. Third, through further advancement, one opposes their manifest karma.
"What is the contributory cause? Ānanda, these twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves by their own power;

they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment, namely: edible food, contact-food, volition-food, and consciousness-food. For this reason, the Buddha said that all sentient beings abide by means of nutriment.
Ānanda, all sentient beings live because they consume what is sweet and die because they consume poison. Thus it was said.
Sentient beings who seek *samādhi* should sever the consumption of the five kinds of pungent vegetables. These five pungents, when eaten cooked, arouse lust;

when eaten raw, they increase anger. Thus, in this world, those who eat pungent things—even if they can expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures—will be shunned by the celestial beings of the ten directions because of their foul stench. Furthermore, various hungry ghosts, on account of them...
While eating, they lick their lips; they constantly dwell with ghosts, and their merit and virtue daily diminish, resulting in no long-term benefit.
When those who eat pungent roots practice *samādhi*, the Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and virtuous deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them.
A powerful Mara-god, seizing this opportunity, manifests in the form of a Buddha to preach the Dharma to them, disparaging the prohibitions and precepts while praising sexual misconduct.
Driven by anger and delusion, at the end of their lives they become members of the retinue of Māra. Once their demonic blessings are exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Ānanda, those who cultivate Bodhi must forever renounce the five pungent vegetables; this is called the first stage of progressive cultivation.

"What is right nature? Ānanda, for such sentient beings to enter samādhi, they must first strictly maintain pure precepts, forever sever lustful thoughts, abstain from wine and meat, consume food purified by fire, and never eat raw or living things. Ānanda," [he said].
For such a practitioner, if they do not sever sexual desire and abstain from killing, it is impossible for them to transcend the three realms.
One should regard sexual desire as being like a venomous snake or as encountering a hostile enemy; first, one must uphold the four parājikas and eight parājika-like offenses of the śrāvaka.
Holding the body motionless, one subsequently practices the pure discipline of a bodhisattva; holding the mind so that it does not arise, one achieves the perfection of the prohibitive precepts.
Thus, within the world, there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing; theft and robbery will not occur, and there will be no mutual burdens of debt.
Furthermore, in this world, they do not fail to repay their past debts; such are pure persons who cultivate samādhi.
Without needing the divine eye, their physical bodies naturally perceive the worlds of the ten directions, behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and personally receive the holy instructions.
Attaining great supernormal powers, wandering through the worlds of the ten directions, with a pure past life and freedom from all hardships—
this is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.
What is manifest karma? Ānanda, when a person thus purely upholds the prohibitive precepts, their mind is free from lustful desire and does not flow excessively toward the six external sense objects.
Because they do not flow outward, they revolve back to the source and return to themselves. When the sense objects are no longer conditioned, the faculties have nothing with which to pair.
The flow is reversed and the one essence is restored; the six functions cease to operate. The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like—
A bright moon hangs within the lapis lazuli; body and mind are blissful. Wondrous, perfect, equal, and impartial, one attains great peace and stability.
All the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of all Tathāgatas appear therein. This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
From this point on, they gradually cultivate, establishing themselves in the stages of sagehood according to their initial practices. This is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.
Gradually, we were shrouded by ignorance and failed to recognize the causes of transgression within the twelve classes of beings and their karmic retributions.
Now that we have encountered this site of enlightenment, we are finally able to awaken to this knowledge. We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy sages.
I burn incense and scatter flowers. I confess and repent all karmic retributions of the twelve classes of beings, not daring to conceal anything.
By these causes and conditions, may all karmic retributions of myself and the ocean of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm be entirely purified.
Next, the mudrā for repentance and the eradication of transgressions: Oṃ sṛmbara-pabha-mi-sphuṭa-natha-namadra-ye svāhā.
(Recite this three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas are entirely swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
All that has arisen from my body, speech, and mind, I now confess it all.
Having confessed, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Recitation: May the assembly listen to these verses on impermanence from the Sūtra:
Just as one awakens from sleep and experiences [the dream], So too, when performing various Buddha-activities for the Saṃgha, One takes this as the object of focus; No past events are seen.
In this present body of mine, immeasurable enemies and kin have already passed away;
for the karma created by them, which is truly terrifying, I must now face it.
Knowing that this body is not firm or enduring, I do not yet understand this matter.
All are caused by ignorance, greed, and hatred, Through which immeasurable karmic offenses are committed.

The Liturgical Rite for the Constant and Universal Prostration and Repentance Based on the Tenfold Vows and Practices of the Sea-Seal Bodhimanda from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huìjué, the National Preceptor Hùfǎ of Cí'ēn Temple at Yúnyán on Mount Lán during the Táng Dynasty, based upon the Sūtra.
