Next is the Night Goddess who Protects All Cities,

Namo to her, the Night Goddess who is the Sovereign of Increasing Power who Protects All Cities, having attained the liberation door of the Profound and Sovereign Sublime Sound within this assembly of Tathāgatas at this site of enlightenment.
All in the ten directions take refuge; Sins are extinguished and pure faith increases. May they be born in the Flower Treasury Sea and the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Next is the Repentance of the Blind Dragon and the Starving Dragon.
I only pray that the inexhaustible jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha within the celestial net, Vairocana Tathāgata,

and the assembly of holy beings of Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the ocean-like gathering— through the compassionate original vows of worldly and world-transcending deities— may emit great radiance to illuminate this dharma assembly.
May you bear witness and protect us with your mindful care; may you look upon us with compassion and grant your acceptance.

I pray that for myself and the ocean of all sentient beings, from the beginningless past until this very moment, throughout the inexhaustible ocean of karma—with its infinitely nested Indra-nets of merit and demerit and their retributions within the dragon realm—I now reveal and repent.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: At that time, within the assembly gathered before the Buddha, there was a blind nāga named Phalaki-riśa who raised his voice and wept bitterly, saying:
"O Great Sage, World-Honored One, I pray you save me! I pray you save me!
All Buddhas are compassionate and take pity on all beings; yet now, within my body, I endure great suffering and affliction day and night."
They are devoured by various insects, small snakes, and frogs; dwelling in hot water, they find no pleasure for even a moment.
The Buddha said, "Reṣa, in a past life, you were once a bhikṣu within the Buddha-dharma.

You violated the prohibitions and precepts, harboring deceit within while outwardly manifesting various signs of virtuous conduct and dignified demeanor. You greedily sought after a vast circle of relatives and disciples."
His fame spread far and wide, such that there was no one who did not hear of it. His disciples spoke thus: "Our preceptor has attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Because of this, he received great offerings; yet having received these offerings, he consumed them all alone.
When he saw those who maintained the precepts, he instead treated them with harsh words. Those people were distressed and thought to themselves: "In birth after birth..."
"In the midst [of this], I pray that wherever I may be, I shall eat the flesh of your body. Because of such evil karma, you died and were born among the dragons.

It is due to the vows made by sentient beings in your previous lives that they devour your body. Through the causal conditions of this evil karma, you have received the retribution of being a blind dragon, dwelling in hot water.
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, you were within the hell of molten red copper, constantly [suffering] for the sake of all..."
As they were being devoured by the insects, the assembly of nāgas, having heard these words, wept in sorrow and lamentation, saying:
"We now, with all our hearts, together offer repentance; may we be swiftly liberated from this suffering."
If there are any sentient beings who, though having obtained a human body,
commit all manner of evil deeds and fail to make offerings to the Triple Gem,
after death they will gather all manner of suffering and fully experience the torments of hell and the hungry ghosts.
Even if one should obtain the body of a nāga king, yet one’s retinue, wife, and children are all impoverished, hungry,
and afflicted by various torments; lacking the wish-fulfilling jewel upon the crown of the head,
one dwells in empty marshes teeming with venomous insects, where the waters are parched and perpetually dry.
All this is due to the past: having once been a bhikṣu in the Buddha-dharma,
or having seen an ascetic practicing austerities in an araṇya, one harbored jealousy and stinginess, begrudging food and drink,
and when a visiting bhikṣu came to stay, one felt anger and resentment, with a heart full of displeasure.
The donor gives food and drink with impartiality, yet therein he obstructs [the recipient] and reviles him, saying:
"Even if there were pure, fine flowing water, it would be filled within with excrement, urine, and filth;
all places where one dwells, walks, or sits would be foul, stinking, and utterly impure."
Should there be those who maintain pure precepts, upon seeing such [a place], they will all avoid it;
even if there are virtuous people elsewhere who hear of this, they have no desire to come here.
Because of the causes and conditions of their own evil karma, those people will fall into hell for immeasurable eons after death.
In the Ash River and the Boiling Excrement, they endure the burning of red copper; for immeasurable billions of years, they suffer such agonizing torment.
Among such hungry ghosts, they are parched with hunger and thirst, never having heard even the name of water or gruel.
As a further retribution, they are born again within the realm of dragons, where they undergo suffering and hardship for many long years.
Though they have obtained the bodies of nāgas, they are constantly hungry;
wherever they are born, there is no water—be it in parched marshes or on treacherous mountains of withered reeds.
Deprived of water, eternally dry, and lacking food or drink, once dead they repeatedly enter the hells, where great fires and scorching torments pervade their entire bodies.
Having wandered thus through hungry ghosts for immeasurable years,
there is no means of rescue other than practicing dhyāna; by revering and making offerings to the Buddha Tathāgata,
observing the precepts, cultivating wisdom, studying the vast teachings, and exerting diligence to abandon thoughts of stinginess and pride.
The poisonous mind of jealousy is the most evil; One must sever the causal conditions of this karma.
Recall that at the time of death you will suffer this calamity; Without any doubt, repent early!
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, twenty-six billion hungry nāgas from among the assembly of nāgas...
Recalling their past bodies, they all shed tears and spoke thus: "We only pray that the World-Honored One of Great Compassion will take pity on us and deliver us.
We recall that in a past life, although we had left the household life within the Buddha-dharma,"
Having committed such various evil karmas, because of those evil deeds, he has spent immeasurable lifetimes in the three evil realms.
Furthermore, due to the remaining retribution, he was born among the nāgas and undergoes extreme suffering, just like the Blue Nāga; I am also like this.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the nāgas, "You may take water to wash the Tathāgata’s feet, so as to cause your calamity to end."
Their sins were gradually extinguished. At that time, all the nāgas reached into the water with their hands, but the water turned entirely into fire;
it transformed into great stones that filled their palms and burst into fierce flames. Even after they cast them away, the stones would reappear. This occurred as many as seven times.
When the entire assembly of nāgas saw this, they were struck with terror and anguish, weeping and shedding tears like rain. The Buddha addressed the nāgas: "You have committed these transgressions."
Through karma, one receives this evil retribution; those who cultivate wholesome karma receive good fruits. I now instruct you to speak a vow of truth:
"If the Buddha, the Guide, out of compassion for all, has been without duplicity toward sentient beings throughout his life, may these words not be false;
by this truth, may the flames of my dragon-fire be extinguished. Having made this vow, the flames were all extinguished. At that time, the starving dragon...
They repeated this up to eight times, cupping water in their hands to wash the feet of the Tathāgata, and with sincere hearts they repented:

"From this day forward, we shall no longer commit evil. Having thus repented, each addressed the Buddha, saying: "The Tathāgata is greatly compassionate; we pray that you will save us. The Buddha said:
"O nāgas, the remainder of this evil karma of yours is not yet exhausted. In the age of Maitreya Buddha, you shall attain human birth."
He was born with a physical body and encountered a Buddha, whereupon he left the household life. Through diligent application and upholding the precepts, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.

At that time, the various nāgas gained the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvajātismṛti*) and, reflecting upon their own past karma, wept until their faces were drenched in tears. Each spoke thus:

"I recall how, in the past, within the Buddha-dharma, whether due to the causal conditions of being relatives of laypeople, or again due to the causal conditions of coming and going to hear the Dharma, all..."
With faith, they offered various flowers, fruits, and food and drink, which they shared with the bhikṣus and consumed together.
Some said, "I have partaken of the flowers, fruits, food, and drink of sentient beings from the four directions.
Others said, "I went to the monastery and gave alms to sentient beings," or "I prostrated to them," and thus partook. Or again, some said, "I [partook of the offerings of] the Vai..."
In the Dharma of Vipaśyin Tathāgata, he once served as a layperson; or again, some say that in the Dharma of Viśvabhū Tathāgata, he once served as a layperson;
or again, some say that within the Buddha-dharma of Krakucchanda, [he once served as a layperson].
Some say that I was once a layperson during the teachings of Vipaśyin Buddha;
others say I was once a layperson within the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Tathāgata;
and still others say I was once a layperson within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha. Or, he may be questioned by former acquaintances.

Regarding the causes and conditions: perhaps due to the circumstances of coming and going to hear the Dharma, or traveling to and from monasteries, there were faithful people who, in order to make offerings to the Sangha, gave gifts of flowers, fruits, and various kinds of food and drink. When the bhikṣus received these, they shared them with me;
having received them, I ate them. By reason of that karmic cause, within the great fierce fires of hell, I have passed through immeasurable kalpas. Or...
They are burned or boiled; they drink molten copper and swallow iron balls. Emerging from the hells, they fall among the animals.
Shedding their animal bodies, they are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). Thus they undergo all manner of bitter sufferings.
As their evil karma remains unexhausted, they are born among these *nāgas*, constantly enduring affliction: hot water rots their bodies, hot winds blow upon them, and there is hot sand and hot soil.
Excrement, heat, and ashes—when food enters their mouths, it turns into copper needles or iron balls.

At all times, whatever they eat causes their mouths to burn upon entering, their throats to rot upon passing through, and their bellies to seethe upon reaching them; it passes straight through and falls to the ground.
Their entire bodies are pierced with holes, and they undergo such suffering that it is unbearable. We pray only that the Tathāgata will take pity and deliver us from this. The Buddha [responded].
He addressed the nāgas: "This evil karma is no different from stealing the property of a Buddha.
Although the monk who committed this deed bears only half the guilt, because he has not yet exhausted the retribution for this sin, it is difficult for him to attain liberation.
You all should now fully receive the Three Refuges and cultivate goodness with a single mind. By virtue of this cause, during the Bhadrakalpa, you shall encounter the final Buddha, named..."

He replied, "Lohita. In the world of that Buddha, your sins shall be extinguished. When the dragons heard these words, they all with sincere hearts, for the remainder of their lives, each received the Three Refuges and repented for the retribution of their sins.
At that time, within that assembly, there was a blind nāga girl whose mouth was festering and rotting, filled with various kinds of worms;
it was like excrement and urine, even as foul and loathsome as the impurities within a woman’s private parts, unbearable in its stench and putridity, and being devoured by all manner of creatures.
Pus and blood flowed from all her limbs, which were constantly being bitten by mosquitoes, gadflies, and various venomous flies.

The stench of her body was such that it was difficult even to look upon or hear of. At that time, the World-Honored One, with a heart of great compassion, saw that the female nāga was blind and suffering in this manner, and asked: "Sister, for what reason did you obtain this wretched body? In a past life..."
"What karma did I perform in the past? The nāga wife replied, "World-Honored One, this body of mine is now oppressed by manifold sufferings without a moment's respite.

Even if I wished to speak, I am unable to do so. I recall that for thirty-six billion hundred-thousand years in the past, I was born among the evil nāgas and underwent such suffering, which continued day and night, without ceasing even for a single kṣaṇa. For my sake...
In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, she was a bhikṣuṇī.
Her thoughts on sensual desires were more intense than those of a drunkard; although she had left the household life, she could not practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Within the monastery, she prepared beds and mats, repeatedly committing unchaste acts. Driven by a mind of eager desire, she gave rise to feelings of great pleasure, or was greedy for them.
He sought the property of others and accepted many offerings from the faithful.

Because of this, for ninety-one kalpas he was constantly unable to receive a body as a deva or human, remaining perpetually in the three evil realms where he underwent various forms of burning and boiling. The Buddha asked again: "If it is so..."
"When this kalpa comes to an end, Sister, where will you be reborn? The nāga woman replied, "By the causal conditions of my past karma, I shall be born in another world.
When that kalpa there comes to an end, driven by the winds of evil karma, I shall return here to be born again. At that time, the nāga woman—
Having spoken these words, she said: "O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, please rescue me! Please rescue me!
At that time, the World-Honored One scooped up water with his hand and addressed the nāga girl, saying: "This water is called *kṣetrapati* mixed with medicinal herbs.
I now speak these words in truth: in the past, for the sake of saving a pigeon, I relinquished [my own body]."
"Regarding my body and life, I shall never harbor doubt or give rise to a mind of stinginess. If these words are true, may all your malignant afflictions be completely cured.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, took water in his mouth and sprinkled it upon the body of that blind nāga woman.
All her malignant afflictions and foul odors were entirely healed. Once she had recovered, she spoke these words: "I now beg the Buddha to grant me [the precepts]."
The Three Refuges. At that time, the World-Honored One immediately conferred the three refuges upon the dragon girl and had her repent for her karmic retribution.
At that moment, there was another dragon among the assembly whose mouth was filled with all manner of foul-smelling insects.
Pus and blood flowed from his throat and mouth. Those who saw or heard of this all fled and abandoned him.
When the Buddha saw this, he immediately asked, "Good son, what evil karma did you commit in the past to receive such retribution?
That nāga opened his mouth, and from within it emerged various kinds of worms; pus and blood overflowed like a blazing fire. Although...
He opened his mouth again, but was ultimately unable to speak, and immediately closed it once more. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of that nāga:
"Because of the karmic conditions of theft in the past, And having treated a holy person with levity, you have received this retribution."
"Listen with utmost sincerity to these words of truth, and you shall immediately attain coolness and extinguish all suffering.
At that time, having spoken these words of truth, the World-Honored One poured a small amount of water into the dragon's mouth;
the fire, as well as the worms and pus, were all completely extinguished, and his mouth became cool. He then spoke these words: "O Great Sage Tathāgata, I recall the past..."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I was once a layman plowing a field. A bhikṣu came and begged from me for fifty coins.
I replied at that time, "Wait until the grain is ripe; I shall give you food then. The bhikṣu spoke again:
"If even fifty coins cannot be obtained, I pray you will grant me ten.
At that time, I became angry with that bhikṣu and said to him, "I will not give you even ten coins. Then, that bhikṣu felt deep distress in his heart.

Furthermore, at another time, he went to a monastery and entered beneath a grove of trees, where he immediately stole ten *āmra* fruits belonging to the resident monastic community and ate them in private.
Due to the causal conditions of that karma, he suffered in hell; as his evil karma was not yet exhausted, he remained there.
Born in a wild marsh, he takes the form of a starving dragon, constantly being devoured by various kinds of insects. Pus and blood flow profusely, and he suffers the torments of hunger and thirst.

Furthermore, due to the causal conditions of his evil karma and a mind of wrathful anger, that bhikṣu dies and immediately becomes the body of a small venomous dragon, born beneath my armpit. It sucks at my blood, and the touch of its hot breath upon my body is unbearable.

"Therefore, my body is burning and filled with pus and blood. The nāga addressed the Buddha, saying, "Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, I pray that you will take pity on me and rescue me, so that I may be liberated from that vengeful, venomous dragon. At that time, the World-Honored One scooped up some water with his hand.
He utters words of truth, speaking thus: "In the past, during a time of famine, I made a vow to become a being of great body, vast and immeasurable in length and breadth.
By means of my supernormal powers, I proclaimed these words from within the midst of space:"
"In that marsh there is a large-bodied insect named 'Non-Anger. You all should go and take its flesh for food and drink;
thus you shall not suffer from hunger. When the humans and non-humans of that world heard these words, they [acted accordingly].
Everyone went there to compete for and eat them. When these words of true and sincere faith were spoken, the small dragon from the armpit of that [great] dragon emerged.
Then these two dragons both addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how long will it be before we leave this dragon body and are liberated from our calamity and transgression?
The Buddha told the dragons: "This karma is extremely heavy, second only to the five actions of immediate retribution. Why is this?"
Therefore, if there is property belonging to the permanently resident Sangha of the four quarters, or property belonging to the present Sangha, or items bestowed with deep faith by a donor—
whether flowers, fruits, trees, gardens, food and drink, means of livelihood, bedding, mats, or medicinal decoctions for illness, or anything else required—
and one privately consumes these or takes them outside to give to acquaintances or relatives; [this constitutes an offense].
"O lay followers, this offense is heavier than the retribution suffered in the Avīci Hell. Therefore, you should receive the Three Refuges.
Only after taking refuge in the Triple Gem may you remain within these cold waters. Thus he spoke three times, and they received the precepts three times.
His body immediately became peaceful and secure, and he was able to enter the water.
Having repented for his karmic retribution, at that time the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of the nāgas:
"Better it would be to cut one's own body with a sharp blade— The limbs, joints, flesh, skin, and muscles."
It is truly difficult for a layperson to consume any gift offered out of faith;

it would be better to swallow a large, glowing red iron ball until flames burst from one's mouth than to privately use for oneself any food or drink belonging to sentient beings that has been offered to the Sangha. One must not use such things for private purposes.
It would be better to take up a great fire as large as Mount Sumeru with one's own hands and eat it oneself;
it is not right for lay householders to divert food intended for the Sangha to eat themselves.
It would be better to use a sharp blade to butcher one's own body and devour one's own flesh, skin, and membranes.
There are laypeople among the householders who should not accept mixed food from the Saṃgha;
it would be better to cast one's own body into a room filled with a great, raging fire than to do so.
There are also those among the householders who should not sit or lie upon the beds and mats belonging to the Saṃgha.
It would be better to grasp a red-hot iron spike with one's own fist until it is scorched and charred,
than for a layperson living at home to privately appropriate the property of the Sangha.
It would be better to use a sharp, excellent blade and a block to cut the flesh from one's own body, piece by piece.
One should never give rise to even a single thought of anger toward a person who has left the household life for purity;
it would be better to gouge out both eyes with one's own hands and cast them away upon the ground than to look upon one who practices the wholesome Dharma with a mind of resentment and malice.
It would be better to wrap one’s body in glowing iron sheets than, while moving, rising, walking, sitting, or lying down,
to harbor a mind of anger, resentment, or envy toward sentient beings who have offered pure robes.
It would be better to drink alkaline brine or salt water that is boiling hot and searing the mouth like fire.
"One should not harbor the poisonous mind of greed; one should partake of the pure medicine offered as a gift to the Sangha.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, fourteen thousand dragon hosts all received the Three Refuges.
They shall attain liberation from all past and present karmic retributions and various sufferings, and with deep faith in the Triple Gem, their resolve shall never regress.
Furthermore, there were eight billion nāgas who likewise gave rise to a heart of refuge and reverence toward the Triple Gem.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya: "Observe these evil sentient beings; they have deceived themselves."
With the mind—whether out of fear of poverty, or out of dread regarding the evil realms—one practices wholesome dharmas.
Whatever various requisites for life a bhikṣu may obtain are all gifts bestowed by faithful donors;
yet these sentient beings either consume them themselves, give them to others, or steal and hide them away from the community.
Storing [wealth] for private use—due to such karma, one falls into the three evil realms and undergoes diligent suffering for a long time.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are poor, lowly, and without autonomy; for this reason, they leave the household life in the hope of attaining abundance, liberation, and peace.

Yet, once they have left the household life, they become indolent and lazy, failing to recite the scriptures or to apply themselves diligently to meditative concentration and wisdom, abandoning these practices.

He took pleasure in attending to the affairs of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, day and night, applied himself with diligence, delighting in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas, reciting the sūtras, practicing dhyāna, and training in wisdom without ceasing for even a moment.
Because of these causes and conditions, he moved the fourfold assembly to provide him with various kinds of offerings.
When the administrators saw that such gains and sustenance had been obtained, they either consumed them for their own private use or stole them to give to their relatives and old friends.
Worldly people, due to such causes and conditions, dwell for a long time in the evil realms; having emerged, they enter them again.
Thus deluded and ignorant, they do not perceive the lightness or gravity of future retributions. I now exhort you, my śramaṇa disciples:

mindful of the Dharma and maintaining it, you must not claim of yourselves, "I am a śramaṇa, a true practitioner of the Dharma," nor, relying upon the Saṃgha, [misappropriate] the offerings of others' faith, whether they be cakes...
Whether it be vegetables, fruits, or flowers—whatever items are for the consumption of the Sangha—one must not give them to any layperson at will.
Nor should one say, "This is my own property," and eat separately from the assembly.

Furthermore, one must not use the property of the Sangha to accumulate wealth, engage in various forms of trade, or claim such activities are beneficial; to do so invites the world's censure and reproach. Moreover...
It must not be so. To buy low and sell high, competing with the world for profit, causes all sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.

We repent of these karmic retributions. Enshrouded by ignorance, we failed to recognize the causes of sin within the dragon realm; only now, having encountered this site of enlightenment, do we finally awaken.
I know. I take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy and holy ones. I offer incense and scatter flowers.
I confess and repent for the karmic retributions of my dragon rebirths; I dare not conceal them.

By these causes and conditions, may the karmic offenses of the dragon realm—my own and those of the ocean of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, as vast as the layered net of Indra—be entirely purified.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for repentance and the eradication of transgressions: Oṃ sarvapa-pame-si-put-nadaha-nadama-draya svāhā.
(Recite three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas are all swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose entirely from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
I now repent of everything produced by my body, speech, and mind.
Having repented, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Recitation: Listen, all of you, to these verses on impermanence from the Sūtra:
"At the time when this present life and one's kinsmen Must all be abandoned in this way, And one goes alone toward a single destination, Of what use are friends and those who are not?"
Because of committing unwholesome deeds, one gives rise to suffering and affliction; how may one attain liberation from them?
Now, throughout the day and night, I shall constantly and exclusively focus my mind upon this single matter:
the Ritual for Constantly and Universally Paying Homage and Repenting According to the Tenfold Vows and Practices of the Sea-Seal Dharma-Assembly in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Scroll Thirty-Five.
Compiled by the Dharma Master Huguang of Yunyan Cien Monastery on Mount Lan during the Tang Dynasty; based on the scriptural records by the Śramaṇa Huizhao;
supplemented with annotations by the Śramaṇa Pueri of Caiguang Monastery on Mount Cang during the Song Dynasty.
Enlightened by the Emperor’s decree honoring loyalty and righteousness, compiled by the Buddhist disciple Mu Zeng, Provincial Governor of Sichuan;
revised by the śramaṇa Du Che of Jiguang Temple on Mount Ji;
and finalized by the śramaṇa Zhengzhi, who studied the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school.
The thirty-fifth session:
Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), during the fourth assembly with the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*),
one pays all-respectful homage to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
All these people knelt on their right knees, reverently holding incense and flowers to make offerings according to the Dharma.
May this ocean-like cloud of offerings pervade the worlds of the ten directions. Or again, they may bestow solid incense-carts with wheels made of various jewels, magnificent and grandly adorned;
with jeweled canopies covering them above and jeweled nets hanging down below, various precious garments spread within, all pure and stainless.
The fine incense flows with its fragrance penetrating far and wide; its scent is exquisite and pleasing to the hearts of men.
Immeasurable devas attend him as he travels, carrying him with precious treasures provided at all times.

Or again, they grant him radiant jeweled chariots, wherein various jewels of wondrous colors shine through, and nets of diverse exquisite gems are spread over them, while necklaces of assorted jewels encircle them on every side.
Hanging down, they are sprinkled with powdered incense, making both the interior and exterior fragrant and pure. With such various wondrous jewel chariots, one constantly makes offerings.

Layer upon layer like Indra’s net, the oceans of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages receive these clouds of offerings as luminous terraces, vast as boundless realms, immeasurable and inexhaustible; may they perform the work of the Buddha.
Having made these offerings, they all paid homage with reverence.
Next, they presented the most excellent Seven-Jeweled Mountains, consisting of vast oceans of the nature of precious lattices and jewels.
I bring forth such clouds of offerings as these and present them to all the Buddhas. Oṃ sarva-tathāgata-arcanā-pracāra-samaya-śrīye hūṃ.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: There is a dhāraṇī called the "Spell of Immeasurable Varieties," which can accomplish all things and possesses great efficacy.
The dhāraṇī is: Oṃ sīmala sīmala mīmada sigrāmaha liṅga huṃ.
Next, Mahamati, the mantra is: Oṃ namaḥ sarvatathāgatānām avalokiteśvara-sambara sambara hūṃ.
The Brahma-voice praises the Buddha:
Just as all phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions, so too is the vision of the Buddha;
it must depend upon various virtuous deeds. Like a wish-fulfilling jewel, he is able to satisfy the hearts of sentient beings.
Such is the nature of all Buddhas: they fulfill every aspiration.
When the Guides arise in the world within immeasurable lands, by virtue of their power of vows, they universally respond throughout the ten directions;
I now speak these words in praise of the Buddha.
Upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head is the mark of a Great Man adorned with thirty-two jewels.
Among these marks of a Great Man is one named "Illumination," which universally pervades the infinite nets of great light throughout the ten directions.
It is adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels, encircled by jeweled garlands that are soft, dense, and finely woven, each emitting the radiance of *maṇi* gems that fill [the space].
They fill all boundless worlds, manifesting everywhere the body of a Buddha with perfectly complete physical marks. This is the first [major mark].
Furthermore, there is a major mark named "Universal Illumination," which is the supreme locus of clouds of adornments for the entire dharma-realm.
Within it, Jāmbūnada-gold Indra-nets gradually rise up in succession as adornments, emitting clouds of pure light.
They fill the dharma-realm. In every thought-moment, they constantly manifest within all worlds at the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is the thirty-second. O Son of the Buddha, upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, there are these thirty-two kinds of marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), which serve as his adornment.
Homage to the Buddha Vairocana, the Original Honored One of Unobstructed Ten Bodies in the Flower Treasury World-Ocean of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha,
who with great kindness and compassion made five hundred vows to save sentient beings from suffering in the five turbidities.

Homage to the Buddha Bhaisajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha-rāja, King of Medicine with Lapis Lazuli Light, who possesses twelve supreme vows to save beings from suffering in the world-system of Pūrṇacandra in the eastern direction.
Homage to the Buddha Amitābha, who possesses forty-eight vows to save beings from suffering in the world-system of Sukhāvatī in the western direction.
Homage to the Perfect Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, throughout all lands as numerous as atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time;
homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, who presides over the truth of the Vows and Conduct within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*.
Homage to the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who presides over faith, understanding, and realized wisdom within the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara of a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes, who possesses great kindness and great compassion, rescues from suffering in the five turbidities.

Homage to him whose great vows are profound and far-reaching, who rescues from suffering in the five turbidities, appears in worlds where no Buddha dwells, and constantly abides to comfort the hearts of sentient beings.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbharāja in the realm of Yama;

homage to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment, throughout all the lands as numerous as atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Homage to the assembly of all oceans of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in the oceans of lands throughout the entire Dharma-realm;
and homage to the fifty-five holy ones who realized and manifested the five stages of practice during the final assembly of the Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra.

Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sudhana, who, as a vessel of perfect capacity and superior faculties within the final assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, sought the Dharma through a hundred cities;
who, within a single lifetime, perfected the practices of a bodhisattva, and serves as the model for cultivation and realization for the sudden teaching of the final age.

Homage to all Buddha-activities— including the *dharmakāya*, the physical forms, the relic-sharīra, the precious stupas, and the monasteries— within all dust-mote lands throughout the entirety of space across the ten directions and the three periods of time;
and further, to the ocean-like assemblies of Bodhisattvas, worthy ones (*ārya*), and sages within the Dharma-treasury and at all places where the Dharma is preached.
Namo to the Great Vow, Clad in Armor, Seeking Rebirth in the Pure Land, Protector of the True Dharma in the Degenerate Age, Guardian of the Nation, National Preceptor. With a sincere heart,
I take refuge and pay homage to the Bhagavān, the World-Honored One, the Honored One of the Flower Treasury Ocean World-System within the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya.

To Vairocana Buddha, throughout the ten directions, I take refuge; May my transgressions be extinguished and my pure faith increase; May I be born within the Lotus Treasury Ocean, in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The *Saptamī Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasvāminī-rātridevatā-bodhisattvotpādavipulaprītiprabhā-vimokṣadharmaparyāya-sūtra* states:
"At that time, the youth Sudhana [arrived]... (omitted)... gazing up at her with earnest devotion, he took his leave and departed."
Vowing to be reborn together with all sentient beings in the Flower Treasury Ocean within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss;
next, the place where the Night Goddess Who Causes All Tree Blossoms to Open first resolved her mind:
Homage to the Buddha [of this land]. Within the ocean of worlds called Universal Radiance True Gold Mani Mountain, there are as many worlds as there are atoms in a world.
In every single world-system of the world-realms, a Tathāgata appears in the world;
each such Tathāgata bestows predictions of enlightenment upon as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field.
To all the ocean-like assemblies at these sites of enlightenment—namo to the Tathāgata Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm, Wisdom Mountain, Tranquil Majesty King!
Next, I pay homage to the Night Goddess who Causes All Tree Blossoms to Bloom,
who attained the liberation door of the "Vast and Great Joyful Light of the Birth of Bodhisattvas" within this assembly of the Buddha at the site of enlightenment.
I pay homage to the Night Goddess who Causes All Tree Blossoms to Bloom.
All in the ten directions take refuge; Sins are extinguished and pure faith increases. May they be born in the Flower Treasury Ocean and the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Eighth Great Vow: The Power of Diligence to Rescue and Protect All Sentient Beings. The Night Goddess who Knows the Teachings.
The *Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of Transforming Sentient Beings to Give Rise to Roots of Goodness and Attain Liberation* states:
"At that time, the youth Sudhana (having arrived... joined his palms, gazed up with reverence, took his leave, and departed."
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the ocean of the Flower Treasury and within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Next, [I pay homage] to the Buddhas of the initial stage of excellence in the eon of Radiant Light, in the world of Jewel Radiance, at the place where the Night-Spirit Great Vow and Diligence Power first generated the mind of enlightenment.
Homage to the Tathāgata Dharmacakraghoṣagaganapradīparāja.
Homage to the five hundred all Tathāgatas. Homage to the Tathāgata Mahākāruṇika.
Homage to the Tathāgata Lokahitāvaha. Homage to the Tathāgata Mahākāruṇikasimha.
Homage to the Tathāgata Savior and Protector of Sentient Beings; homage to the Tathāgata King of Physicians;
homage to Krakucchanda and the other thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, as well as all the great Bodhisattvas, numbering one million asaṃkhyeyas.
Homage to the Tathāgata Immeasurable Vigor Power Renown Merit Wisdom;
homage to the Tathāgata Dharma-Emptiness King; homage to the Tathāgata Heavenly King Treasury;
homage to the Tathāgata Great Earth Power Mountain; homage to the Tathāgata Dharma-Wheel Light Sound King.
Homage to the Tathāgata King of Space-like Wisdom; homage to the Tathāgata Invincible Banner;
homage to the Tathāgata King of the Thunderous Sound of All Dharmas; homage to the Tathāgata Universally Manifesting the Transformed Proclamation of Dharma-Sound;
and homage to these ten thousand Tathāgatas such as these.
On the following day, during the Kalpa of Radiance, [I pay homage] to all the Buddhas:
Namo to the Tathāgata Wondrous Appearance Mountain; Namo to the Tathāgata Perfect Shoulders;
Namo to the Tathāgata Stainless Youth; Namo to the Tathāgata Valiant Sustainer.
Homage to the Tathāgata Sumerukūṭa. Homage to the Tathāgata Vimalabāhu.
Homage to the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrāntagāmī. Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin.
Homage to the Tathāgata Dharmottarasaṃghuṣṭa. Homage to the Tathāgata Prabhāketu.
Homage to these sixty billion Tathāgatas and so forth;
homage to all the ocean-like assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of these immeasurable Buddhas;
and next, homage to the Night Goddess Great Vow and Power of Diligence.

Homage to the Night Goddess, Sovereign Who Protects All Sentient Beings through the Power of Great Vows and Diligence, who is surrounded by a sea-like assembly before and behind her at this site of enlightenment, and who has attained the liberation door of teaching and transforming sentient beings to cause them to produce roots of goodness.
Homage to the Night Goddess who possesses the power of great vows and diligence, who protects all sentient beings, who guides and transforms according to their capacities,
who brings practices to fruition through the teachings, and who accords with reality by departing from obstacles—

homage to her twenty-four bodies. Homage to all such [goddesses], as many as they are unspeakably unspeakable, who manifest boundless transformations according to sentient beings and move throughout the world.
The eighty-nine kinds of quiescent non-duality, even unto a hundred bodies pervading all form-bodies throughout the ten directions—to all these I take refuge.
May my sins be extinguished and my pure faith increase; may I be born within the Flower Treasury Ocean in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The *Dharmaparyāya on the Liberation Door of the Sovereign Power of Manifesting Birth Everywhere Known by the Ninth Night Goddess,
Perfectly Virtuous Excellence* states:
"At that time, the youth Sudhana (proceeded until) he gazed up at her with earnest devotion and took his leave to depart."
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Next, [I take refuge in] the Buddha from whom the Night Goddess Samantaguṇaviśuddhavyūhā attained the Dharma:
in the world-system Sarvaratna, during the eon of Rati, eighty nayutas of all Buddhas appeared.
Homage to the Buddha Sovereign Merit Banner.
Next, to the Night Goddess Sublime Virtue Perfection.

Homage to the Night Goddess Subhūṣitā, Sovereign of Perfect Virtue, who attained the liberation door of the sovereign manifestation of birth in all places throughout immeasurable eons within the Lumbinī Grove of this Jambudvīpa;
she to whom the ten directions all turn for refuge— may she extinguish my sins, increase my pure faith, and may I be born in the Flower Treasury Ocean.
The Tenth: The Dharma Gate of the Liberation for Observing the Ocean of Samādhis of All Bodhisattvas, Attained by Gopā’s Daughter within the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the youth Sudhana (until) circumambulated him countless times, took his leave, and departed.
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean and within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Next, [the section] explaining the place where the maiden Gopā attained the Dharma and the Buddha [therein].
Homage to the Buddha Victorious Sun-body at the Dharma-Cloud Radiance Bodhimanda in the world-system Fearless during the first *vīrya-caryā-kalpa*.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Jewel Flower of the Bodhimanda, who manifests the bodies of all world-protectors;
next, to the Buddhas who appeared after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Sun Body;
homage to the Buddha Pure Body; homage to the Buddha Moonlight Body of All-Knowledge.
Homage to the Buddha Jāmbūnada-suvarṇa-prabhāsa-rāja. Homage to the Buddha Sarva-lakṣaṇa-vyūha-kāya.
Homage to the Buddha Candra-prabha. Homage to the Buddha Jñāna-darśana-dhvaja.
Homage to the Buddha Mahājñāna-prabha. Homage to the Buddha Vajra-nārāyaṇa-vīrya.
Homage to the Buddha Invincible Power of Wisdom. Homage to the Buddha Universal Serene Wisdom.
Homage to the Buddha Cloud of Stainless Supreme Wisdom. Homage to the Buddha Lion Wisdom Radiance.
Homage to the Buddha Radiant Topknot. Homage to the Buddha Banner of Merit Radiance.
Homage to the Buddha Wisdom-Sun Banner. Homage to the Buddha Body-Blossomed-Jewel-Lotus.
Homage to the Buddha Virtue-Adorned-Pure-Light. Homage to the Buddha Wisdom-Flame-Cloud.
Homage to the Buddha Universal-Illumination-Moon. Homage to the Buddha Adorned-Coverlet-Wondrous-Voice.
Homage to the Buddha Lion-Valiant-Wisdom-Light; Homage to the Buddha Dharma-Domain-Moon;
Homage to the Buddha Who Manifests the Reflections of Space to Awaken the Minds of Sentient Beings;
Homage to the Buddha Constantly Inhaling the Fragrance of Quiescence; Homage to the Buddha Universal Resonance of Tranquil Sound.
Homage to the Buddha Amṛtaparvata. Homage to the Buddha Dharmasāgaraghoṣa.
Homage to the Buddha Dṛḍhajālā. Homage to the Buddha Buddhacandrakeśin.
Homage to the Buddha Candrābhā-ūrṇākośa. Homage to the Buddha Pratibhānavaktra.
Homage to the Buddha Awakening Flower Wisdom. Homage to the Buddha Jewel Flame Mountain.
Homage to the Buddha Merit Star. Homage to the Buddha Jewel Moon Banner.
Homage to the Buddha Samādhi Body. Homage to the Buddha Jewel Light King.
Homage to the Buddha Samantaprajñācaryā. Homage to the Buddha Jvālārṇavapradīpa.
Homage to the Buddha Vimaladharmaghoṣarāja. Homage to the Buddha Anupamaguṇakīrtidhvaja.
Homage to the Buddha Dīrghabāhu. Homage to the Buddha Mūlapraṇidhivimalacandra.
Homage to the Buddha Śārdhārthapradīpa. Homage to the Buddha Gambhīrodātaghoṣa.
Homage to the Buddha Vairocanavijayagarbharāja.
Homage to the Buddha Sarvayānadhvaja. Homage to the Buddha Dharmasāramanipuṇapuṣpa.
Homage to all these sixty billion, hundred thousand nayutas of Buddhas;
homage to all these immeasurable Buddhas and their ocean-like assemblies at their sites of enlightenment.
Next, [the account of] Gopā’s daughter.

Homage to the Bodhisattva Sudhana, who was accompanied by eighty-four thousand celestial maidens and the goddess Śāntamati, and who attained the liberation of the ocean of samādhis for observing all bodhisattvas within this city of Kapilavastu.

Homage to the Deity of the Hall of Universal Manifestation of Dharma-Light within the Assembly of Bodhisattvas, who is surrounded by ten thousand palace-deities welcoming and praising the youth Sudhana; homage to the deity Śāntamati-guṇa.

Homage to those of the highest capacity, like perfect vessels, who sought the Dharma through a hundred cities and perfected the bodhisattva practices within a single lifetime for the sake of future generations.
To the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sudhana, the exemplar of the sudden gate of practice and realization in this world,

to whom all ten directions pay homage— I prostrate and pray that my transgressions be extinguished, my pure faith increased, and that I may be reborn within the ocean of the Flower Treasury and the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Next, for the confession of the karma of sentient beings receiving the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), I pray that the inexhaustible Triple Gem of the Dharma, the Buddha, and the Sangha; Vairocana Tathāgata;

the assembly of holy ones of Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the ocean-like gathering; and all mundane and supramundane deities, by virtue of your compassionate original vows, may emit great radiance to illuminate this dharma assembly.
May you bear witness and protect us with your mindful attention; may you compassionately accept and take us into your care.

I vow that for myself and the ocean of all sentient beings, from beginningless time until this very moment, throughout the succession of intermediate state bodies—vast as the infinite reaches of space, like Indra’s net, beyond end and fullness, visible to the Buddha-eye yet unknown to ordinary beings—I now repent them all.
The *Akṣobhyavyūha-mūlatantra* states: "If one practices the ten virtuous actions of the highest degree, one proceeds directly to the Pure Land by way of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).
If one commits the five crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) of the highest degree, one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.

These two types of persons do not undergo an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "In the case of extreme goodness or evil, when the present aggregates cease..."
The next body arises swiftly, like thrusting a spear that immediately strikes the ground. In this regard, if one’s evil karma is heavy, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
at the time of death, if the wind element disperses first, it is as if one's body were being sawn apart;
if the fire element departs first, it is as if one's body were being boiled in scalding water. These are summoned by one’s own evil karma. If the earth...
Regarding the statement that "the water element disperses first among the four elements": one will naturally experience peace and happiness, free from suffering and affliction;

this is the result induced by virtuous causes. If virtue and non-virtue are intermingled, then the phenomena of the four elements merging with one another as described in the *Akṣobhyavyūha Tantra* (Mi g.yo ba’i rgyud) and other such texts apply.
Furthermore, the meaning of the four elements merging at the time of death is also taught in various secret tantras. This is the composition... [end of fragment].

Those who possess a mixture of wholesome and unwholesome karma receive three kinds of intermediate state bodies (*antarābhava*). Compared to their previous original body (*pūrvakālabhava*), these are forty-six times more acute and intelligent. What are the three?

When a shadowy being—the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) subject to the karmic retribution of birth and death—hears the fierce and malevolent sounds of those kalpa-ending fires and black winds, it frequently manifests signs of terror, fear, and alarm; yet, while that intermediate state life has not yet come to an end, [it remains].

One immediately receives this retribution. Furthermore, whenever one sees lice, fleas, humans, animals, or others engaged in sexual desire, one immediately conceives a mind of attachment and delight toward them, desiring rebirth therein.
One takes great pleasure in death and finds no joy in life. This is the confession of such karmic offenses.
The second [type] consists of the seeds of the consciousness of a greyish, intermingled spirit, which possesses a body within a dream-like state.

During the interval before the arising of the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*), within that continuous process of rebirth, all the seeds of good and evil that have been perfumed within the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are activated, like the mental conceptions in a dream.
This is just as when one is currently asleep in this present life, even while experiencing sweet...
While eating and drinking, one is unaware of it. At the time of death, earth, water, fire, and wind successively dissolve into one another.

Then, wind and fire enter into consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness enters into manifestation (*ābhāsa*); manifestation enters into the gross; the gross enters into the subtle; the subtle enters into the extremely subtle.
Once that manifestation and the others have ceased in succession, like the state of sleep, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), objects, and so forth are like those in a dream at the moment of death.
After death, the arising of consciousness within the intermediate state (antarābhava) is likewise like this:
it is just as a drunken man who lacks all awareness and remains in a state of total delusion. [This concludes] the confession of karmic retribution.

Regarding the third type, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a white-colored deity, that which possesses a body is not like the first two types of intermediate states which abide in a state of mental obscurity;
rather, its mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is sharp and clear. The verse says:
Among those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are sentient beings;
their gathered sense faculties pass through mountains, rocks, walls, and barriers without obstruction. In a single instant, they can travel ten thousand *li*;
their karmic supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) possess great majesty. These seven types of intermediate bodies are seen by the pure eye.
Thus one should repent for the karmic retribution of the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) experienced therein.
First, the intermediate state body of those in hell has an appearance as ugly and foul as a charred stump.
Second, the intermediate state body of hungry ghosts (*preta*) is smoke-colored. Third, the intermediate state body of animals (*tiryagyoni*) is water-colored. Fourth, that of humans and...
The intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*) of the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens have bodies as magnificent and brilliant as gold.
Those of the six realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) have complexions like white silver. Those of the asuras and other such beings have complexions like the color of the blue sky.
These intermediate state beings may have two hands and two feet, or four feet and many feet, or four hands and two feet, or...
They are footless. Depending on the karma created in previous lives, they arise wherever they are destined to be born;

at the time of their cessation, the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) is also similar to the respective original body (*pūrvakālabhava*) of that particular realm. [This concludes] the repentance for karmic retribution.
If those among the gods possess an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), they are born moving upward with their heads facing up.

Those among humans, non-humans, animals, and hungry ghosts who possess an intermediate state body are born moving horizontally. Those in the intermediate state body of the hells are born moving downward with their heads facing down.
Due to these karmic causes, these seven types of intermediate state bodies undergo transformation; they all traverse through the air.
With the divine eye, one sees the place of one's own rebirth;

having repented for the retribution of one's transgressions, one observes that the person who previously received karmic retribution exists as an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) during the transition between birth and death.

Since at this time the objects of the previous stage have already ceased and the characteristics of the objects of the subsequent stage have not yet arisen, by performing superior roots of goodness for that deceased person, one will obtain great merit.
They do not undergo karmic retribution; like the rising sun dispelling darkness, all sufferings are entirely absent, and they experience great joy as if it were the present moment.

By the power of their previous merit, they transform that intermediate state body (*antarābhava*)—which is heavy and of an indeterminate nature due to evil karma—into an intermediate state body that is light and of a virtuous nature.
At the end of the first seven days, when that arising-and-ceasing intermediate state life comes to its conclusion, they pass away from that state.
Within the intermediate state of dream-like appearances, the mental body arises; this continues until one is reborn in a Buddha-land.
After one's original physical body has died, during the first seven-day period, for the first three days, one perceives that one’s own original body has already died.

Furthermore, for half a day thereafter, while still remaining [in that state], if one is a person who has cultivated merit and goodness, they will have no sense of fear. If, however, one has committed [evil deeds]...
The wicked experience great terror; if they see pits, ravines, fissures in the earth, or the interiors of stone caves and the like, they are filled with dread.
Within the state of taking birth in the realm of pleasure, there is the body. Furthermore, the *Śrīparamādya-tantra* states:
Abandoned by his kingdom and palace, separated from his wives, concubines, sons, and daughters,
he realizes that his consciousness has departed; struck with terror as he suddenly reaches the summit of Mount Sumeru,
he wails three times with a mournful cry, at which time the one who produces evil harm appears.
If its body remains as it was before, And when the body is absent, one awakens to its original nature—where was it in the past, and where has it gone?
It pierces mountains, penetrates walls, crosses great waters, and in the space of a single kṣaṇa, it roams through the realm of empty space. Furthermore, the *Tattvasaṃgraha* asks: "Where is it?"
Now, at this time of passing away and death, during the third watch of the night,
may I clearly perceive the circumstances of my own demise; I now repent for the retribution of these past karmic causes and conditions.
Furthermore, three and a half days after the first seven-day period has ended, those who have committed evil deeds manifest the signs of the three terrors and four fears.

The three terrors are the three evil destinies. The four fears are the sound of the waves of the great ocean, the sound of the sun, moon, and celestial deities, the sound of the arising of the kalpa-ending fire, and the sound of the rising of great winds. When these sounds emerge, [the following] arises:

Fearing [this], one receives such retribution. Thereafter, if one's relatives and others cultivate goodness and perform meritorious deeds, one should likewise cultivate merit oneself, as if one were an infant.
If one's relatives and others commit transgressions, one adds suffering to their suffering and further gives rise to fear, receiving the retribution of great suffering.
One must repent for these karmic offenses.
If one truly cultivates goodness, it is like raising a bright lamp that illuminates those deceptive evil habits and karmic obstructions; thus, the darkness of ignorance is utterly destroyed.
Through the accumulation of merit, the cultivation of goodness, repentance, and so forth, one should diligently perform the rites of dedication during the first seven-day period with utmost urgency.

Then, during the subsequent seven-week period, it is easier to attain liberation. If one does not diligently perform the rites of posthumous dedication during the first seven-week period, it will be difficult to rescue them during the subsequent seven-week periods. Why is this?

Because for those who have cultivated superior merit, as well as for those with lifespans in the human realm, the heavens of the desire realm, the heavens of the form realm, or among the intermediate states (*antarābhava*), [the duration] of the third seven-week period...

Within a day, one will certainly undergo rebirth. At that time, when distinguishing between the paths of good and evil, the manifestation of the *antarābhava* (intermediate state) body is not fixed in its nature.

Because the *antarābhava* body during the first seven days is entirely a transformation of one's own essence, sentient beings therein are likewise indeterminate, and their perfect awakening is also indeterminate, like empty space. If this is not understood, one wanders in saṃsāra; through realization, [one is liberated].

The mind is thus pure and perfectly awakened; therefore, its state is not fixed. As for those of middling virtue who cultivate wholesome deeds—humans, non-humans, and so forth—who receive an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) and possess a lifespan, they undergo birth and pass away within five or seven days.
If they have committed unwholesome deeds, they fall into the three evil realms; their lifespan in that intermediate state lasts for seven times seven, or forty-nine days.
The retribution is received at the time of death. The verse says:
Within the body that exists in the dream-like realm of arising and ceasing, that which exists among these three types dwells sequentially for seven days;
in the first seven days, it is the body of karmic retribution.
In the seventh day of the second week, one goes to receive retribution within a cave or stone crevice;
seeds are sown and infused, and evil objects appear, giving rise to fear.
In the seventh day of the third week, the mental body manifests, appearing amidst the three fears and four terrors. Thus, the first three weeks for humans and devas are completed.
The three types of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) arise through the convergence of conditions; from the seeds of karmic retribution, two bodies manifest.
When the mental body (*manomaya-kāya*) reaches the end of its lifespan, it is reborn. The same applies to the non-divine intermediate existence.
Beginning from the third seven-day period, up to the middle of the fourth and fifth seven-day periods.
Each [being] dwells, gathers, is born, and departs; the three intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of hell are likewise.

From the fifth week onward, as before, they dwell, gather, reach the end of their lifespan, and are born into the non-gods (*asura*), the evil destinies, or the two intermediate states. These are the two [periods of] the second week.
Dwelling in the hells and the states of no leisure, one undergoes the retribution of suffering.

Regarding the confession of these karmic offenses, it is most clearly explained in the *Mūlatantra* that there are five types of bodies: First, the present body (*pratyutpanna-kāya*). This arises through the power of virtuous and non-virtuous karma;
it is the manifest body appearing in the present, a composite of physical form and consciousness. This is the current physical body. Second, the body of death (*maraṇa-bhava-kāya*).
The manifestation of the body at the end of life refers to the appearance of a corpse. There are three types of intermediate state bodies (*antarābhava*).
Due to the power of negligence, one may turn from evil to good or regress from good to evil; thus, good and evil are intermingled.
From the first half-day until the sixth part of the final seventh day, because they are sustained by seven kinds of karma, those who abide here—during the first week—remain for the first three days.
For the first half [of the seventh day], because the signs of conscious awareness have not yet arisen, one does not abide within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
On the subsequent three and a half days, the signs of the intermediate state of hell arise. On the second week, the signs of the intermediate state of hungry ghosts arise.
On the third week, the signs of the intermediate state of animals arise. On the fourth week, the signs of the intermediate state of the human realm appear. On the fifth week...
On the first day, the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the asuras appear. On the sixth week, the signs of the intermediate state of the celestial realms (*devagati*) appear.
During the seventh week, in its upper six parts, the body of the intermediate state of liberation arises.

Regarding the bodies of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), the location during the seventh week constitutes the final part. As for the subsequent body of existence (*paścima-bhava-deha*), this refers to the body received thereafter.

If one has performed superior-grade great goodness or committed grave offenses, within the first seven-day period, the ascent for the good and the descent for the evil will each be clearly manifested according to their respective retributions.
If the causes and effects of middling-grade good or evil, they will be clearly manifested within the third seven-day period.
If the causes and effects of inferior-grade good or evil, the ascent and descent will be clearly manifested within forty-nine days. If it is of the lowest grade...
The superior grade becomes clear within one hundred days; the third, the middling of the inferior grade, becomes clear within one year;

and the fourth, the lowest of the inferior grade, becomes clear upon the completion of three years. During those intervals, the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) appear, and one remains in a state of incessant terror.
After experiencing the fear of the intermediate state, the body of that person will not quickly arise [again]. This is the repentance for karmic retribution.
[The intermediate state being] repents. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) by way of nine aspects:
it is visible to the pure divine eye; it possesses karmic supernormal power and speed; its faculties are complete; it is non-obstructive; and it cannot be turned back.
Those who subsist on fragrance do not remain for long; with inverted minds, they pursue the realm of desire. Those born from moisture and transformation are attached to fragrant places;
among the heavens, the first three have their heads upward while the others are horizontal. As for those in the hells, their heads are turned downward.
Regarding those born from a womb or an egg, those possessing an intermediate body (antarābhava) obtain eyes through the power of their karma and see their place of birth from afar.
At the time when the parents unite, they give rise to perverted thoughts and quickly undergo rebirth.

Among those born from moisture who possess bodies, whenever they encounter the conditions for rebirth, regardless of whether those conditions are near or far, they all perceive a fragrance; because they smell that fragrance, [they proceed to be reborn].
A mind of attachment arises; at that moment, due to the distinct power of karma for taking birth, the fragrances are likewise either pleasant or foul and are not the same.
Among those born by transformation who possess a body, when the conditions for rebirth converge, they do not discriminate between near and far;

seeing the place of rebirth, they give rise to craving and attachment, and thus immediately take birth. According to the goodness or evil of their karma, they are divided into pure or impure realms. This is the retribution of sin.
[The opponent] offers an apology.
Furthermore, the Venerable Vasumitra says: "That intermediate state body (antarābhava), at the very longest, remains for seven days and then takes birth.
The Dharma Master refutes this, saying: "The duration of the intermediate state body is not fixed; it depends on whether the conditions for taking birth are met sooner or later."
Therefore, if the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) persists. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* records that Maudgalyāyana stated:

"The intermediate state lasts at most seven times seven days—forty-nine days—within which one will certainly undergo rebirth. Question: If the conditions for rebirth converge within these forty-nine days, then this may be so.
But if the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged, does that [intermediate state] perish? Answer: [It does not.]
That [intermediate state] is likewise indestructible. If the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged, one undergoes repeated deaths and births without interruption or destruction.
Furthermore, it is said that if the conditions for rebirth do not converge for a long time, this intermediate body (antarābhava) remains for a long duration;

only when the conditions harmonize does one finally undergo birth. If the conditions are not encountered, one is born among those of a similar class. Moreover, the Buddha spoke of the consecration (abhiṣeka).
The *Zhongmu yinyuan sifang shenzhou jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Tombs and the Four-Directional Divine Spells) states:
Ānanda asked the Buddha, "If a person has died and is placed in the mountains or wilds, and a tomb is constructed for them, does their soul remain within that tomb? The Buddha said:
"There is existence and there is non-existence. Ānanda asked again, "In what way is there existence and non-existence?
The Buddha said, "'Existence' refers to when a person, while in the present life, neither plants roots of goodness nor recognizes the Three Jewels, yet likewise does not commit evil."

Regarding good, there is no merit to be received; regarding evil, there is likewise no suffering to be experienced. Furthermore, there is no one who cultivates goodness, because of [the presence of] spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
It is said that they "are" within those tombs because, having no place to go, they remain there. Ānanda asked again, "What does it mean to 'not be'?

The Buddha said, "To 'not be' means that if, in a previous life or during the present life, one performed great meritorious deeds and exerted oneself [in virtue, yet failed to meet with spiritual friends]."

Because he practiced the Path, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three to enjoy meritorious bliss. If he were to be born among humans, he would be born into a noble family and naturally experience happiness, taking birth according to his own will;
therefore, it is said that he does not remain [in this world]. This was when he was previously in the present life.

Because they slaughtered living beings to sacrifice to the gods, lacked faith in the truth, held perverse views, and nourished themselves through flattery, deception, and concealment, they fell among the hungry ghosts (preta) and underwent manifold sufferings, wandering through the hells; therefore, it is said that [the spirit] does not reside at that grave site. The Buddha further said:

"As for those who say it resides there, if one becomes a ghost or a malevolent spirit (*bhūta*) of the five grains, there remains a trace of a subtle soul for as long as the marrow and bones have not yet decayed."
Spirit: "If the bones have already decayed, the soul perishes immediately; there is no longer any vital heat, and it can no longer bring fortune or calamity to humans.

However, while the soul-consciousness has not yet perished, if relatives and others do not cultivate merit and goodness for those who have died recently, and instead engage in perverse and deluded acts, they will fall among the ghosts and spirits, or become *chimei* (goblins) haunting trees and miscellaneous objects."

They do not receive celestial blessings, nor are they gathered among those in hell. Surveying the world and wandering through villages, because they lack celestial food, they afflict and provoke humans by manifesting various transformations that cause people’s minds to become deluded.

If such false teachers rely upon them as deities to seek the status of a field of merit, aspiring for long life, they act out of ignorance and false views, seeking [their ends] through the taking of life.
After death, one will fall among the denizens of hell, hungry ghosts, and the like, with no prospect of escape. Therefore, one should not be negligent;
one must repent for the retribution of one's transgressions.
Even the youth of the Śākya clan addressed the Buddha again, saying: "Is it true that spirits and deities dwell within the foundations of ordinary people's burial mounds?

The Buddha replied: "Regarding what I previously stated—that there are souls within the foundations of ordinary people's burial mounds—they all transform into the ghosts and demons of the five grains.
However, those who died by unnatural means and have no place to rely upon take refuge in the grasses, trees, and forests."
These trees become *chi-mei* ghosts. If they lack food and drink, they wander among human beings, manifesting various transformations to terrify people.
When ordinary sentient beings hear of this, they immediately seek merit, believing these to be heavenly deities, and repent for their karmic offenses.
Thus far, we have meticulously investigated the intermediate state (antarābhava) as described in the sūtras, śāstras, and the root tantras.
May all who hear this not let it pass by in daily frivolity, but instead give rise to a sense of wearying regret.

Since one may not be of the highest capacity for cultivating virtue, others should practice this essential gateway for the transference of consciousness. Open the pure Brahma-eye and seek rebirth in a pure land. This is [the instruction].
Swift Path: We were shrouded by ignorance; amidst the karmic retributions of the evil realms, we did not recognize the causes of our transgressions.
Now that we have encountered this site of enlightenment, we have finally awakened to this knowledge. We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean of all worthy sages.
[Assembly: We burn incense and scatter flowers. Regarding the karma of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that we have received, we openly confess and repent, not daring to conceal it.

By these causes and conditions, may all the various transgressions—the karma of the intermediate state leading to evil realms—that I and the ocean of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm have received, be entirely purified.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for repentance to extinguish transgressions: Oṃ sarvapa pame sputanadahanadarmaya svāhā.
(Recite three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred eons are all swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose entirely from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion.
I now repent of everything produced by my body, speech, and mind.
Having repented, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Proclamation: Listen, all you people, to these verses on impermanence from the Sūtra:
The three realms are all unstable; One should not remain attached to them.
Enveloped by the fire of craving throughout all worlds, Desire burns those who lack self-mastery, Driven as they are by lust and delusion.
Just as adding dry fuel to a fire causes the flames to increase and blaze forth, so too for one who indulges in pleasure,
the fire of craving increases further. But if a person can escape the net of craving and remain far removed from desire and hatred,
that wise one crosses over the afflictions and is forever freed from all suffering and distress.

In the thirty-sixth session,
during the stage of Equal Enlightenment, [I] pay respectful homage with all reverence to Queen Māyā and the entire assembly of the hundred Buddhas, and to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
All these people knelt on their right knees, solemnly holding incense and flowers to make offerings according to the Dharma.
May this ocean-like cloud of offerings pervade the worlds of the ten directions. Upon immeasurable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel thrones, Buddhas sit and let out the great lion’s roar.
Immeasurable jewel lamps constantly radiate the pure light of wisdom. Immeasurable jewel *tāla* trees, in succession...

The first row was encircled by jeweled cords, pure and magnificent. Those trees further possessed incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jeweled trunks, which rose upward from their bases, straight, round, and pristine.
They had incalculable jeweled branches, densely adorned with various kinds of jewels.
Inconceivable birds flew and gathered among them, constantly emitting wondrous sounds to proclaim the True Dharma. Incalculable...

Jewel leaves radiate the light of great wisdom, pervading all places. Upon each of the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewel flowers, immeasurable bodhisattvas sit in the full lotus posture, traveling everywhere throughout the dharma-realm.
From the incalculable jewel fruits, those who behold them always attain the wisdom of omniscience and the fruit of non-retrogression.
From the incalculable jewel villages, those who behold them abandon the worldly settlements.
The Dharma of Falling Away. Within it, there are *asaṃkhyeya* jewel cities filled with unimpeded sentient beings;
within them are *asaṃkhyeya* jewel palaces where kings reside, possessing the Nārāyaṇa bodies of bodhisattvas—valiant, firm, clad in the armor of the Dharma, and with minds that never regress.
There are *asaṃkhyeya* jewel houses, entering which one can eliminate the mind that clings to dwellings.
There were *asaṃkhyeya* precious robes; those who wore them were able to understand and realize non-attachment.
There were *asaṃkhyeya* precious palaces, filled with renunciant bodhisattvas. There were *asaṃkhyeya* precious curiosities and playthings, which all who saw them felt immeasurable joy.
Incalculable jewel wheels emit inconceivable light of wisdom and turn the wheel of non-retrogression.
Incalculable *bhadra* jewel trees and Indra-nets are pure and magnificent. Incalculable jewel grounds are adorned with the intermingling of inconceivable jewels.
Incalculable jewel winds blow, their sounds clear and resonant, filling the entire Dharma-realm. Incalculable...

The precious drum alone produces wondrous sounds that harmonize perfectly, continuing without ceasing for the duration of kalpas. With such various articles of offering, one constantly makes offerings.
Within the infinitely layered Indra-nets, the ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages receive these clouds of offerings.
I conceive of it as a Terrace of Radiance, vast beyond the boundless realms, immeasurable and inexhaustible. May it perform the work of a Buddha.
Having made this offering, all pay homage with reverence.
Next, I offer clouds of supreme offerings such as these— vast oceans of the nature of jewels and precious gems, and mountains of the seven treasures—
which arise in this most excellent manner; I present them to all the Buddhas and their assemblies.
Oṃ sarvamata-dhāraṇī-prabodhana-samagra-siddha-samayam hūṃ. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"There is a dhāraṇī named 'Innumerable Varieties of Spells,' which can accomplish all things and possesses great power."
It can. The *dhāraṇī* says:
Oṃ sīmala sīmala mīmada sigrāmaha liṅga hūṃ. Next, bind the seal of the Great Amoghapāśa-maṇi (the method for binding the seal is the same as before).
Oṃ amoghapāśa mahāvidyārāja tathāgatamaitrīkṛta sarvaduṣṭān saṃharā hūṃ.
(In Sanskrit, this is a hymn of praise to the Buddha.)
From within the Tathāgata’s radiance, there constantly issues forth a profound and wondrous sound,
praising the ocean of the Buddha’s merits and the practices of the Bodhisattvas. As the Buddha turns the wheel of the True Dharma,
the teachings he proclaims are immeasurable and boundless, peerless, and unfathomable to those of shallow wisdom throughout all worlds.
Manifesting their bodies as perfectly awakened ones, each displays miraculous transformations that completely fill the entire dharma realm.
Speaking directly, they praise the Buddha’s perfect awakening; having realized all phenomena, they are non-dual, free from duality, and entirely equal.
Inherently pure like space, making no distinction between self and non-self;
Like the ocean-seal manifesting the bodies of sentient beings, it is for this reason called the great ocean.
The Bodhisattva universally seals all mental activities; Therefore, he is called by the name of Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksambuddha).
Just as in the world there is success and failure, yet space neither increases nor decreases;
so too, when all Buddhas appear in the world, bodhi is of a single mark, eternally without marks.
It is like a person who, through mental transformation, conjures a Buddha; whether manifesting or not manifesting, there is always no difference.
All sentient beings attain enlightenment; Whether they attain it or not, there is no increase or decrease.

The Buddha has a samādhi named "Excellent Awakening"; Entering this concentration beneath the Bodhi tree, He emits immeasurable light equal to all sentient beings, Awakening the multitudes like the blooming of lotuses.
Just as there are kalpas, lands, and sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, and all their thoughts, faculties, and desires—
manifesting bodies equal in number to these— he is therefore called the Immeasurable Perfectly Awakened One.
