revised by the Buddhist disciple Mu Zeng, Minister of Public Works (Sichuan Provincial Governor) and devoted follower of the Buddha, who was loyal and sincere in his service to the state during the Ming dynasty.
Sandaṃśa No. 40: Compiled by the śramaṇa Duce of Jikō-ji on Mount Kei, who studies the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school;
finalized by the śramaṇa Shoji.
Next, to manifest the vastness of the cause, bringing the branches back to the root, the assembly of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva universally honors and pays respect to the inexhaustible Triple Gem.
All members of this assembly kneel with their right knees on the ground, solemnly holding incense and flowers, making offerings according to the Dharma. May this ocean of offerings...
Clouds [of offerings] pervade the worlds of the ten directions. There are arranged incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) precious robes; there are set up incalculable precious canopies.
There are incalculable precious seats, upon which are spread incalculable precious silken cloths. There are incalculable images of Jāmbūnada gold youths and maidens;
there are incalculable images of various forms made of diverse jewels; there are incalculable images of Bodhisattvas made of exquisite jewels, located everywhere.
It was completely filled with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) flocks of birds uttering harmonious and elegant sounds;
it was adorned with incalculable precious *utpala* flowers, incalculable precious *padma* flowers, incalculable precious *kumuda* flowers, and incalculable precious *puṇḍarīka* flowers;
and there were incalculable precious trees arranged in successive rows. Incalculable *mā*...
The Bhikṣuṇī Ratna emits great radiance; with such immeasurable asaṃkhyeya ornaments as these, she adorns herself.

With such articles of worship as these, she constantly makes offerings. Within the infinitely layered Indra-nets, the ocean-like assemblies of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages receive these clouds of offerings, taking them as luminous pavilions that extend beyond the boundless realms.
Immeasurable and inexhaustible, may you perform the work of a Buddha.
Having made this offering, all pay homage with reverence.
Next, the mantra for the offering of the jeweled casket is recited.
With clouds of offerings such as these— vast oceans of the intrinsic nature of precious jewels and the most excellent emergence of the mountains of the seven treasures—
I offer them to all the Buddhas and others. Oṃ sarva-tathāgata-udana-bhujaṅga-samaya-hūṃ.
*Phraṇat-samaye hūṃ*. The *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī Sūtra* states:
"There is a dhāraṇī called the 'Spell of Immeasurable Varieties,' which can accomplish all things and possesses great efficacy.
The dhāraṇī says: [as above].
Oṃ smara smara me manaḥ siddhara-mahā-liṅga hūṃ. Next is the mantra for bestowing great wisdom: Oṃ dharma-saṃkrama-tathāgatāvalokite saṃmārjaya.
(raṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ hūṃ) In the Sanskrit voice,
I praise the Buddha:
The Buddha’s body emits radiance That pervades the ten directions, Manifesting according to the needs of beings.
The forms and marks are not of a single kind; within each and every atom, radiance completely fills them, and one universally beholds the lands of the ten directions. Each variety is distinct;
throughout all the lands of the Dharma-realm, one travels everywhere without obstruction. Amidst all assemblies, one constantly turns the wondrous Wheel of Dharma.
Speaking directly in praise of the Buddha,
whose body universally radiates great light— His physical marks are boundless and utterly pure,
like clouds filling all lands; Everywhere he extols the virtues of the Buddha.
Within a single atom are many oceans of lands, Each location distinct and entirely pure;
Thus, the infinite enters into one, Each division distinct without confusion or overlap.
Equal in number to the atoms within a Buddha-field, Such are the lands contained within these atoms.

They are all likewise able, within a single thought-moment, to manifest within every single atom and within every single pore of the Tathāgata’s body, the thrones of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of all lands,
surrounded by assemblies of Bodhisattvas, proclaiming the supreme conduct of Samantabhadra.
Within a single pore, one clearly perceives Buddhas as numerous as the inconceivable and the immeasurable;
All pores are likewise so, As one universally pays homage to all the Lamps of the World.
Within a single minute dust-pore, Inexpressible lands enter in succession.
The pores can contain all those lands, yet those lands cannot pervade a single pore;
The Tathāgata sits upon the seat of enlightenment, manifesting many oceans of lands within a single hair;
Every single hair manifests in this same way, thus pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Just as one sees objects and seats within this assembly, so it is in all assemblies;
the Buddha-body neither goes nor comes, yet all lands appear clearly therein.
Within the number of atoms of all buddha-fields, clouds of bodies are constantly seen to completely fill them all.
Universally emitting great rays of light for all sentient beings, Each raining down the rain of Dharma according to their inclinations;
Within every single atom, infinite bodies appear, As the Buddha manifests various adorned lands;
In a single thought-moment, he vanishes and reappears for all to see— He who has attained the adornment of unimpeded intent.
Within a single atom, there are entirely present unspeakable numbers of lotus realms;
within each and every lotus world, there are unspeakable numbers of Tathāgatas named Bhadramukha.
Within a single pore, there are inconceivable lands as numerous as atoms, existing in various locations throughout the entire realm.
In each and every one there is the Honored One of Universal Radiance, Proclaiming the wondrous Dharma amidst the great assemblies.
All buddha-fields enter my body, And the Buddhas dwelling therein are likewise so.
You should observe all my pores; I now reveal to you the realm of the Buddhas.
Homage to the Vairocana Buddha, the Original Honored One of Unobstructed Ten Bodies in the Flower Treasury World-Ocean of the Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha,
who with great kindness and compassion made five hundred vows to save sentient beings from suffering in the five turbidities.

Homage to the Buddha Bhaisajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha-rāja, King of Medicine with Lapis Lazuli Light, who possesses twelve supreme vows and rescues sentient beings from suffering amidst the five turbidities in the Pūrṇacandra World of the East.
Homage to the Buddha Amitābha, who possesses forty-eight vows and rescues sentient beings from suffering amidst the five turbidities in the Sukhāvatī World of the West.

Homage to the Perfect Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Extensive Flower Ornament*, throughout all lands as numerous as atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, who presides over the truth of the Vows and Practices within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Extensive Flower Ornament*.
Homage to the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who presides over faith, understanding, and realized wisdom within the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Thousand Hands and Thousand Eyes, who possesses great kindness and great compassion, rescuing those suffering in the five turbidities.

Homage to him whose great vows are profound and vast, who rescues those suffering in the five turbidities by appearing in worlds where no Buddha dwells, comforting the hearts of sentient beings, and remaining forever present.
To the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha-Rāja in the realm of Yama;

to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, and Equal Enlightenment within all the lands as numerous as atoms in the entirety of space throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; Namo! To these and all others...
Homage to the assembly of all oceans of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms within the oceans of lands pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
and homage to the fifty-five holy ones who cultivated and realized the five stages in the final assembly of the Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sudhana, who, in the final assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, was a vessel of perfect capacity and superior faculties;

who sought the Dharma through a hundred cities and perfected the bodhisattva practices within a single lifetime, serving as a model for cultivation and realization for the sudden teaching of the final age.

Homage to all Buddha-activities— whether in the form of Dharma-bodies, physical bodies, relics, stūpas, temples, or monasteries— within every dust-mote world-system throughout the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time;
and further, to the Bodhisattvas, worthy ones, and sages within the ocean-like assemblies at the treasuries of the Dharma and the places where the Dharma is preached.
Homage to the Great Vow, Donning Armor to Seek Birth in the Pure Land, Protecting the True Dharma in the Degenerate Age of the Xia Kingdom, State Preceptor for the Protection of the Nation.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the World-Ocean of the Flower Treasury within the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, and to the Honored One [Vairocana].
To Vairocana Buddha,

throughout the ten directions, I take refuge; may my transgressions be extinguished and my pure faith increase, and may I be born within the ocean of the Flower Treasury and the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The fifth assembly, which reveals the Dharma-gate of the liberation of the vast characteristics of causes, states in the *Sūtra on the Liberation of the Playful Supernatural Powers of All Tathāgatas*: "At that time, the youth Sudhana [proceeded] to the playful supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas."

May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean, within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, before the lion throne of the Tathāgata Vairocana at this Vajra-Treasury Bodhimanda, where all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Samantabhadra and others sit upon precious lotus thrones. Namo!
To this Vajra-Treasury Bodhimanda, before the lion throne of the Tathāgata Vairocana, where all sit upon precious lotus thrones, [I take refuge in] the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra.

Homage to the Tathāgata Vairocana here; homage to all the Tathāgatas in all worlds of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below; homage to all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas Samantabhadra.
Homage to the Dharma that exists within every single atom of every Buddha-field in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
In each of the assemblies of Buddhas throughout all realms, at the presence of every Buddha, there are Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
I pay homage to each Samantabhadra. From every single pore, in every moment of thought, they emit clouds of pure Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields.

Homage to Samantabhadra, from every single pore of whose body, in every moment of thought, there emerge clouds of bodies of all perfectly awakened ones, as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields.
Homage to Samantabhadra, from every single pore of whose body, in every moment of thought, there emerge [clouds of] one... as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields.

I take refuge in the clouds of bodies of all Bodhisattvas, and in each and every part of their bodies, and within each and every pore, there are the sites of enlightenment where Buddhas appear in the three thousandfold world-systems,
together with all the assemblies of the ocean-like multitudes.

Homage to each and every pore of Samantabhadra, wherein there are worlds such as these, all likewise containing Buddhas appearing in the world and assemblies of all oceans at their sites of enlightenment;
from all ten directions, we take refuge. May our sins be extinguished, may our pure faith increase, and may we be born in the Flower Treasury Ocean.
The Sutra on the Land of Ultimate Bliss states that when the youth Sudhana beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, [their] liberations and masteries were entirely equal. May I,
together with all sentient beings, Vow to be born within the Flower Treasury Ocean, In the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, who sits upon a seat of universal jewel lotuses before the lion throne of the Tathāgata Vairocana within this Vajragarbha Bodhimaṇḍa;
homage to all the worlds within every single seat throughout all the worlds of the ten directions in this Sahā world-system.
I pay homage to all Buddhas and to all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Samantabhadra.
By virtue of the power of Samantabhadra’s true contemplation and the power of the wisdom-eye of all dharmas, one attains this ultimate,
pure Dharma-body, which is equal throughout the three periods of time.

Homage to the power of Samantabhadra’s assistance on the path, the power of all roots of goodness, the power of great resolve and aspiration, and the power of cultivating merit, by which this pure, unsurpassed Dharma-body is attained.
Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; within each and every pore of his physical marks and limbs, there are [innumerable...]
I take refuge in Samantabhadra, who proclaims that within each and every ocean of unspeakably many Buddha-fields, there are oceans of Buddha-fields where Buddhas appear in the world,
all surrounded by assemblies of great Bodhisattvas;
and who, in each and every world, manifests as many bodies as there are atoms in an ocean of all Buddha-fields.
The emanation of all Buddhas,
Yun Nan Wu Yuanqi, a person of the highest capacity who sought the Dharma across a hundred cities; within a single lifetime,
he perfected the conduct of a Bodhisattva and became a model for practice and realization in the sudden gate of the final age— the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sudhana.
Homage to all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, such as Sudhana, who stand before Samantabhadra in the presence of Vairocana Buddha beyond the three thousandfold world-system of this Sahā realm;
homage to all worlds within the ocean of lands, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Before all Buddhas and in the presence of Samantabhadra, I take refuge in all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, such as Sudhana, throughout the ten directions.
May my transgressions be extinguished and my pure faith increase; may I be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean and the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Next, for those who have not yet awakened to the realm of the single reality,

we offer this repentance: We pray that the inexhaustible Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, which is like a celestial net, the Tathāgata Vairocana, and the holy assembly of Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the ocean-like gathering of sages,
together with the compassionate original vows of mundane and supramundane deities, will emit great radiance to illuminate this dharma assembly.
Bear witness and protect us with your mindful regard; out of compassion, please accept and sustain us.

I and the ocean of all sentient beings, from time immemorial until this very moment, have been shrouded by the veil of ignorance and failed to awaken to the realm of the single reality. I now openly confess and repent.
The *Sūtra on the Divination of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma* states: At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Firm Pure Faith (*Dṛḍhaśuddhādhimukti*).
Rising from his seat, he adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to ask a question within this assembly; I pray that the World-Honored One will deign to listen and grant me permission. The Buddha said: "Good son, as you please..."
"You may now explain what you have asked. The Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith said: "As the Buddha previously taught:

when I have passed away and the True Dharma has been extinguished, when the Semblance Dharma is nearing its end and one enters the Final Age—at such a time, the merit of sentient beings will be meager."
There will be much decline and affliction; the lands will frequently be in turmoil; calamities will arise repeatedly; and various misfortunes and terrors will oppress and harass them.
My disciples will lose their wholesome mindfulness, and they will only increase greed, anger, jealousy, and pride, speaking of things that merely appear similar [to the truth].

Those who practice wholesome dharmas seek only worldly gain and reputation, making these their primary concern; they are unable to devote themselves single-mindedly to the cultivation of the essential methods for transcendence.
At that time, sentient beings, beholding the calamities and chaos of the world, are constantly timid and weak of heart;
they are filled with anxiety and fear for themselves and their kinsmen, and are unable to obtain clothing or provisions to sustain their lives. Due to such numerous obstacles as these—
Due to these causes and conditions, within the Buddha-dharma there are few of dull faculties, and those who attain the Way through faith are extremely rare.
Even those who gradually achieve confidence in the Three Vehicles are likewise exceedingly few.

As for those who cultivate and study worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and develop various supernormal powers (*abhijñā-karman*), such that they know their own past lives—such people will subsequently disappear. Thus it shall be in the final age.

Within the Dharma, after a long time, one attains the Way and acquires faith, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the various karmas; yet in all these, there is absolutely no self.

Now, for the sake of those with even a slight root of goodness in this future evil age when the Semblance Dharma (*sāṃketika-dharma*) is nearing its end and during the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*), we ask:

By what skillful means (*upāya*) does the Tathāgata provide instruction, transformation, and guidance, so that they may give rise to faith, eliminate their decline and afflictions, and [attain liberation]?
Those sentient beings, encountering an evil age and being beset by many obstacles, have regressed from their wholesome resolve.
Within the teachings on worldly and world-transcending causes and effects, they repeatedly give rise to doubt and are unable to seek the wholesome Dharma with steadfast and single-minded devotion.

Such sentient beings are pitiable and worthy of rescue; may the World-Honored One, possessing great compassion and all-encompassing wisdom, deign to employ skillful means to instruct and enlighten them.

This shall cause them to leave the net of doubt, remove all obstacles, and increase their faith, so that they may swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression regardless of which vehicle they follow.
The Buddha said to Dṛḍhaśraddhā: "Excellent, excellent! You have asked about this matter most skillfully; it deeply accords with my own intention.
Now, within this assembly, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Kṣitigarbha. You should request [the teaching] regarding this matter from him."
He was questioned about it. He shall establish for you the skillful means and reveal and expound them.

When the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith had thus expressed his earnest wish, he addressed the Buddha again, saying: "Tathāgata, World-Honored One, Possessor of Unsurpassed Great Wisdom, for what reason do You not speak of this?"

The Buddha then intended for that Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha to expound it. The Buddha said to Dṛḍhaśuddhādhimukti: "Do not give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority regarding this son of good family.
Since he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed;
he has long since been able to cross the ocean of *sarvajñatā*, and his merits are fully perfected. He does so merely in accordance with his original vow."
By the power of his sovereign mastery, he manifests through skillful means and appears as reflections throughout the ten directions.
Although he constantly performs meritorious deeds while traveling universally through all lands, his transformative benefits are particularly profound in this world of five turbidities.

This is because it accords with the habitual perfuming of his original vows and is due to the karmic conditions of sentient beings who are ready to receive his transformation. He has been thus for eleven kalpas. Ornamented...

He adorns this world and brings sentient beings to maturity; therefore, within this assembly, his physical form is upright and majestic, and his awesome virtue is preeminent—none can surpass him except for the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, regarding all transformative activities in this world, with the sole exception of Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and other great Bodhisattvas, none can equal him. This is because of this Bodhisattva’s fundamental...

By the power of their vows, they swiftly fulfill all the requests of sentient beings, can extinguish all the heavy sins of sentient beings, remove all obstacles, and grant them peace and security in the present life.
Furthermore, these Bodhisattvas are called "skillful consolers," meaning they are adept at expounding the profound Dharma;
they are able to skillfully guide beginners who have first resolved to seek the Mahāyāna, ensuring they do not become timid or weak.
For these and other such reasons, the sentient beings of this world yearn with thirsting longing; they receive transformation and attain deliverance.

Therefore, I now cause him to speak it. At that time, the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith, having understood the Buddha’s intention, immediately exhorted and requested the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"Excellent, O True Being who saves the world! Excellent, O One of Great Wisdom!"

“Bodhisattva, regarding what I have asked—by what skillful means should one transform and guide the sentient beings of the evil age so that they may leave behind all hindrances and attain firm faith? Now, the Tathāgata wishes for you to explain these skillful means;
you should know the proper time. Out of compassion, please speak. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhaprasāda:
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva said: "Good son, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.

In the evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who have not attained decisive faith in the laws of worldly and world-transcending cause and effect, and who are unable to cultivate the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, or the perception of non-self."

They cultivate and bring to manifestation the perception of impurity, yet they are unable to diligently contemplate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths or the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Furthermore, they do not diligently contemplate such dharmas as True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Reality Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), non-arising, and non-ceasing.
Because they do not diligently contemplate these dharmas, they are unable to ultimately refrain from the fundamental transgressions of the ten unwholesome paths of action regarding the Three Jewels.
Regarding virtue, they cannot place exclusive faith in various realms; among the three vehicles, they have no fixed direction.
For such persons, if there are various obstructing matters, their anxieties increase, and they become either doubtful or regretful.
Their minds are not clear in any respect; they seek much and suffer much, entangled by manifold affairs. Their actions are unstable, and their thoughts wander.
[They were] distracted. They neglected the practice of the path and did not awaken to this Dharma; now they all repent.

Good son, if there are sentient beings in future ages who wish to seek liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and who have newly begun to cultivate the resolve, practicing meditative concentration and signless wisdom, they should first contemplate the deeds performed in their past lives.
Regarding the quantity and gravity of evil karma: if one's evil karma is great and thick, one must not immediately study meditative concentration and wisdom.

One should first practice the method of repentance. Why is this? Because this person’s habitual evil mind from past lives is so fierce and sharp that they will inevitably commit many evils in the present life and violate the heavy prohibitions. Because they have violated these heavy prohibitions—
If one practices dhyāna-concentration and wisdom without first repenting to bring oneself to purity, there will be many obstacles and one will be unable to achieve success.
One may suffer from loss of mind or mental derangement, be afflicted by external malevolent spirits, or accept false teachings that increase wrong views.
Therefore, one should first practice the method of repentance.
The collection of the six sense faculties of all sentient beings arises from the single reality realm of the *tathāgatagarbha*, the intrinsically pure mind.
It takes this single reality realm as its basis. That is to say, because it relies upon the single reality realm, there exists that ignorance which fails to comprehend the one dharma-realm;
through erroneous conceptualization and reflection, it manifests delusive realms and engages in discrimination.
Through grasping and attachment, the causal conditions for the accumulation of karma give rise to the six sense faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Because one relies upon these six internal faculties, the six consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—arise in relation to the six external objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Because one relies upon these six consciousnesses, thoughts of aversion and thoughts of attraction arise toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
“Not perceiving things as either contrary or conformable, eighteen kinds of sensation arise; failing to awaken to this dharma, we now repent it all.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Firm Pure Faith asked the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying, “How should one instruct those who seek to advance toward the Mahāyāna regarding the skillful means for their progress? The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha replied:
"Good son, if there are sentient beings who wish to proceed toward the Mahāyāna, they should first know the fundamental practice that must be undertaken at the outset.
That fundamental practice undertaken at the outset is as follows: by relying upon the realm of single reality (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*), one cultivates faith and understanding;
through the cultivation of the power of faith and understanding, it increases, whereby one swiftly attains entry into the lineage of the Bodhisattvas."
Regarding the nature: what is called the "single reality realm" refers to the essence of the minds of sentient beings. From the very beginning, it is neither born nor extinguished;
its self-nature is pure, unobstructed, and unhindered, like empty space. Because it is free from conceptual discrimination, it is equal and all-pervasive, reaching everywhere.
It is perfectly complete throughout the ten directions, ultimately a single characteristic, non-dual and without distinction, immutable and...
They are distinct, yet there is neither increase nor decrease. Failing to awaken to this Dharma, we now repent all together.

This is because the minds of all sentient beings, the minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the minds of all bodhisattvas, and the minds of all buddhas are identical in their aspect of true suchness (tathatā)—which is unborn, undying, unstained, and quiescent. Therefore...
Why is this? All that possesses mind and gives rise to conceptualization is like a magical illusion; it has no reality.

That is to say, the dharmas such as consciousness, feeling, perception, mental formations, recollection, objective consideration, and cognition—these various mental factors are neither blue nor yellow.
It is neither red nor white, nor is it of variegated colors. It has no length or shortness, nor squareness or roundness, nor largeness or smallness.
Even searching throughout the entirety of the ten directions of empty space and all worlds, not a single distinct portion of the mind's shape or form can be found.
It is solely due to the causes and conditions of the habitual perfuming of sentient beings' ignorance and the darkness of delusion that false objects appear, causing them to give rise to attachment.
That is to say, this mind cannot know itself; it falsely claims to exist and gives rise to the notion of cognition, calculating "I" and "mine."
In reality, there is no perception or conceptualization of awareness, for this deluded mind ultimately lacks substance and cannot be seen.
Failing to awaken to this Dharma, I now repent it all.
If there were no cognizing subject capable of discrimination, then there would be no differentiated characteristics of the various realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
This is because all phenomena cannot exist of themselves; they exist only through the discrimination of the deluded mind.
That is to say, among all these realms, none think of themselves as existing, nor do they know themselves as "this" or perceive others as "that."

Therefore, all phenomena cannot exist of themselves; thus, they possess no inherent distinction. It is solely due to the deluded mind—failing to know and failing to realize that they are internally non-existent—that one speaks of external objects of knowledge as existing.

One falsely gives rise to various conceptions of phenomena, asserting "it exists" or "it does not exist," "that" or "this," "right" or "wrong," "good" or "bad," and so forth, even to the point of falsely giving rise to the notion of "non-existence."
Contemplate the boundless nature of all phenomena. One should understand that all dharmas arise from false conceptualization and take the deluded mind as their root.
Failing to awaken to this truth, I now repent for them all.
However, because this deluded mind lacks its own intrinsic characteristics, it also exists in dependence upon objects.
That is to say, it is called "mind" because it conditions, recollects, and cognizes preceding objects.

Furthermore, although this deluded mind and the preceding objects arise in mutual dependence without priority or sequence, this deluded mind is able to serve as the source and master of all objects. Why is this so?
This means that because the deluded mind does not realize that the dharma-realm is of a single characteristic, it is said that the mind possesses ignorance;
by virtue of the power of ignorance as its cause, false objects appear. Furthermore, because ignorance ceases, all objects cease;
it is not that objects exist because they do not themselves realize [their own nature]. Nor is it that ignorance arises because it depends upon objects. It arises [from the mind].
Regarding ignorance: because all Buddhas do not give rise to ignorance regarding any object, and furthermore, because it does not depend on the cessation of objects, the mind of ignorance ceases.

This is because all objects have, from the very beginning, been self-extinguished in their essential nature and have never truly existed. For this reason, it is said that all phenomena depend [on conditions].
The mind is the root. One should know that all dharmas are entirely called "mind," because their essential nature is not different from it and they are subsumed within the mind.
Not having awakened to this dharma, I now repent for all of it.
Furthermore, all phenomena arise from the mind and are in accord with it as its characteristics; they arise and perish together with it, and likewise lack any abiding.
This is because all objective spheres merely follow what the mind takes as its object, continuing in succession from moment to moment.
Thus it remains sustained, existing for a mere moment. Failing to awaken to this dharma, I now repent for all [of these].
Regarding the meaning of "mind" as thus explained, there are two kinds of characteristics. What are the two? First, the internal characteristic of mind.
Second is the external aspect of the mind. As for the internal aspect of the mind, there are again two kinds. What are these two? First is the real;
second is the delusory. That which is called "real" refers to the fundamental nature of the mind's essence, which is suchness without variation, pure and perfect.
It is unobstructed and unhindered; subtle and secret, it is difficult to perceive. Because it pervades all places, it is eternal and indestructible, for it establishes and brings forth all phenomena.
What is called "delusion" refers to such things as the arising of discursive thought, discernment, objective consideration, and recollection;
although these continue in succession and can produce all manner of diverse objects, they are internally hollow and false, having no [inherent existence].
It is real, because it is invisible. That which is called "external appearances" refers to all phenomena, various objects, and so forth;
because these objects appear before one according to whatever is being contemplated, one knows that there is an internal mind and the distinctions within that internal mind.
Thus it should be understood: internal false appearances constitute the cause and the essence; external false appearances constitute the effect and the function.
Based on these meanings, I therefore say that all dharmas are entirely named "mind. Failing to awaken to this dharma, I now repent for all of it.
Furthermore, one should know that external appearances are like the various objects seen in a dream; they are merely constructed by the mind and have no real external existence.
All objective realms are likewise so, for they are all produced by the deluded thoughts perceived by the dream-consciousness of ignorance.
Moreover, one should know that because the internal mind does not abide for even a single moment, whatever is seen or taken as an object [is likewise unreal].
All objective realms likewise follow the mind; they do not abide for even a single thought-moment.

This is because when the mind arises, various phenomena arise, and when the mind ceases, various phenomena cease. These characteristics of arising and ceasing exist only as names; in reality, they cannot be apprehended.
Failing to awaken to this dharma, I now repent for all of it.
Because the mind does not go to the sense objects, nor do the sense objects come to the mind; they are like images in a mirror, neither coming nor going.
Therefore, when one seeks the fixed characteristics of arising and ceasing within all phenomena, they are utterly unfindable.
This is because all phenomena are ultimately without essence, originally and eternally empty, and truly subject to neither birth nor cessation. Thus it is for all things.
The Dharma, being truly without arising or ceasing, is devoid of all characteristics of differentiation among objective realms. It is quiescent and of a single flavor;
this is called *tathatā* (suchness), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*).

That intrinsically pure mind is profoundly still and perfect, because it is free from the characteristics of conceptual discrimination. Being free from the characteristics of conceptual discrimination, it has no [attachment] toward anything whatsoever.
It is not non-existent; that which is nowhere not present is so because it can serve as the support and basis for the establishment of all phenomena.
Failing to awaken to this Dharma, I now repent for all [transgressions].
Furthermore, that mind is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. This means it is fully endowed with immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and untainted pure merits and karmic activities.

Because of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*, from the beginningless limit of time, it has been unobstructed, unhindered, sovereign, and indestructible, constantly and intensely manifesting all manner of transformative deeds and accomplishments. It has never...
He has rested, in the sense that he manifests various transformative benefits through his activities throughout all worlds.
A single Buddha-body is the body of all Buddhas, and the bodies of all Buddhas are a single Buddha-body.
All activities performed are likewise identical; that is to say, they are characterized by non-discrimination, without thinking of self or other, equal and non-dual.
This is because, by relying on the single *dharmatā*, their activities are the same, for the body of spontaneous transformation is without distinction.

In this way, the Dharma-body of all Buddhas pervades all places; because it is perfectly complete and immovable, it constantly serves as a support for sentient beings as they die here and are born there.
It is like space, which can fully contain all material forms and various types of shapes, for all material forms and various types of shapes are established by depending upon space.
It grows and develops, abiding within empty space and being subsumed by the sphere of empty space (*ākāśa-dhātu*). Taking empty space as its essence, there is nothing that can emerge from it.
One should know that the constituent part of the sphere of empty space is the realm of empty space within material forms, which cannot be destroyed.
When the forms and appearances perish, they return to empty space; yet that fundamental realm of empty space neither increases nor decreases, being unmoving and unchanging.

The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is likewise: it is able to contain and receive the various karmic fruits and retributions of all sentient beings, for all the various karmic fruits and retributions of sentient beings are established in dependence upon the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
It grows and develops, abiding within the *dharmakāya* and being encompassed by the locus of the *dharmakāya*. Taking the *dharmakāya* as its essence, there is nothing that can transcend it.
Regarding the constituent parts of the *dharmakāya*, one should know that the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas within the bodies of all sentient beings is likewise indestructible.
When afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed and destroyed, they return to the *dharmakāya*; yet the original realm of the *dharmakāya* neither increases nor diminishes.

It is without decrease, immovable, and unchanging. However, from time immemorial, due to the power of habitual perfuming by the causes and conditions of ignorance and the deluded darkness of the mind, false objects appear.
Because of the causes and conditions of habitual perfuming based upon these false objects, a false correspondence arises;
the mind conceives of "self" and "what belongs to self," accumulates various karmas, and undergoes the suffering of birth and death. This is what is called the Dharmakāya.
They are called sentient beings because they do not awaken to this Dharma; we now repent of all such [failings].

Among these sentient beings, those who possess the power of the Dharma-body’s perfuming gradually thin their afflictions, become able to weary of the world, seek the path to Nirvana, take refuge with faith in the single reality, and cultivate the six *pāramitās* and all other factors of enlightenment.

The classification of dharmas is as follows: one who is called a bodhisattva is so named because they practice all wholesome dharmas within the state of a bodhisattva and bring them to ultimate fulfillment;
when such a person attains liberation from the sleep of ignorance, they are further designated as a Buddha.

One should know that these distinctions among sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas exist only by relying upon worldly conventional designations and verbal expressions. As for the essence of the *dharmakāya*, however, there is no difference.
Ultimately equal, without any marks of difference. Son of good family, this is called the brief explanation of the meaning of the single reality realm (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*).
If one wishes to rely upon the single reality realm to cultivate faith and understanding, one should train in two kinds of contemplative paths.

What are these two? First, the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*citta-mātra-vijñapti-darśana*); second, the contemplation of the true suchness of reality (*tathatā-bhūta-darśana*). One should study the contemplation of mind-only consciousness.
This means that at all times and in all places, one should thoroughly examine every action performed by body, speech, and mind, knowing them to be nothing but the mind.
Furthermore, regarding all objective spheres, if the mind dwells upon them, one should observe and know them all as such.
Do not allow the mind to remain in a state of neutral indifference (*avyākṛta*) such that it clings to objects without self-awareness. At every moment of thought, one should investigate thoroughly.
Whenever the mind has an object of focus, mindfulness should follow that object, causing the mind to know itself. One should realize that within one's own mind, thoughts arise spontaneously;
it is not the case that all objective realms possess inherent thought or conceptual discrimination. This is what is called "internal."
The mind itself gives rise to views of long and short, beautiful and ugly, right and wrong, gain and loss, decline and profit, existence and non-existence, and so forth;

it gives rise to immeasurable perceptions. Yet, within all objective realms, there has never been a perception that gives rise to such discrimination. One should know that all objective realms are thus.

Because one is free from conceptual discrimination, one is oneself neither long nor short, neither beautiful nor ugly, and so forth, up to neither existent nor non-existent, being detached from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus one observes that all phenomena arise solely from the mind’s perceptions.
If they were separated from the mind, not a single phenomenon or mark could be seen to possess any distinction. One should always maintain this practice.
One should maintain mindfulness within the mind, knowing that there are only deluded thoughts and no real objective realm, and must not allow this practice to cease or decline;

this is called the cultivation and study of the contemplation of consciousness-only. If the mind is indeterminate and does not recognize its own mental states, one will perceive the existence of external objects and it cannot be called the contemplation of consciousness-only. Failing to awaken to this Dharma, I now repent for all such faults.
Furthermore, one who guards and records the internal mind recognizes thoughts of greed, thoughts of hatred, and thoughts of delusion or false views;
it recognizes what is wholesome, what is unwholesome, and what is indeterminate. It recognizes mental fatigue and the various anxieties of suffering.

When sitting, one observes and knows according to whatever the mind takes as its object, moment by moment, that it is merely the arising and ceasing of the mind—like the flow of a river or the flicker of a lamp’s flame, which does not abide for even an instant.

From this, one shall attain the Samādhi of the Tranquility of Form. Having attained this samādhi, one should next train in faith regarding the contemplation of the mind through śamatha, and faith regarding the contemplation of the mind through vipaśyanā. As for training in faith regarding the contemplation of the mind through śamatha:
one contemplates that the internal mind has no visible characteristics; it is perfectly still, without coming or going, and its original nature is neither born nor...
It ceases, because it is free from conceptual discrimination. One who practices the contemplation of the mind through *vipaśyanā* perceives internal and external forms;
these arise with the mind and cease with the mind. Even the practice of perceiving the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddha is likewise:

they arise with the mind and cease with the mind, being like an illusion, like a magical transformation, like the moon reflected in water, or like an image in a mirror—neither the mind itself nor separate from the mind.
Neither coming nor not coming; neither going nor not going; neither arising nor not arising; neither acting nor not acting.
Good son, if one can practice and believe in these two contemplations of the mind, one will swiftly attain entry into the path of the One Vehicle.
One should know that this contemplation of mind-only consciousness is called the supreme gateway of wisdom;
for it enables the mind to develop sharp and powerful strength of faith and understanding, swiftly enters into the meaning of emptiness, and gives rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.
I now repent for all instances of failing to realize this Dharma.
If one studies the true contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*), one contemplates the nature of the mind as being without arising or ceasing,
not abiding in seeing or hearing, and forever free from all conceptualizations of cognition. Gradually, one is able to transcend the meditative states of the sphere of infinite space,
the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attaining a semblance of the *śūnyatā-samādhi* and its signs.
At the time of the *ākāśa-samādhi*, the coarse marks of discrimination regarding perception, feeling, and mental formations do not manifest before one.

From this point, one trains under the guidance of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who possess great compassion; they protect and nurture [the practitioner], whereby one leaves behind all obstacles and practices diligently without ceasing.
Consequently, one is able to enter progressively into the *citta-śānti-samādhi*. Having attained this samādhi, one is then further able to enter...
The Samādhi of One Practice. Having entered this Samādhi of One Practice, one beholds countless Buddhas and gives rise to profound and vast conduct.
The mind abides in the stage of firm faith, which is the definitive faith and understanding regarding the two paths of contemplation: śamatha and vipaśyanā.
It is able to definitively incline toward them; and according to whatever worldly dhyānas and samādhis one practices and studies, there is nothing [that is not accomplished].

Free from cowardice and fear, they take no pleasure in the Two Vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*). Because they rely on the capacity for cultivation, they direct their minds toward the two types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

This is the most subtle and skillful means, the basis of all wisdom, and the root of practice. Furthermore, regarding those who cultivate and study as described above in their faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), there are two kinds of persons.

What are these two? First, those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*); second, those of dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*). As for those of sharp faculties, they have already been able to know the One [Vehicle] previously.
All external objects are merely products of the mind; they are deceptive and unreal, like dreams and illusions.
Those who are certain of this, free from doubt, whose hindrances and obscurations are slight, and whose distracted minds are minimal—such persons should engage in this study.
Regarding the true contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*), those of dull faculties have not yet been able to realize that all external objects are merely the mind, deceptive and unreal;
consequently, their defiled attachments are deep-seated, hindrances arise frequently, and the mind is difficult to subdue.

They should first study the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti*). Even if such a person studies and develops this faith and understanding, if their roots of goodness and karma are weak:
Unable to advance further, they cannot gradually subdue their various evil afflictions. Their minds are filled with doubt and timidity;

they fear falling into the three evil realms or being born in the eight difficult states. They fear not constantly encountering Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, and thus being unable to make offerings or hear and receive the True Dharma.
They fear that the practices for awakening will be difficult to accomplish. Such are their doubts and terrors, as well as their various obstacles.
One should, at all times and in all places, constantly and diligently recite and keep in mind my name. If one attains single-mindedness and the roots of goodness increase,
such that the will becomes sharp and keen, one should contemplate that my Dharma-body and the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas are equal in essence to one's own body—
non-dual and undifferentiated, unborn and unceasing, eternal, blissful, self, and...

It is pure; its merits are perfected, and it is worthy of being a refuge. Furthermore, one should observe that the characteristics of one's own body and mind are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure—like an illusion or a magical transformation—and thus they are to be reviled and abandoned. If one can practice and study such contemplation, [one will attain liberation].
One will swiftly increase one’s mind of pure faith, and all obstacles will gradually diminish. I now repent for all instances of failing to awaken to this Dharma.
Furthermore, if a person wishes to be born in a pure land currently existing in another direction, they should follow the Buddha of that world.
If one recites and contemplates these names with focused intent, with a single mind free from distraction, and observes as described above, one will certainly be born in that Buddha’s pure land.
One’s roots of goodness will increase, and one will swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression.

You should know that among all roots of goodness, the practice of single-mindedly binding one's mindfulness to contemplate the equal Dharma-body of all Buddhas is the most supreme; this is what is called diligence.
As for the practitioner: by gradual cultivation, they are able to incline toward the *ekavyūha-samādhi*. If one reaches this *ekavyūha-samādhi*, then a vast and subtle mind of practice is perfected;
this is called attaining the "conformity to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anulomikī-akṣānti*). Failing to awaken to this Dharma, I now repent of it all.
We have been shrouded by ignorance and failed to awaken to the single reality realm. Now that we have encountered this site of enlightenment, we have finally come to realize it.
We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy sages. We burn incense and scatter flowers.
Failing to awaken to the various karmic retributions with single-mindedness, I now reveal and repent them, not daring to conceal anything. By virtue of these causes and conditions,
may I and the ocean of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who have failed to awaken to the realm of one reality have all their karmic retributions purified.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for repentance to extinguish transgressions: Oṃ sarvapāpam me kṣayaṃ kuru svāhā.
(Recite three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas are entirely swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose from beginningless greed, anger, and delusion.
I now confess all that has arisen from my body, speech, and mind;
having confessed, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.

Throughout the ten directions, all take refuge; Sins are extinguished and pure faith increases. May they be born within the Flower Treasury Ocean, In the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[From] "The Chapter on Entering the Sphere of Inconceivable Liberation through the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra."
The Sūtra says: "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva... (up to) "...tenth, universally dedicating all.
First, regarding "paying homage to all Buddhas," the Sūtra says:
"Sudhana said, 'O Great Sage... (up to) ...in the actions of body, speech, and mind, there is no weariness or fatigue."
Having paid homage, with a sincere heart, take refuge and pay obeisance to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Second, regarding the praise of the Tathāgata:
furthermore, O son of good family, as for the "praise of the Tathāgata," it refers to [the state] up to having no weariness in the activities of body, speech, and mind.
Having offered praise, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Third, regarding the extensive cultivation of offerings:
furthermore, O son of noble family, "extensive cultivation of offerings" refers to [the practice] until body, speech, and mental actions are free from weariness.
Having made these offerings, with a sincere heart, take refuge and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Fourth, regarding the repentance for karmic obstructions:
furthermore, O son of good family, as for what is called "repenting and eliminating karmic obstructions," [it extends] until one’s actions of body, speech, and mind are free from weariness.
Having performed the confession, with a sincere heart, take refuge and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Fifth, regarding the merit of rejoicing (*anumodana*):
furthermore, the man says that as for the merit of rejoicing, [it extends] until one’s actions of body, speech, and mind are free from weariness.
Having expressed sympathetic joy, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Sixth, the Request to Turn the Wheel of Dharma:
Furthermore, O son of good family, that which is called "requesting the turning of the wheel of dharma" [extends] until the point where there is no weariness in the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Having made this request, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Seventh, regarding the request for the Buddha to remain in the world:
furthermore, O son of good family, that which is called "requesting the Buddha to remain in the world" [extends] until the point where there is no weariness in the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Having made this exhortation, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Eighth, "Constantly Following the Buddha’s Example":
Furthermore, O son of good family, as for what is called "constantly following the Buddha’s example," it means that one's actions of body, speech, and mind are never weary or exhausted.
Having studied accordingly, one should with a sincere heart take refuge in and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Ninth, "Constantly Accord with Sentient Beings.
Furthermore, O son of good family, as for what is called "constantly accords with sentient beings," it means that one's actions of body, speech, and mind are never weary or indolent.
Having thus accorded with constancy, one should, with a sincere heart, take refuge and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Tenth, regarding universal dedication:
furthermore, son of good family, as for what is called "universal dedication," it extends until one’s actions of body, speech, and mind are free from weariness.
Having performed the dedication, with a sincere heart, take refuge and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
As the Sūtra says: "Good son, this is for the Bodhisattva... (up to) "...all were greatly rejoiced, believed, accepted, and practiced accordingly."
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
With a sincere heart, I make this vow:
by virtue of our cultivation of the merit of the ten inexhaustible vows and practices of Samantabhadra, may we swiftly be able to eliminate [all obstacles].

The five deeds of immediate retribution shall be extinguished; all worldly diseases of body and mind, various afflictions and sufferings, and even all evil karma as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, shall all be eliminated.
All demonic armies, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, pūtanas, and other such malevolent spirits that drink blood and devour flesh—[shall all be subdued].
The gods will all keep their distance; yet at times they may resolve to approach and provide protection.
Therefore, if a person recites this vow and moves through the world, they will encounter no obstacles, like the moon in the sky emerging from the clouds.
They shall be praised by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; all humans and devas should pay them homage, and all sentient beings should make offerings to them.
Nurturing this son of good family, if he attains a human body, he will fully manifest all his merits and, before long,
shall quickly achieve accomplishment like the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, obtaining a subtle and wondrous physical form endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Whether born among humans or devas, wherever he may be, he will always dwell in noble lineages and will be able to utterly destroy all evils.
They are able to distance themselves from all evil associates, subdue all non-Buddhists (tīrthika), and liberate themselves from all afflictions (kleśa).
Like a lion king, they crush and subdue the host of beasts and are worthy of receiving the offerings of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, when such a person approaches the end of life, at the final moment, all their faculties (indriya) will completely dissolve.
All kinsmen shall perish; all power and majesty shall be utterly abandoned and lost;
and all such things as ministers, high officials, the inner and outer palace, elephants, horses, chariots, precious treasures, and hidden hoards shall no longer follow him.
Only this King of Vows shall not forsake him, leading him at his side at all times, even for a single moment.
Immediately upon passing away, one attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Having arrived there, one beholds Amitābha Buddha, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and others.

These bodhisattvas possess majestic and upright physical forms and are fully endowed with merit; they surround [the practitioner] together. That person, acting with sovereign ease, is born within a lotus flower.

In the midst [of this], he received a prophecy from the Buddha. Having received the prophecy, for incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, throughout unspeakably unspeakable worlds in the ten directions, he benefited sentient beings according to their minds by the power of his wisdom.
Before long, he shall sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), subdue the armies of Māra, and attain equal and perfect enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhi).
He awakened and turned the wondrous wheel of Dharma, enabling sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
According to their faculties and natures, he taught and brought them to maturity, continuing until the end of the ocean of future kalpas, extensively benefiting all sentient beings.
Thus, even when the realm of empty space is exhausted, the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, and the karma of sentient beings is exhausted—[he continues to act].

Until the afflictions of birth are exhausted, may this vow of mine never come to an end; may it continue from thought-moment to thought-moment without interruption, and may my actions of body, speech, and mind never grow weary or discouraged.
Having made this vow, take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Next, perform the mudrā and mantra for repentance and the eradication of transgressions: *Oṃ sarvapāpam me kṣayaṃ kuru svāhā*.
(One should recite this three times:
That which has been accumulated over a hundred kalpas Is entirely swept away in a single thought-moment; Like fire consuming dry grass, it is extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed,
hatred, and delusion, Produced through body, speech, and mind— I now confess it all. Having confessed,
I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Proclamation: May the assembly listen to these verses on impermanence from the Sūtra:
All who are born must return to death; Their countenances utterly change and decay. The powerful are assailed by illness; None can escape this fate.
Even if it were Mount Sumeru, At the end of the kalpa, it would all be destroyed and scattered.
The great ocean, deep and bottomless, shall likewise be completely exhausted; the great earth, the sun, and the moon, when their time comes, all return to extinction.

There has never been a single dharma that has not been swallowed by impermanence—from the Peak of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception above, down to the Universal Monarch below, whose seven treasures are ever present with him.
Constantly surrounded by a thousand sons, yet when their lifespan is exhausted, they do not pause for even a moment;
drifting once more upon the ocean of birth and death, they undergo manifold sufferings according to conditions,
as they address the Worthy and Holy Ones.
I look up and pay homage to the Buddha of Ten Bodies who shines everywhere, To all the Tathāgatas of the Flower Treasury World,
And to Śākyamuni, the Honored Original Teacher of this Sahā world, To Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and all the foremost leaders,
To the holy assembly of the ocean of lands and their retinues, And to all the noble beings within the Flower Treasury Assembly.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the multitudes of devas and spirits, Who have attained the path of the knowledge of others' minds and the divine eye—
May you all not forsake the power of compassion, And grant that we two people may realize the gate of dhāraṇī for the practice of vows.
At this time, with a sincere heart, we together prostrate and repent.
May the merit thus produced be used entirely to adorn the Dharma-realm, the oceans of lands, and all sentient beings.
May the celestial beings and immortals not fall into attachment to the pleasures of awakening, but instead recognize the true vehicle within the eternal, pure, and peaceful lands.

May these eminent officials always abide in their positions of honor and rank, all of them rejoicing in the Sudden and Perfect Teachings. May the people enjoy perpetual peace and security, and may they all cultivate the path of enlightened illumination.
May the preceptors, monks, parents, and all who bestow offerings and alms enjoy vast and boundless blessings and prosperity.

May their myriad practices reach perfection, and may those in the three miserable realms simultaneously be freed from suffering while the eight difficulties are entirely eliminated. May the cauldrons of boiling water transform into pools of cool clarity, and the iron beds into lotus seats.
May the sounds of lamentation cease and be replaced by the voices of reciting the Buddha’s name. May every person possess the aspiration to return to their original source. Each...

May each return to the illumination of their original source; may our present vows and future aspirations, together with our non-regressive resolve and contemplative practice, lead to the same realization within the ocean-like assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra as a supreme and auspicious condition.
The Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha; the Perfect Sambhogakāya Rocana Buddha;
the thousand, ten-thousand, and hundred-million transformation bodies Śākyamuni Buddha;
the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Buddha of the twelve supreme vows; and Amitābha Buddha of the forty-eight vows.
The Great Sage Samantabhadra Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
the Great Sage Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Great Sage Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
and the Great Sage Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Pervading the Dharma Realm.

The Vairocana Consecration Light Mantra:
Oṃ ā ma ā (repeated) me (repeated) rañja dharma amogha māne pāṇe mātsarya phala pravartaya hūṃ.
Abiding in the world like empty space, Like a lotus flower unsullied by water,
With a mind pure and transcending all, I prostrate and pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One;
I circumambulate you while reciting your name.
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the Dharma-realm. Homage to the Dharmas of the ten directions throughout the Dharma-realm.
Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions throughout the Dharma-realm. Homage to Vairocana Buddha.
