The Forty-Second Session:
A Separate Invocation of the Compassionate Light to Gather Beings, from the Assembly of Amitābha Buddha.
First, one should learn to pay homage to all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions always draw near to the Buddhas,
serving and making offerings to them without interruption; may they hear and receive the true Dharma and constantly practice its study,
and thereafter learn to pay homage to the treasury of the Dharma.
May all sentient beings in the ten directions draw near to the Dharma, constantly receiving, upholding, reading, reciting,
and contemplating it, practicing according to the Dharma, and further expounding it to others; thereafter,
they shall learn to pay homage to the worthy and holy ones.
May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions always draw near to the noble Sangha, making offerings and serving them without weariness; may their bodhicitta never regress.
Next, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha and make vows.
With a heart of devotion, recite the name of Amitābha; Thus chanting the name up to ten recitations, I pray that your compassion will protect and sustain me, As well as all sentient beings.
Next, one should practice repentance and dedication of merit.
May heavy karmic offenses from past lives be swiftly extinguished; May all obstacles and defilements be abandoned, and pure faith increased;
May all sought-after virtuous aspirations be fulfilled, And may one behold the face of Amitābha and be born in the Pure Land.
Next, the mantra for offering the jeweled lattice:
With clouds of offerings such as these— vast oceans of the intrinsic nature of precious jewels, the most excellent emergence of the seven-jeweled mountains,
and so forth— I offer them to all the Buddhas and others. Oṃ sarva-tathāgata-arcana-pratimaṇḍita-samantālaṃkāra-siddhi.
*Phraṇatsamaṃ hūṃ*. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"There is a dhāraṇī called the 'Mantra of Immeasurable Varieties,' which can accomplish all things and possesses great efficacy. The dhāraṇī says:
Oṃ smara smara mīna smara mā hāṃ phaṭ hūṃ. Next, the mantra of the Ākāśagarbha mudrā:
Oṃ gaganasvabhāva-vajra hoḥ dṛṃ svabhāva svabhāva hūṃ.
Furthermore, bind the Ākāśagarbha mudrā and recite the mantra. Thereafter, from the mudrā there flow forth immeasurable offerings—robes, food, drink, pavilions, and so forth.

Although the power of one's contemplative practice may be slight, the majestic spiritual power of the empowerment through mantra and mudrā is profound and difficult to fathom, even in its extensive yogic explanations.
May the accepted offerings become reality; may each one individually appear as the pure land of Sukhāvatī.

May the offerings currently presented fulfill the essence of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, remaining eternally pervasive. Furthermore, may these incense and flowers be identical with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Pervading all Buddha-fields, they perform the work of Buddhas with pervasive fragrance;
directing their minds in offering,
they provide every kind of offering for the ten directions as required, constantly and universally present, leaving nothing unfulfilled.
Incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, flags, and canopies; all implements of offering, the sounds of various musical instruments, food, drink, clothing, bright lamps and candles;
bedding, medicinal ointments, palaces, and so forth—all such offerings as exist, one should bring to mind and offer them together with all the Tathāgatas.
I rejoice in those who offer worship in all lands, and now, with great joy, I rejoice in them all;
as for those who have not yet practiced such offerings, I shall instruct and guide them so that they may cultivate them.
I make this vow of offering:
may I universally pervade all buddha-fields, providing various ornaments and articles of worship at the sites of all the Triple Gem— the Buddha, Dharma,
and Sangha— and may I serve and uphold them for the sake of all sentient beings.
I offer worship to the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, To their physical forms and images,
as well as to their relics, stūpas, and shrines; And to these places of the Buddha’s work,
As well as the Dharma-throne and the sites where the Dharma is preached, And the abodes of the assembly of noble Saṅgha throughout the Dharma-realm.
May I and all sentient beings universally make offerings together,
practicing the vast offering;
having practiced such offerings, may we gradually attain the six perfections.
One should recollect that the four immeasurables— compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— are all fully accomplished;
one should practice offering while remaining free from signs, for all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent, without arising or ceasing, and equal in their single flavor.
Free from thought, pure, and ultimately perfected— Contemplating thus with deep awakening and reflection,
one praises the Tathāgata in a single pore of his hair with Brahma-sounds: He emits inconceivable light, Universally illuminating all sentient beings.

The Tathāgata causes all afflictions to be extinguished; from a single pore, he produces inexhaustible flowers that pervade the entire Dharma-realm, eliminating the suffering of sentient beings. When the Buddha utters a single sublime sound, all beings understand it according to their own kind;
he rains down the great rain of Dharma, causing them all to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
To speak directly in praise of the Buddha:
As for Amitābha Buddha, he takes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as his essence and employs prajñā as his mind. His golden countenance is vast and expansive;
his *saṃbhogakāya* dwells in the Pure Land. His wondrous marks are majestic and sublime; his *nirmāṇakāya* manifests according to the capacities of sentient beings. Among all the sages...
He was surrounded [by his retinue] like the bright moon amidst the host of stars. His marks and signs were dignified and majestic, resembling blue lotuses blooming in a verdant pond.
Radiance emanated from the ūrṇā-kośa, its brilliance surpassing that of the five mountains; his deep-blue eyes were clear and pure, their exquisite beauty like the four oceans.
With great kindness and great compassion, he manifests thirty-six hundred thousand emanations, all sharing the same name and title.

He displays nine thousand five hundred transformations, emitting twelve rays of light each day to guide and receive those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Through his forty-eight vows, he never abandons his great compassion.
The Holy One seeks out voices to rescue beings from suffering in this Sahā world; the Bodhisattva Śrī-Ābhāsvara guides all classes of beings with a compassionate heart.
We pray that the holy assembly of Amitābha’s ocean-like retinue, with bodies abiding upon lotus pedestals and minds dwelling in the realm of the Buddha—how excellent is your holy virtue!
It transcends words and thought.

Homage to all Buddha-works—whether in the form of Dharma-bodies, physical bodies, images, relics, stūpas, or temples—within all the lands as numerous as atoms throughout the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time;
and likewise to the treasuries of the Dharma and the places where the Dharma is preached.
To the ocean-like assembly of all Bodhisattvas, worthies, and sages (three times):

Homage to Amitābha Buddha, who, through thirty-six trillion, one hundred and eleven thousand, nine thousand five hundred and forty-eight vows, gathers in living beings with the compassionate light from the Western World of Ultimate Bliss; and to Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Pure Ones.
With a sincere heart, recite "Great Ocean Assembly" ten or twenty-one times and repent:
I pray that all the compassionate Honored Ones of the ten directions, For myself and all sentient beings, [grant your protection].
I pray that you act as my witness and protect me with mindfulness; I now repent and shall not commit again the sins accumulated throughout immeasurable kalpas:
The ten evils, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, slandering the Triple Gem, and the icchantika state— May these be swiftly extinguished so that I may attain coolness and purity.
Furthermore, one should contemplate that such offenses arise solely from inversion and delusion;
they have no fixed existence that can be apprehended. Being primordially empty, quiescent, and eternally pure, may I and all sentient beings swiftly and universally attain the opening of the Way.
Swiftly reaching the fundamental mind without error, may the roots of transgression be forever severed and exhausted without remainder.
[This is appended to the Compassionate Awakening Repentance Text.

We, [Name] and others, universally extend our compassion to the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm. May the life-span of the Dharmakāya and the light of primordial wisdom [be realized].
I am of the same essential nature as Amitābha Buddha; yet, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have failed to realize my own mind, giving rise to delusions and creating karma.
I have been unfilial toward my parents, disrespectful toward my teachers and elders, cruel and devoid of compassion, committing killing, stealing, and impure sexual misconduct.
I have engaged in false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh words, as well as greed, anger, and ignorance—thus the ten non-virtuous actions have blazed intensely within me.
They commit no transgressions [of their own making], yet they follow false teachers and do not believe in the Triple Gem.

They may violate the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the twenty-five precepts, the two hundred and fifty precepts, or the five hundred precepts; they may break the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, the three thousand rules of majestic deportment, or the eighty thousand subtle practices.
Fully possessing the nature of an icchantika, they deny cause and effect and slander the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
They destroy the wholesome deeds of others and lack compassion, refusing to encourage their fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.

They even go so far as to kill their fathers, harm their mothers, kill their preceptors (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya), shed the blood of a Buddha, disrupt the Saṃgha that performs the *karmavācanā* and turns the wheel of Dharma,
kill Arhats, destroy stupas and monasteries, mutilate scriptures and images, and subject the monastic community to forced labor or oppression through tyranny.

Furthermore, they have encroached upon and damaged the wealth and property of the Triple Gem in the ten directions; they have preached the Dharma impurely and defiled those who practice the Brahma-faring life.

In this way, they have committed various offenses against the Triple Gem, the assembly of noble ones, teachers, parents, the dharma-realm, and all sentient beings—whether acting themselves or inciting others to act, or seeing others act and rejoicing therein—repeatedly and inexhaustibly, pervading the entire dharma-realm and filling it to overflowing.
O Ākāśa, we now, in the presence of Amitābha Buddha, confess all our transgressions.

We pray that by the majestic spiritual power of Amitābha Buddha, they may be dissolved like ice melting in hot water, and that through a single thought-moment, they may be transformed into unsurpassed wisdom and enlightenment.

Furthermore, by virtue of the forty-eight vows of Amitābha Buddha, which out of compassion for sentient beings emit pure light to gather them in and never abandon them, we shall dwell in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Adorned with various jewels, when Bodhisattvas are reborn there, they never regress. They practice without interruption until they reach Bodhi.
Their original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, as well as all Buddhas of the ten directions, earnestly exhort and praise them.

Whether it be one thought-moment up to ten thoughts, or one day up to seven days, by invoking the name and maintaining mindfulness, rebirth there is certain. We, who are ignorant and deluded, do not...

Their faith is not compliant. Sometimes, having heard [the teaching], they laugh it off with contempt in their hearts. Upon seeing those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they harbor malicious thoughts and slander them.

Even if they possess some degree of faith, it lacks a resolute mind; it wavers between existence and non-existence, advancing and retreating. Their karmic conditions are deep and heavy, entangled by worldly affairs.

Though their bodies reside in the place of practice, their minds dwell upon mundane truths. Their mouths speak of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, yet their hearts long for this Sahā world. Regarding this—

When reciting the Buddha’s name, the mind is often distracted; thus, among the three types of pure karma, not even a fragment of goodness is accomplished, and the sixteen contemplations of the mind fail to penetrate at once.
At the time of death, one may meet with an untimely demise—such as when walls collapse, houses fall, trees break, or cliffs crumble;

or by being swept away by water or consumed by fire; or by being injured by insects or bitten by beasts; or when weapons suddenly arrive, or one is violently harmed by poison; or when a sudden illness strikes the body. Not...

How could one have leisure to mind the Buddha? Or, when entangled by a grave illness, the body and mind are oppressed by suffering; one wallows and wails, making it difficult to maintain right mindfulness.
Or, lacking virtuous friends to assist in generating pure causes, through these various karmic conditions of transgression, at the time of the end of life—

They shall not behold the Buddha, nor attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Instead, they will once again circulate through the five turbidities and evil worlds of Sahā, encountering the three miserable realms and eight difficulties.
Reborn according to their karma, they will experience the five pains and five burnings as their ultimate suffering throughout future births and deaths.
There will be no end to this. Some may fall into the hardship of being born with golden chains, unable to see a Buddha for five hundred years.
All of these result from having, since ancient times, lacked faith in Amitābha Buddha and lacked faith in rebirth in the Pure Land;

they treated the body, speech, and mind with negligence, contempt, and slander. Due to these causes and conditions, although they may now resolve to practice, they encounter many obstacles and difficulties. I, now...
I prostrate to Amitābha Buddha. I pray that Your celestial eye may behold me, Your celestial ear may hear me, and Your knowledge of others' minds may perceive me.

With great kindness and great compassion, have pity and accept me; grant me the opportunity to repent, so that I may universally eliminate the karmic obstructions, afflictive obstructions, cognitive obstructions, and the obstruction of disbelief in the Buddha’s words for all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm—the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence—removing even my sloth.
May all obstacles to the practice of cultivation, obstacles of the long night of the three miserable realms, obstacles of the five turbidities of this evil age, obstacles of doubt in remote lands,
and obstacles to hearing of the Triple Gem— indeed, every single hair’s breadth of obstacle to rebirth— be entirely eliminated and purified.
With right faith manifest before them, free from doubt and without regression, they will certainly be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss, swiftly attain perfect enlightenment,
and turn the Great Dharma Wheel to fulfill their vast and expansive vows and practices.
With a sincere heart,
I entreat you: may all bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions who have not yet attained perfect enlightenment quickly achieve equal and right awakening, for the benefit of all sentient beings.
May all those who have attained perfect enlightenment remain forever in this world,
constantly turning the vast and sublime Wheel of Dharma; we entreat you not to enter nirvana, and with sincere hearts,
we rejoice in your virtue.
May I and all sentient beings, who have been perfumed by the unwholesome states of envy,
pride, and arrogance arising upon seeing the superior achievements of others, now utterly abandon them;
and may we likewise abandon all merits acquired through study and practice throughout all the buddha-fields of the three times.
And all those who have attained accomplishment— I now rejoice in them all with my whole heart.
Dedicate these merits I have cultivated To benefit all sentient beings.
May all together dedicate this toward the Buddha’s wisdom, And swiftly reach the city of Nirvana.
This supreme conduct of mine, Samantabhadra, And its boundless, excellent merit, I dedicate entirely:
May all sentient beings drowning in suffering Swiftly proceed to the buddha-field of Amitābha.
With a sincere heart, I make this vow:
may my disciples extend [this merit] universally to the four debts of gratitude and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm of the three realms of existence.

From this day forward, may they abide in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), cultivate the primary cause for the pure karma of a Buddha, provide filial support to their parents, serve their teachers and elders, and maintain a compassionate heart that refrains from killing.
Cultivate the ten wholesome karmas; receive and uphold the Three Refuges; be fully endowed with the various precepts; do not violate the rules of dignified conduct;
arouse the bodhicitta; have deep faith in cause and effect; read and recite the Mahāyāna; exhort practitioners of purity; be mindful of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;

be mindful of the precepts, of giving, and of the ultimate heavenly realm (paramārtha-deva). With a sincere mind, a profound mind, and a mind of dedication and aspiration, invoke the name of the Buddha.
Recite the Name; praise the Name of the Buddha; praise the radiance of the Buddha; contemplate the sixteen sublime realms of the Buddha’s primary and secondary marks;
recollect the forty-eight original vows of the Buddha; deliberate upon the three grades of rebirth; enter deeply through the five gates; accord with the three kinds of bodhi-gates;
and faithfully accept the teachings of all Buddhas of the ten directions. Whether with a distracted mind or a concentrated mind, I only pray that Amitābha Buddha...
May your Dharma-power augment your supernatural faculties to manifest great benefit, so that we may concentrate our minds on the path of awakening and tread in the dark toward the Great Vehicle.

In every movement and posture, may we never be separated from the vision of the Buddha—just as one sees one’s own face in a bright mirror—and may we constantly behold the myriad wondrous joys of that land even within our dreams.
May this comfort our hearts, causing us to progress ever further; out of compassion, please protect and shield us with the Dharma.
Their seeds increase. Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they remain far removed from demonic activities.

Furthermore, the karmic afflictions and worldly toil accumulated over immeasurable kalpas all become pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Through these roots of goodness and merit, they enter together into the great cause;

having fully dedicated all accumulated conditions toward this end, they are free from all obstacles at the time of death. Seven days prior, they know in advance that their time has come, and their bodies are free from pain.
With diligent effort free from delusion, body and mind are peaceful and blissful, as if entering meditative concentration.

Upon meeting a virtuous friend who instructs one to maintain ten recitations of "Amitābha Buddha," the Buddha and his assembly of holy ones appear before one, emitting great radiance and extending their hands to welcome them.
One sees oneself mounted upon a diamond pedestal, following behind the Buddha; in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, one is reborn there.
Having arrived at the land, he beheld the physical body of the Buddha, complete with all its marks; he beheld the bodhisattvas, their forms and features fully perfected.
As the jewel groves radiated light and the sublime Dharma was proclaimed, upon hearing it, he immediately realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

His body became the color of pure gold, indistinguishable [from the Buddhas], endowed with the thirty-two marks, mastery of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and great eloquence, as he expounded all-encompassing wisdom. Nara...

Their bodies are elongated and their lifespans are immeasurable. Their needs are met according to their wishes, and exquisite garments appear spontaneously. They never hear ill repute and do not cling to the view of a self.

They gather together with all superior and virtuous people, dwelling in the stage of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), never regressing, until they finally reach the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).
There, they enjoy the pure Dharma-joy of the Mahayana, making offerings throughout the six periods of day and night.
Amitābha Buddha. Every morning at dawn, you shall serve the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, hear the Dharma, and receive predictions of enlightenment.
You will attain dhāraṇīs and achieve mastery over emanation bodies, pervading the ten directions. In buddha-less lands, you shall realize equal and perfect awakening;
in places of extreme suffering, you shall sport with supernatural powers, manifesting physical forms according to the minds of sentient beings and the scope of their understanding, day and night.
He preaches the Dharma without ceasing. In every moment of thought, he causes unspeakably many, unspeakably many sentient beings to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
In every moment of thought, he causes unspeakably many, unspeakably many sentient beings to abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra.
May the provisions of merit and virtue be fully perfected, so that we may together attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
May each of us adorn a pure land and gather and transform sentient beings, exactly like Amitābha Buddha, without any difference.
I pray that Amitābha Buddha will compassionately bear witness to this.
I only pray that I may seek rebirth within the Pure Land, Free from all illness and always dwelling in peace and joy;
That all karmic offenses confessed shall be utterly extinguished, And all vows made shall be fully perfected.
May I constantly give rise to the aspiration to seek rebirth in Sukhāvatī, And constantly practice the conduct for seeking rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
May all my practices and vows, even those as small as a single flower, be fulfilled for both myself and all sentient beings.
May I and all beings vow to be born upon the lotus pedestals of the nine grades.
May we constantly cultivate the sixteen sublime contemplations and the three types of pure karma; may I and all beings fulfill these vows.
The forty-eight kinds of vows I have made, And the two hundred and ten billion practices,
Even down to the single thought-moment of all practices and vows— May I and all sentient beings fully accomplish them all.
When I am about to reach the end of my life, May every single obstacle be completely eliminated.
Having personally beheld that Buddha Amitābha, one immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Once I have been reborn in that land, may this great vow be fulfilled before my very eyes,
entirely and without exception, for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all realms of sentient beings.
The assembly of that Buddha was entirely pure; at that time, I was born from a supreme lotus and beheld the Tathāgata Amitābha face-to-face.
Having received the prophecy of enlightenment from that Tathāgata, he manifested countless hundreds of koṭis of emanation bodies.
The power of wisdom is vast and pervasive throughout the ten directions,
universally benefiting the realms of all sentient beings until the exhaustion of empty space, the exhaustion of sentient beings, and the exhaustion of karma and afflictions.
As long as all such things remain inexhaustible, may your ultimate wisdom likewise never cease.
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Flower Treasury Ocean, within the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Regarding the masters of the *Avataṃsaka* who first transmitted it to the Western Regions:
the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna was originally the Buddha *Meghasvara*. He manifested his traces at the stage of the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*). He was from the South.
He was of Brahmin descent from the land of India. His family was wealthy and noble; he was exceptionally intelligent from childhood, surpassing all others without peer.
He was born with the wisdom of omniscience and understood the four Vedas, astronomy, geography, astrology, divination, and all manner of magical arts, none of which remained unknown to him.
By smelling the scent of medicinal herbs, he could identify those from five different kingdoms. Having realized that desire is the root of suffering, he swiftly made his vow. Ninety.
At midday, he recorded all the scriptural texts of the Five Indias and expounded their meanings and principles with a fluency like flowing water.
He claimed to be an omniscient person and resided in a crystal palace. The Great Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, having become aware of him, [acted accordingly].
By means of his supernatural power, he summoned [the assembly] to the sea and opened the treasuries of the seven precious jewels.
He revealed the Vaipulya Sūtras; upon seeing this Great Inconceivable Sūtra, it was found to have three versions.

The Superior Version consists of verses as numerous as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and chapters as numerous as the atoms in one four-continent world system. As for the Middle Version, it has four...

It consists of one hundred and nine thousand eight hundred and eighty verses and one thousand two hundred chapters. As for the "Shorter Version" of the sutra, it contains one hundred thousand verses and thirty-nine chapters;
Nāgārjuna recited this and transmitted it to the world. Having obtained the Shorter Version, the brilliant sun of wisdom shone upon the celestial realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Plying the oars of the boat of compassion, he traveled across the ocean of the nature of *tathatā*, realizing the thirty [stages].

The second [master], Dharmakṣema, compiled various sūtras and composed the *Mahā-acintya-śāstra* (Great Inconceivable Treatise) in one hundred thousand verses, which was widely disseminated throughout the Western Regions.

He also compiled the teachings on the signless emptiness (*animitta-śūnyatā*) of the Mahāyāna and composed the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in five hundred verses, the *Mahāvyūha-buddhamārga-śāstra* in fifty stanzas, the *Mahākaruṇopāya-śāstra* in fifty stanzas, and the *Abhayasūtra-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses. Mahā...
The *Vyākhyāyukti-śāstra* in ten fascicles and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* in one hundred fascicles; he whose name is the Omniscient One— now, as we, the assembly,
pay homage and praise his meritorious virtues, we dedicate the roots of goodness thereby obtained to the ocean of all sentient beings,
wishing that they may forever be free from the veils and hindrances and swiftly awaken to Bodhi.
Homage to the Great Master Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, the Omniscient One, who composed the *Great Inconceivable Treatise* based on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*.
Homage to the one who composed the *Treatise on the Ten Stages* based on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, [a work] consisting of a thousand sections that perfectly integrates the six aspects.
To the Master of Treatises, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
and to the various masters who successively transmitted and translated the Avataṃsaka Sūtra in the Eastern Land,
including the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra (Jue Xian) from Northern India during the Jin Dynasty— homage to them!
Homage to the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Bharukaccha, who came from Central India during the Tang Dynasty, and whose sun-like radiance illumined the land;
homage to the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, who realized the holy [truth] and delighted in study;
and next, homage to the patriarchs of the Huayan school, the authentic transmitters of the Dharma in this eastern land.
Homage to Dharma Master Shun, the Third Patriarch within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, who composed the *Dharmadhātu Contemplation* (Zao fajie guan).
Homage to Yunhua Zhi, the Fourth Patriarch within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, who composed the *Ten Mysterious Gates* (Shixuan men).
Master Yan:
Homage to the *Tanyuan ji* (Record of Exploring the Profundities) composed by the Fifth Patriarch, Master Xianshou Fazang, within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Homage to the Sixth Patriarch’s Great Commentary and Sub-commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, composed by the Dharma Master Qingliang Chengguan.
Homage to those within the lineage of Qingliang who have attained the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision as found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Homage to the Great Master No. 38 and over one thousand other Dharma masters who,

following the Seventh Patriarch of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, composed the *Huayan lúnguàn zhù* (Commentary on the Essential Themes of the Avataṃsaka) and the *Guifeng Zongmi Chanshi* (Chan Master Zongmi of Mount Gui).
Homage to the Great Master Guangzhi, the author of the *Guanzhuji* commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
homage to the successive masters who propagated the *Avataṃsaka* in the Great Xia state;
homage to the various masters who lectured on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, and who translated the various sūtras of the True Vehicle.
To the National Preceptor of the True Meaning, the Pure Precepts of the Xianbei,
the Tripitaka Master Rudu Zhiyun, who translated the scriptures within the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, I pay homage.
Homage to the Imperial Preceptor of True Nation’s Wondrous Enlightenment, who causes the gates of contemplation to flourish within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya*;
homage to the New Yuan,
who transmitted and produced the great commentaries and sub-commentaries within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya*.
The True Realizer Imperial Preceptor, Namo;
the Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, long transmitted through the land of Woli Hwaŏm;
the National Preceptor Hwaŏm.
Homage to the National Preceptor Haiin, the Sovereign of Oral Transmission and Exposition within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya*, who is like an ocean seal;
homage to the Most Venerable One of Unobstructed Wisdom and Eloquence in the Exposition and Dissemination of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya*.
The National Preceptor Jue (Jue Guoshi) of the Eastern Land bows to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* of the Great Vaipulya Buddha;
in accordance with the ten kinds of Dharma-practices of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he exhorts, praises, and rejoices in all Dharma masters.

Homage to the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*. This is the ritual for the propagation of the Dharma at Lánshān Yúnyán Cí'ēn Monastery, performed by the National Protector, the Dharma Master Hǎiguó Yīxíng Huìjué;
next follows the repentance for eighty-four thousand afflictions and karmic deeds.
I only pray that the inexhaustible Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha jewels of the celestial net, Vairocana Tathāgata,

and the assembly of holy beings of Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the ocean-like gathering— by the compassionate original vows of all mundane and supramundane deities— may emit great radiance to illuminate this dharma assembly.
I pray that you will bear witness to my protection and mindfulness, and compassionately embrace me with pity.

May I and the ocean of all sentient beings, from beginningless time until this very moment, confess and repent for our inexhaustible ocean of karma—the myriad layers of delusions and karmic actions, as vast as Indra’s net.

Now, within the various schools concerning nature and characteristics, there are eighty-four thousand Dharma gates, eighty-four thousand merits, eighty-four thousand afflictions, and eighty-four thousand ten-fold evil karmas. In this present age of decadence, every person commits unwholesome karma;
each performs evil deeds without remorse. Consequently, through these resentful Māras and non-Buddhists, the True Dharma is destroyed and extinguished. Its...
Regarding the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), there are two interpretations. The first is that the fundamental afflictions of sentient beings are tenfold:

(1) greed, (2) hatred, (3) pride, (4) ignorance, (5) doubt, (6) the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), (7) the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), (8) false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), (9) the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and (10) the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Since each of these delusions possesses ten further aspects, they constitute one hundred. These should be divided into nine [categories].

As for the categories: because the superior grade is heavy, it is divided into three grades; because the middle and inferior grades are light, each is treated as a single grade. Combined, these constitute five hundred.

Regarding one’s own five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), five hundred arise in total; regarding the five sense objects of others, another five hundred arise in total. Each of these bases thus totals one thousand.

Furthermore, if one separately gives rise to five hundred for each of the individual five sense objects—both one's own and those of others—there are five thousand. This constitutes the distinct delusions.

Five thousand are deluded specifically regarding the Truth of Suffering; five thousand are deluded specifically regarding the Truth of Origination; five thousand are deluded specifically regarding the Truth of Cessation;

and five thousand are deluded specifically regarding the Truth of the Path. Thus, these specific delusions regarding the Four Truths amount to twenty thousand, and together with the original one thousand, they total twenty-one thousand.
Furthermore, there are twenty-one thousand based on those who predominantly act out of greed; twenty-one thousand based on those who predominantly act out of hatred;
twenty-one thousand based on those who predominantly act out of delusion; and twenty-one thousand based on those who possess an equal proportion of all three.
These together constitute eighty-four thousand. Second, taking the ten unwholesome actions as their objects, they gradually form combinations such that each one becomes tenfold.
One hundred [delusions] regarding oneself and others in relation to the five sense objects constitute one thousand.

Regarding those who are deluded concerning the tenfold Dharma-gate of the Truths—namely, the Four Truths, Three Truths, Two Truths, and One Truth—if one is deluded such that each Truth is explained as having ten aspects (such as the Truth of Delusion), this constitutes ten thousand.
Now, being deluded regarding these ten Truths, there are differences in their emptiness, which divides them into twenty thousand. Some say "deluded."
The ten wholesome paths of action and the two truths are divided into twenty thousand, plus the original one thousand, as explained in other sutras.

Such phenomena within the Indra’s Net of the Dharma-realm, the ocean of delusions, and the ocean of karma, are infinitely layered and inexhaustible. If one wishes to reveal and repent these transgressions, one should recognize the ten minds of contrariness and compliance.

The *Tiantai Mohe Zhiguan* states: "If one wishes to repent for the heavy obstacles of the two worlds [past and present], one should recognize the ten minds that follow the current of samsara and clearly understand their faults;
one should then mobilize the ten minds that flow against the current as an antidote. These twenty minds constitute the foundation for all forms of repentance.
As for the ten minds that follow the current: first, from time immemorial, the consciousness has been deluded and obscured by afflictions..."

Intoxicated by afflictions (*kleśa*), they falsely conceptualize a self and what belongs to a self (*pudgala-ātman*). Because of this conceptualization of self and what belongs to a self, the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) arises.
Due to the view of a self-body, there is deluded inversion; due to inversion, greed, anger, and ignorance arise. Because of greed, anger, and ignorance, one extensively creates various karmas.

Karma leads to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Second, internally possessing afflictions and externally encountering evil friends who fan and stir up false teachings, they are urged and deluded.

The mind becomes doubly more flourishing [in its corruption]. Third, when internal and external adverse conditions are fully present, they are able to extinguish wholesome states of mind within and extinguish wholesome deeds without;
furthermore, one feels no sympathetic joy whatsoever toward the virtues of others. Fourth, one gives rein to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, committing every kind of evil.
Fifth, although their transgressions may not be extensive, their evil intentions are pervasive. Sixth, their evil intentions continue in succession, uninterrupted day and night.
Seventh, they conceal and deny their faults, unwilling for others to know them. Eighth, they are obstinate and aggressive, showing no fear of the evil realms.
Ninth is the absence of shame and the absence of remorse. Tenth is the denial of cause and effect, becoming an icchantika.

These are the ten kinds [of states] that follow the stream of birth and death; through delusion they commit evil, like a latrine worm delighting in its dung, neither perceiving nor knowing as they accumulate heavy burdens.
They are beyond measure and calculation. From the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes, down to the most extreme icchantikas, the cycle of birth and death is vast and boundless.
Now, wishing to repent, one must turn against this. One should employ ten kinds of mind within the flow of transgressions to overturn and eliminate evil dharmas.
First, one must correctly believe in cause and effect with absolute certainty; though the seeds of karma may be ancient, they do not perish over time, and ultimately there is no escape.
One acts; others receive the fruit. One clearly discerns good and evil and gives rise to no doubt or confusion—this is profound faith. It overturns and destroys the mind of an icchantika.
Second, one feels self-reproach and censures oneself as an utterly base sinner, shameless and devoid of modesty, practicing the ways of beasts and abandoning the pure, supreme adornment.
Alas, being without the hook, one has committed such grave offenses. May the heavens behold me!

One should conceal one's transgressions. Therefore, one feels shame before gods and humans who know of one’s manifest offenses; this is what is meant by "humility" (*hrī*). By means of this, one overturns and destroys the mind of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of remorse (*anapatrāpya*).
Third is the fear of the evil realms. Human life is impermanent; with a single breath not yet returned, one departs forever for a thousand years.

The dark path is vast and distant, and there are no provisions for the journey. The ocean of suffering is wide and deep; where can one find a boat or raft to rely upon? [Thus, one should take refuge in] the sages and saints.
Reproached and cast aside, with no one to rely upon, as the years gradually pass and the "wind-sword" of death does not wait, how can one remain complacent while awaiting pain?
It is like a jackal that has lost its ears, tail, and teeth, feigning sleep in hopes of escaping, yet suddenly hearing that its head is to be severed; its heart is struck with great terror.
Having encountered birth, old age, and sickness, one does not even regard them as urgent; when the matter of death is imminent, how could one not be afraid? This is the mind of fear.
When rising from meditation, one should feel as if treading upon boiling water or fire; there is no leisure for greed or defilement regarding the five sensory objects or the six desires.

Like King Aśoka, who heard that a caṇḍāla would ring a bell every morning to announce that one day had passed and that he would die on the sixth day—despite possessing the five desires, he did not harbor a single thought of attachment—the practitioner should be filled with dread and repent with such intensity that they do not spare even their own body or life, just as that jackal was determined.
One must be entirely free of all thoughts and recollections, like that King Bhīṣma. By this, one overturns and destroys the mind that does not fear the evil realms.

Fourth, one should confess and reveal [one's faults] rather than concealing them; do not harbor the thorns, poisons, and evil weeds of one’s defects. One must urgently eliminate them, for when the roots are exposed, the branches wither;
when the source dries up, the flow ceases. If one conceals their transgressions, they are an ignoble person. Kāśyapa, the dhūta practitioner, shall cause [them] to confess before the great assembly.

One should confess [the transgressions] according to the Vaipulya sūtras, causing oneself to disclose them before a single person. As for the remaining methods of practice, one should simply reform before an image of the Buddha with a sincere heart.

It is like having an abscess hidden in a dark place; if it is covered up and ignored rather than treated, one will die. By this means, one overturns and destroys the mind that conceals and hides its offenses.

Fifth, regarding the "mind that severs the continuity": if one resolutely cuts off the old karma and completes the rite of dedication so as not to create new karma, this is indeed [the true repentance].
Repentance. If one commits an offense again after having already repented, it is like the law of kings: the first offense may be pardoned, but a repetition is treated as a grave crime.

Likewise, the fault of entering the *maṇḍala* for the first time is easily extinguished, but a repetition is difficult to eliminate. Having already been able to vomit it out, why would one swallow it again?

By this means, one overturns and destroys the mind that constantly dwells upon evil matters. Sixth, the arousal of the *bodhicitta*: formerly, one’s own safety was at the expense of others, universally causing them distress.
Regarding all objects: now, extensively giving rise to universal salvation, pervading the realm of empty space, one acts for the benefit of others.

This reverses the previous state of giving rise to an evil mind that pervades all places. Seventh, as for cultivating merit to compensate for past faults: formerly, one committed offenses through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind without regard for day or night;
now, with a virtuous body, speech, and mind, one exerts oneself without ceasing. It is not a matter of moving mountains or filling rivers and seas.

This is refuted by the following: those who formerly gave rein to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, and who themselves destroyed their own roots of goodness as well as the goodness of others—neither rejoicing in them themselves nor rejoicing in others doing so—now protect all roots of goodness and employ skillful means to increase and expand them.

One must not allow this to be severed, just like the merit of protecting an entire city. The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "To guard the True Dharma and to embrace the True Dharma is the foremost [virtue].
By this, one overturns and destroys the absence of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*). Ninth, as for "recalling the Buddhas of the ten directions":

formerly, one was intimately associated with evil friends and believed their words; now, one recalls the Buddhas of the ten directions and recollects their unimpeded compassion, acting as an unsolicited [teacher].
Friend, contemplate unimpeded wisdom and act as a great guide. Reverse and shatter the mind that follows evil friends. Regarding the tenth contemplation on the emptiness of the nature of offenses:
realize that the minds of greed, anger, and delusion are all gates of tranquility. Why is this? When greed and anger arise, where do they abide?
Know that this greed and anger abide in deluded thoughts; deluded thoughts abide in inversion. Inversion...
The view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is invertedly established within the body; the view of a self-body is established within the view of a self. Yet the view of a self has no place of abiding.
If one seeks it thoroughly throughout the ten directions, a self cannot be found. My own mind is inherently empty; there is no master over sin or merit.

Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, one illuminates the ten directions, causing this wisdom of emptiness to be in accord with the mind. It is like when the sun rises: the morning dew vanishes in an instant.
All minds are gates of tranquility, for they demonstrate tranquility. By means of this, one overturns and destroys the darkness of ignorance;

these constitute the ten kinds of repentance. They accord with the path to Nirvana and flow against the current of birth-and-death, capable of extinguishing the transgressions of the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes.
If one does not understand these ten minds, one has no recognition at all of right and wrong; how then could one perform repentance? Even if one were to... [the text continues].
To enter the *maṇḍala* and practice asceticism in vain brings no great benefit in the end. This is precisely what is meant in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states:

"If one says that the diligent practice of asceticism is a proximate cause for the Great Nirvāṇa, such a thing is impossible. This refers to what is called a grave offense within the context of repentance.
Next is the repentance for the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*). Because of the delusions of view, one follows the current of birth and death, as previously described.

One should direct the ten mental states (*daśa-citta*) toward this and perform the repentance by means of concrete objects (*vastu*), thereby repenting for the offenses of the dull proclivities (*mṛdu-anuśaya*). Now, supporting this with principle (*yukti*), one repents for the views themselves, thereby repenting for the offenses of the sharp proclivities (*tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*).

However, because the mind of views is fierce and its power gives rise to heavy afflictions (*kleśa*), one should employ concrete objects as auxiliary aids. It is like taking a purgative medicine that requires the addition of *bhallātaka* (castor bean) to ensure its efficacy.

To cause [the defilements] to be completely drained away to the very bottom, one therefore returns to summarizing the ten dharmas to clarify the repentance for the first instance of breaking faith through views.

This specifically points to the mind of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity), causing one to recognize ignorance (*avidyā*) and the suffering of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*). Just as Udraka Rāmaputra failed to attain the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), yet the world revered him;
or as the Buddha did not recognize that the retribution of suffering and its origin was exhausted, and thus fell back into the error of Subhadra. One must attain...

Regarding the meditative state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*): although coarse perception is absent, subtle afflictions remain. Even those with long nails and sharp intelligence may accept or reject [this state], yet they remain attached to external paths;
they have not yet emerged from views. This is not *nirvāṇa*, much less so for those who are coarse and shallow, who do not even reach the level of Bhaṭṭaputra.
To claim that this is the true path—how could this not be a great perversion? Such a person is attached to it; they do not understand the wisdom that contemplates emptiness.

This is called ignorance (*avidyā*), from which [the other links] arise. Contrary to the truth, following views, one performs formative actions (*saṃskāra*); based on these views, one performs further actions. Based on form (*rūpa*) is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*);

name-and-form is suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth. Deluded regarding suffering, one gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) for existence (*bhava*). From this, there arises birth (*jāti*) and the future flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The continuous succession of rebirths—how could this be quiescence? To claim that birth and death have been exhausted is but a boastful word.

To call the mind of ignorance and false views the Way, to take what is not the Way for the Way, and to reckon what is not a cause as a cause, is called "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); is this not the theft of causes?

To call the future retributions of suffering in the three miserable realms "nirvāṇa" is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). To regard what is not a fruit as a fruit is the grasping for a fruit (*phalābhiniveśa*).

The nature of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) can be understood through these examples. A mind with such views is itself the origin of suffering (*samudaya*), not its cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*).
It does not even accord with the path or cessation of the Tripiṭaka; how much less could it be the path or cessation of the Mahāyāna? If one can understand it in this way, then—

Because one knows the causes and effects of the world and further recognizes the causes and effects of transcending the world, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Prajñā can demonstrate the characteristics of the world;
that is to say, it demonstrates what is the path and what is not the path. This constitutes a profound recognition and vision of the mind’s suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*).

Furthermore, "profound" means not only knowing the accumulation of suffering that is ignorance, but also recognizing the causes and effects of the Three Baskets (*Tripiṭaka*) and recognizing the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

This refers to the emptiness of the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, that which is "profound" also means knowing that dependent origination is itself the provisional, immeasurable causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, that which is "profound" also means knowing that dependent origination is itself the middle way, the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths.

Because within a single moment of seeing the mind, one fully cognizes all causes and effects, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Within a single thought-moment, one is able to weigh and measure them all."

The immeasurable cycle of birth and death is called the inconceivable; therefore, it is said that "profound faith destroys lack of faith. Second, regarding the cultivation of profound shame and remorse:
not perceiving the principle of the Three Truths within one's own mind is what is termed shame and remorse. This is explained here according to the contemplation of principle (*li*).

Regarding the discussion of humans and devas: one feels shame before those at the stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*); one feels remorse before those of the four fruits of the pure heavens and those of the thirty minds;
one feels shame before the devas of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), those with the five grades of purity of the six faculties, and the devas of the forty-two positions.

For example, those who attain the name through intentional effort are called humans, while those who attain the name through natural fruition are called devas; the two types of humans and devas are likewise so named.
This is so. The path of skillful means is called "human," while the manifestation of ultimate truth is called "divine.

When the mind perceives its own commission of offenses, it obscures the principle of the Three Truths and fails to attain the state of either the three types of humans or the devas. Therefore, shame and remorse serve to overturn and destroy the mind of lack of shame and remorse. Regarding the three fears:
they consist in knowing and seeing that the offenses committed by the mind are profound and grave. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddhas teach the meaning of emptiness for..."

Because one has abandoned all views, yet if one still perceives emptiness, such a person cannot be transformed by any of the Buddhas. Due to my current perception, I have committed a great transgression;
when this kalpa ends, I shall be born in the hells of other realms, and when this kalpa begins again, I shall return to this very place.
Thus it will continue in succession, for immeasurable and boundless eons. As for the body one receives as the retribution for this act, it is said that one shall die from vomiting hot blood.

One knows and sees that the offense is grave and heavy. Since it is not untainted (*anāsrava*), one does not transcend birth and death. When afflictions moisten karma, one falls into ruin—of this there is no doubt.
A single life cannot be reclaimed, and there will never be a day of escape. For this reason, one gives rise to great fear, overturning and destroying the mind that did not fear the evil realms.
Fourth, regarding confession: from time immemorial, various views have given rise to attachment, and these three [afflictions] have been concealed.
Truth. Being unable to decisively give rise to faith, one now recognizes the faults of one's views and eliminates the three doubts; without concealment, one reveals the nature of the Truths.
This is called "confession" (*pratikarman*), which overturns and destroys the mind that harbors secret transgressions. Fifth, regarding the "mind that severs continuity":
through the contemplation of the Three Truths, one must ensure there is no interruption, using the Eightfold Noble Path to treat the mind of the three delusions, severing them so that they do not...
"Practice. This translates as "breaking the continuity of evil thoughts. Sixth, regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta:

this refers to taking the principle of the three truths as one's object; all are like empty space. Since emptiness is boundless, one feels compassion for all beings, universally seeking to deliver them.
Because of past delusion, afflictions have arisen boundlessly; thus, transgressions are also boundless. Now, the bodhicitta pervades the entire dharma-realm, giving rise to [virtue] without limit.

To perform good deeds is likewise to pervade the Dharma-realm; this overturns and destroys the former state of pervading emptiness while committing evil. Playing the *siṃha-vīṇā* (lion lute) causes the other strings to snap—this is precisely that meaning.
Regarding the seventh point, "cultivating merit to compensate for faults": the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) of the three truths are the Bodhisattva’s precious torch.
The *dhāraṇī* is the method for practicing the Path and the gateway to Nirvana. Such factors of the path [should be cultivated] in every thought-moment.

Continuity means cultivating merit to compensate for past faults. Previously, one was attached to views, mistaking them for *nirvāṇa*; thus, while remaining unmoved by those views, one did not cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Even if one were to move from existence toward non-existence, it would be like a centipede: although it moves within its view, it still cannot cultivate the factors of enlightenment.
Now, knowing that both existence and non-existence are merely views and no longer grasping at them as real—this is called "moving within views," yet [not being moved by them].

Regarding the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*): if one analyzes and deconstructs various views while practicing the factors of enlightenment, this is called "moving within views" while cultivating the factors of enlightenment.

Furthermore, when one realizes that the very substance of views is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—since it is said to be "identical" (*ji*), one does not move from the views while cultivating the three kinds of factors of enlightenment;
this constitutes the merit of cultivation, which remedies the fault of indulging in views. Eighth is the protection of the true Dharma.

In the past, he protected [the teachings] by not allowing others to destroy them, employing skillful means to provide exegesis and defense. Now, he protects the Three Truths so that various forms of emptiness do not allow them to be destroyed.

If there is lingering attachment to the wholesome, he skillfully applies himself to propagate and maintain the Dharma at the cost of his own life; he is like parents who guard and praise their child. This is the opposite of destroying and ruining wholesome deeds.
Ninth, as for "recalling the Buddhas of the ten directions": in the past, he was afflicted by the poison of [wrong] views, yet he was ever without...
One becomes weary and dissatisfied, like one who thirsts for drink; yet meeting an evil teacher is like being given salt water.

Seeking to abandon suffering through suffering, with a mind of self-conceit, arrogance, and insincere flattery, one will not hear the name of the Buddha for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Now, to contemplate the Three Truths as neither coming nor going is precisely the Buddha’s Dharma of non-arising; this is the Buddha’s eternal truth, protected by the principle of reality.

This overturns the mind that associates with evil friends. Regarding the tenth [point], contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses: these three types of delusion are fundamentally quiescent;
yet, failing to understand this, I falsely claim they exist—just as a person suffering from a fever sees various dragons and ghosts.
Now, observing them as being like illusions or transformations, they come from nowhere and depart without leaving a trace, nor do they go to the east, west, south, or north.
All sins and merits are likewise thus: one emptiness encompasses all emptiness. Emptiness is the very nature of sin; the nature of sin is emptiness.
This reversal shatters the perverted mind. When performing these ten repentances, one should deeply contemplate the Three Truths while further augmenting them with ritual acts.
With a sincere heart, not sparing even body or life, one is called the second type of "hero. This is termed the dual repentance of both fact and principle.

We have been shrouded by ignorance; we did not recognize the causes of affliction, karma, and transgression. Now that we have encountered this site of enlightenment, we have finally awakened to this knowledge.
We take refuge in the Tathāgata Vairocana and the ocean-like assembly of all worthy and holy ones. We burn incense and scatter flowers.

I openly confess and repent for all delusions and karmic actions, not daring to conceal them. By virtue of these causes and conditions, may the ocean of all delusions and karmic actions of myself and the ocean of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm—the infinitely interpenetrating net of Indra—be entirely purified.
Next, the mudrā and mantra for repentance and the eradication of transgressions: Oṃ sṛmara-pa-pame-spuṭna-hadana-mitrāya svāhā.
(Recite this three times.)
Sins accumulated over a hundred kalpas are entirely swept away in a single thought; like fire consuming dry grass, they are extinguished without remainder.
All the evil karma I have created in the past arose from beginningless greed, anger, and delusion.
I now repent of everything produced by my body, speech, and mind.
Having repented, I take refuge with a sincere heart and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
Regarding the sincere arousal of the vow, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva arouses such great vows as these;
that is to say, they give rise to vast, pure, and resolute understanding. With all manner of offerings, they reverently make offerings to all Buddhas, causing them..."
There is nothing else. Furthermore, I vow to receive the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas; I vow to embrace the bodhi of all Buddhas;
I vow to protect the teachings of all Buddhas; and I vow to uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas.

Moreover, I vow that in all worlds, the Buddhas shall arise in the world—descending from the Tuṣita heaven, passing away, entering the womb, being born, leaving home, attaining enlightenment, teaching the Dharma, and manifesting [these deeds].
They all go to the place of nirvāṇa, where they draw near to and make offerings [to the Buddhas], acting as leaders among the masses and receiving and practicing the True Dharma.
This they do in all places and at all times. Furthermore, they vow that all bodhisattva practices shall be vast, immeasurable, indestructible, and unmixed;

that they shall encompass the purity of the *pāramitās*, and that they shall accomplish the general and specific characteristics, as well as the common and distinct characteristics, of the various stages (*bhūmis*).

He speaks truthfully of all the bodhisattva practices that characterize the marks of disintegration, teaching and transforming all beings so that they may accept and practice them, causing their minds to increase.
Furthermore, he vows for the entire realm of sentient beings—whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, neither with nor without perception;
born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation; bound by the three realms—to enter into the six...
To all places of birth, comprised of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and to all such categories as these, I shall bring them all under my guidance,

causing them to enter the Buddha-dharma, to forever sever all worldly stations, and to abide securely on the path to omniscience (sarvajñatā). Furthermore, I vow that for all the vast and immeasurable worlds—
whether coarse or subtle, whether in states of distracted thought, inverted, or upright, whether entering, proceeding, or departing— [I shall act accordingly].
Just as the distinctions within Indra’s net are infinite and manifold throughout the ten directions, may my wisdom clearly comprehend them all, perceiving them directly before me.
Furthermore, may all buddha-lands enter into a single buddha-land, and a single buddha-land enter into all buddha-lands;
may these immeasurable buddha-fields be universally pure and radiant, adorned with every requisite of excellence, and free from all afflictions.
They have accomplished the path of cool serenity. It is filled with sentient beings of immeasurable wisdom who universally enter the great vows and the realm of all Buddhas.
According to the minds of all sentient beings, they manifest themselves for them, causing them all to rejoice.
Furthermore, they vow to share the same aspirations and conduct as all Bodhisattvas, free from resentment or jealousy, and to gather all roots of goodness together with all Bodhisattvas in equality.
Sharing a single object of focus, they constantly assemble together, never parting from one another. At will, they can manifest various Buddha-minds, abiding within their own minds.
They are able to know the spheres of all Tathāgatas, as well as their majestic powers and wisdom.
Having attained non-retrogression and supernormal powers at will, they travel through all worlds, manifesting forms in all assemblies, and universally enter into all modes of birth.
Abiding in the accomplishment of the inconceivable, they practice the Bodhisattva path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, they vow to achieve non-retrogression and perform the practices of bodhi;
their actions of body, speech, and mind shall never be in vain. Those who see them even for a moment will certainly enter the Dharma;
those who hear their voice even briefly will attain true wisdom; and upon the mere arising of pure faith, they will forever sever the afflictions and attain [the state of] suchness.
This is the body of the Great King of Medicine Tree; it has attained the body of a wish-fulfilling jewel.
It practices all bodhisattva deeds and further vows to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in all worlds without departing from even a single hair-tip.

Abiding within every single hair-tip, they manifest in all places: their initial birth, renunciation, proceeding to the site of enlightenment, attaining perfect awakening, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.
Having attained the power of great wisdom within the realm of the Buddhas, in every thought-moment, according to the minds of all sentient beings, they manifest the attainment of Buddhahood;
yet, mindful of the attainment of quiescence, through a single *samyak-saṃbodhi*, they know one.
The entire dharma-realm is the very mark of nirvāṇa. By preaching the Dharma with a single voice, he causes the minds of all sentient beings to rejoice.
He demonstrates the entry into great parinirvāṇa while never ceasing his bodhisattva practices; he demonstrates the ground of great wisdom and establishes all dharmas.

Through the supernormal powers of the Dharma, the supernormal power of knowledge, the supernormal power of psychic travel, and the supernormal power of illusion, he manifests transformations at will, filling the entirety of the [dharma-realm].
Throughout the entire dharma-realm, taking these ten gates as the foremost, one fulfills a million *asaṃkhyeya* great vows.
Son of the Buddha, these great vows are accomplished by means of ten phrases of totality (*daśa-paryanta-pada*). What are the ten? They are: the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*).

To the end of the world; to the end of the realm of empty space; to the end of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); to the end of the realm of nirvāṇa; to the end of the realm where Buddhas appear;
to the end of the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; to the end of the realm of mental objects; to the end of the spheres entered by Buddha-wisdom;

to the end of the realms of the revolution of the world, the revolution of phenomena, and the revolution of wisdom; to the end of the realm of sentient beings—to the end of my vow, that world shall come to an end.
Until the realms of the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom are exhausted— until my vows are fulfilled and the realm of sentient beings is exhausted;

yet because the realms of the turning of the world, the turning of the Dharma, and the turning of wisdom can never be exhausted, these roots of goodness from my great vow shall likewise never come to an end.
May I, at the time when my life is about to end, Have all obstacles completely removed,
And behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, Thereby attaining rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Having made this vow, with a sincere heart, take refuge and pay homage to the Honored One, Vairocana Buddha.
○ (Proclamation: May the assembly listen to these verses on impermanence from within the Sūtras:
Wandering through the three realms is like the wheel of a well-drawing bucket; It is also like a silkworm making its cocoon, which, once formed, binds itself.
To the Unsurpassed World-Honored Ones and the assembly of Śrāvakas of Perfect Enlightenment: [I take refuge.]
If even [the Buddha] relinquishes this impermanent body, how much more so should ordinary people?
Seeing with their own eyes the urgency of birth and death—parents, wives and children, brothers, and kinsmen—how could they not lament?
Therefore, I exhort all people: listen attentively to the true Dharma and together relinquish the realm of impermanence.
Constantly practice the Gate of Immortality.
One should recite the Verse of the Hundred-Syllable Mantra for Filling Deficiencies:
"I pray that the Seven Assemblies of the Dharma Realm will take pity upon and remember the ocean of sentient beings."
In this assembly of Buddhas at the main and attendant sites of practice, although we perform the ritual of confession,
our deeds are beyond measure. Should there be errors, inversions, omissions,
deficiencies, or redundancies, we fear that these may result in a confused root of virtue.
By the compassionate power of the Buddhas in the assembly at the site of enlightenment, and by the power of the ultimate truth of the hundred-syllable mantra,
may the ocean of sins confessed be purified, and may all performed dharmic practices be brought to fulfillment.
Next, recite the verses for requesting forbearance and accepting the vows.
We, ordinary and ignorant beings, possess but meager power of merit; Having not yet attained right mindfulness, our minds are turbid and distracted.
Our various offerings are incomplete and inferior; Forgetful and disordered, they do not accord with principle.
May we rely upon the compassion of the Three Jewels, which share a single essence, To embrace our roots of goodness and cause them to be perfected.
The nature of conditions is perfectly interfused, commensurate with the Dharma-realm; May the practices and vows of Samantabhadra be fulfilled.
I address the Sages and Worthies, and pay homage to the Buddhas of the Ten Bodies who shine everywhere, And to all the Tathāgatas of the Flower Treasury World.
The Honored Śākyamuni, the Original Teacher of Sahā; Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and all the foremost ones;
The assembly of sages from the oceans of lands along with their retinues; The noble beings of the Flower Treasury Assembly;
The hosts of Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas; And those who have attained the divine eye of knowing the minds of others.
May you both, not forsaking the power of compassion, bear witness to us two as we cultivate this gate of the dhāraṇī of vows.

Whatever merit is produced by our sincere and collective prostrations and repentances at this time, may it all be used to adorn the Dharma-realm and the sentient beings of the oceans of lands. We pray that celestial beings and immortals shall never fall.
Awakening to and realizing joy, they perceive that the land is eternally peaceful and tranquil, and recognize the True Vehicle; thus they excel among their peers.

Constantly abiding in their official positions and emoluments, the people all rejoice in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, remaining forever secure and at peace, as they all cultivate the Way of enlightened illumination.
May the preceptors, monks, parents, and kin enjoy vast and boundless blessings and prosperity. May the donors and patrons who provide offerings have their myriad practices brought to perfection.

May those in the three miserable realms simultaneously leave suffering behind, and may the eight difficulties be entirely eliminated. May the cauldrons of boiling water transform into pools of cool clarity, and the iron beds become seats of lotus flowers.
May the sounds of lamentation cease and be replaced by the chanting of the Buddha’s name. May every person possess the heart to return to the source, each and every one...

May each person’s illumination that returns to its source constantly give rise to present vows and future aspirations; may their non-retrogressive resolve and contemplative practice together bring about the realization of the oceanic assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, serving as a supreme and virtuous condition.
The Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha; the Perfect Sambhogakāya Rocana Buddha;
the thousand, ten-thousand, and hundred-million Nirmāṇakāya Śākyamuni Buddhas; the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Buddha of the twelve supreme vows;

The layman Mao Fengbao commissioned skilled artisans at Jiguge to carve these blocks.
